units.title: Event and feedback kinds, defined outcomes and exceptions
units.feedback:
The suite passes (3116 tests), and ruff and pyrefly are clean. Requeue reasons and rework kinds are now fields, and the dispatch and graph decide from them, which meets group 2. Three things still block. First, two writers that add to saved feedback drop its new source, which breaks the fix-the-checks prompt that tier 1 output used to get. Second, the graph's node spans still record outcomes outside the enum. Third, `UnitState` is declared but nothing uses it.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:481 — Two writers add a new reason to the saved feedback but drop its source, so it resets to `FeedbackSource.NONE`: the restack-conflict path in `prepare` (line 481) and the unaccounted-tests path in `adapt` (line 583). Both also drop `feedback_from_person`.
  Consequence: Take a unit whose last run failed tier 1, so its feedback is `tier 1 failed:\n…` with source TIER1. Its next `prepare` hits a restack conflict, or its `adapt` leaves tests unaccounted. Line 481 or 583 then saves `{waiting}\n\n{why}` with source NONE. On the following attempt `rework` computes `failed_check = False` (line 817), so the tier 1 output goes out under REWORK_PROMPT instead of CHECKS_PROMPT. And when the checks later pass, the TIER1 check at line 668 no longer clears the feedback. Before this change both decisions came from the text prefix, which the append kept. So this is a regression of exactly what task 2.4 moved onto the source field.
  Done when: At both sites, read the stored unit once and pass `source=stored.feedback_source` and `from_person=stored.feedback_from_person` to `set_feedback`, so adding text never changes where the feedback came from. Add a graph test: save feedback with `source=FeedbackSource.TIER1`, make the restack in `prepare` raise, and assert that `store.get(unit).feedback_source is FeedbackSource.TIER1` afterwards and that the next rework runs `claude:fix_checks`. Add the same test for the `adapt` problems path.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:201 — Node spans still record bare-string outcomes: `str(update.get("status") or "ok")` at line 201 and `"waiting"` at line 205. Neither `ok` nor `waiting` is a `UnitOutcome`, and `str()` turns real members back into plain strings.
  Consequence: Task 3.1 says the graph, the CLI and telemetry record outcomes from one enum. Today every node that returns no status, and every interrupt, records an outcome in telemetry that is outside the enum. That also makes the changelog line 'a run ends in one `UnitOutcome`' only partly true.
  Done when: Add the members the node spans need (for example `OK = "ok"` and `WAITING = "waiting"`, or names you prefer) to `UnitOutcome`. Set `outcome = UnitOutcome(update["status"]) if update.get("status") else UnitOutcome.OK` and `outcome = UnitOutcome.WAITING`. Extend `test_the_outcomes_are_the_fixed_set`, and add a test that drives a tick and asserts every `outcome` passed to `spans.record_span` is a `UnitOutcome` instance.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/units.py:64 — `UnitState` is declared but nothing uses it. `PLANNED`, `RUNNING` and the other states are still plain `str` constants, and `Unit.state` is still `str`. `test_the_unit_states_are_the_fixed_set` compares the enum's values with those same strings, so it passes whether or not the enum is ever used.
  Consequence: Task 3.3 says to replace the unit state strings with `UnitState`. As written the enum is dead code, and a test of the wrong kind (`test_passes_regardless`) stands in for the replacement.
  Done when: Define the module constants as members: `PLANNED = UnitState.PLANNED`, and so on for every state. Type `Unit.state` (and anything that annotates a state, such as `set_state`'s `state` parameter) as `UnitState`; pydantic converts the strings in an existing store on load. Replace the tautological test with one that loads a store JSON written with plain state strings and asserts `isinstance(store.get(id).state, UnitState)`, and that `set_state(id, "bogus")` is rejected.

Optional:
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/unit_store.py:85 — `RequeueReason.PARENT_MERGED` is never produced. A parent's merge reaches a child as a `base_moved` event (events.py:315), never as a requeue. `test_every_other_requeue_keeps_the_saved_failure…` builds a PARENT_MERGED event by hand, so for that case it tests a path that cannot happen.
  Consequence: Readers will believe a parent merge is delivered as a requeue carrying this reason.
  Done when: Either have the parent-merged path deliver `requeue=RequeueReason.PARENT_MERGED`, or drop the member and its test case and say in the PR that a parent merge is a `base_moved` event.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:983 — The tier 2 failure path adds `tier 2 failed:` to whatever feedback was waiting and tags all of it TIER2. If a person's words were waiting, they now go out under CHECKS_PROMPT and lose `from_person`. Before this change they went under REWORK_PROMPT, because the text did not start with the tier 1 prefix.
  Consequence: A person's review words could reach the agent through the fix-the-checks prompt.
  Done when: Keep the waiting feedback's source when it is REVIEW (or keep the person flag), or document that tier 2 feedback replaces review feedback here.
- [1.6] CHANGELOG.md:10 — Feedback saved before the upgrade loads with `feedback_source` NONE. A unit that failed tier 1 before the upgrade and is then requeued with `abk requeue --rework` therefore gets REWORK_PROMPT instead of CHECKS_PROMPT for its saved tier 1 output.
  Consequence: After upgrading, an operator using `--rework` on an older failure gets a different prompt, and nothing tells them.
  Done when: Say so in the changelog bullet, for example that saved feedback from before the upgrade is treated as review feedback and `--restart` avoids this. Or list such units in the same `abk status` cutover view.
- [1.7] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/stack_runner.py:215 — `PauseInfo(reason, until)` duplicates `graph.unit.Pause(reason, until)`. `_outcome` copies one into the other field by field.
  Consequence: There are two types for the same fact.
  Done when: Use one type, for example have `Position.pause` be a `PauseInfo`.
- [1.8] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/events.py:1128 — `resume(..., **({"rework": rework} if rework else {}))` passes the kind only when it is set, apparently so older test fakes keep working. In the same way, `feedback_source_of(None)` returns REVIEW while `resume_thread` maps None to NONE.
  Consequence: Two inconsistent defaults, and a conditional call shape the next reader has to reverse-engineer.
  Done when: Always pass `rework=rework` (`_no_thread` and the CLI lambda already accept it) and update the fakes. Pick one mapping for a missing kind.

units.title: The changelog convention and check for any repo
units.feedback:
Most of the unit is in place: the setting, the packaged text, the loader order, the command, the doctor warning, the profile hook, and the runner's tier 1 and prompts. One tier 1 path still skips the check. The tests never run the real command the profile emits, and they never show that the runner wiring passes the repo's setting through.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:1294 — The restack path's tier 1 never runs the changelog check. `build_stack_moves` calls `build_restack(...)` without a `tier1`, so `events.build_restack` falls back to `_default_tier1` (events.py:1555). That calls `build_tier1()` with no `repo`, and `extra = profile.extra_checks(repo) if repo is not None else []` gives no extra checks.
  Consequence: A parent merges and a child branch is rebased cleanly onto it, which is exactly when CHANGELOG.md gets merged. The child is then re-checked and pushed (events.py:1527-1537) without `abk changelog check`, so bullets run together by the merge reach the PR. This breaks the spec requirement 'tier 1 SHALL run it for every repo with the feature on'. It also makes false the docs/architecture.md step 4 sentence ('For a repo whose `changelog` setting is on it also runs `abk changelog check`… on a branch moved cleanly onto a new base, before the push') and the CHANGELOG bullet's 'tier 1 runs the new `abk changelog check`'.
  Done when: `build_stack_moves` passes `build_restack` a `tier1` bound per checkout, the same way `move` is bound through `names[path]`/`installation.repo(...)`. That is `build_tier1(profile=<repo's profile>, root_extras=repo.tests.root_extras, projects=repo.projects, repo=repo)`, looked up from the `cwd` path's repo. Add a test that builds the stack moves (or calls `build_restack` with the wired tier1) for a repo with `changelog` on and a fake `run`, and asserts that the restack's tier 1 ran a changelog-check command. A second case with `changelog: null` asserts it did not.
- [1.2] tests/profiles/test_python_uv_changelog.py:17 — Nothing runs the command the profile actually emits. `is_changelog_check` only looks for the words 'changelog' and 'check', and every tier 1 test fakes `run`. So `[sys.executable, "-m", "agent_build_kit", "changelog", "check", path]`, and the new `__main__.py` it depends on, are never executed.
  Consequence: The tests would still pass if `__main__.py` were missing or broken, if the command were `["abk", ...]` (not installed in a built repo's environment), or if the path argument were wrong. In each case tier 1 would fail every unit with a 'No module named' error or check nothing. The fake stands in for the very boundary in question: a subprocess in another repo's checkout.
  Done when: Add a test that takes `profiles.get("python-uv").extra_checks(RepoConfig(..., changelog="CHANGELOG.md"))[0]` and runs it with `subprocess.run(..., cwd=<tmp checkout>)` (or calls `build_tier1` with the default `run`, scoped so lint/tests are trivial). It runs against a CHANGELOG.md with two bullets run together and asserts exit 1 and `CHANGELOG.md line N` in stdout. A well-formed file asserts exit 0.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/wiring.py:1813 — No test shows that the runner passes the repo's setting to the prompts and review. `UnitRunner.repo_config`, `build_run_review(repo=...)`, `build_restack_onto(repo=...)` and the `in_repo` wrapper in cli/pipeline.py are untested. The prompt tests call `changelog_note(worktree, repo)` directly, and `repo=None` silently behaves as 'on, own section only'.
  Consequence: Task 1.3 asks that a repo with the setting off get no changelog part in its build, rework, test-writing, resolver and review prompts. If `build_runner` dropped `repo_config=repo`, or nodes.py passed `None`, a `changelog: null` repo whose AGENTS.md has a `## Changelog` section would still get the convention and the review paragraph. A repo with no section would get no packaged text. Every current test still passes in both cases.
  Done when: Add a test through `build_runner` (or the existing BuildPath/graph harness in tests/graph/test_build_path.py) for a repo with `changelog: null` and a worktree whose AGENTS.md has a `## Changelog` section. It captures the implementation/test-writing prompt and the review prompt and asserts neither contains the section text. Add the converse for a repo with `changelog` on and no section, asserting the packaged text appears. Add one case for `resolved_move` reached through `build_stack_moves`' `in_repo`, asserting `ConflictContext.repo` is that repo's config.

Optional:
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/changelog_convention.py:83 — The review paragraph still says the form and wording 'follow the convention in this repo's AGENTS.md'. The convention can now come from CLAUDE.md or the packaged text, and the paragraph does not carry the convention itself.
  Consequence: For a repo with no AGENTS.md section, which is now the default case with the packaged text, the reviewer is pointed at a section that does not exist. The spec says the review prompt SHALL carry the convention.
  Done when: Word it as 'follow the repo's changelog convention' and append `changelog_note(worktree, repo)`, or name the source the loader actually used.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/changelog_convention.py:70 — `resolver_changelog_rule` and the packaged text hardcode `CHANGELOG.md`, so the `changelog` setting's path never reaches a prompt.
  Consequence: For a repo with `changelog: docs/HISTORY.md`, the resolver is told the keep-both rule for `CHANGELOG.md`, and the build agent is told `CHANGELOG.md` opens with `## Unreleased`. Both name the wrong file.
  Done when: Substitute `repo.changelog` into the resolver rule and test it with the conflicted file; template the packaged text's file name, or word it as 'the changelog'.

units.title: Init writes the changelog conventions into each repo
units.feedback:
Group 1 covers the spec well: placement, idempotence, stamps, CRLF, the setting off, dry-run lines, the doctor check and docs are all there and tested through public surfaces. Two small fixes are needed before approval. I could not run the suite in this session because the command was refused, so the blank-line finding comes from tracing the code by hand, not from running it.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/init/scaffold.py:494 — The block is appended after two blank lines, not one. For a file ending in a newline, `separator = eol` and then `separator += eol` gives `"# App\n" + "\n\n" + "<!-- abk:changelog ..."`. A file with no final newline gets `eol * 3`, which also leaves two blank lines.
  Consequence: The design ("append at the end of the file (after a blank line)") is not met. Every AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md init touches ends up with consecutive blank lines, which markdownlint MD012 rejects in code repos that lint markdown in their gate. The person committing init's output then hits a failing hook. The test `test_the_block_is_appended_to_an_existing_agents_md_and_the_rest_is_untouched` cannot catch this because it strips every leading newline (`tail.lstrip("\n")`) before matching.
  Done when: Remove line 495 (`separator += eol`) and set `separator = eol if text.endswith("\n") else eol * 2`, so exactly one blank line sits before the opening marker. Tighten the append test to assert `tail.startswith("\n<!-- abk:changelog")` and `not tail.startswith("\n\n")`. Add a case for a file with no final newline (`"# App"`) that asserts the result is `"# App\n\n<!-- abk:changelog ..."`. The CRLF test should assert the same with `\r\n`.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/cli/doctor.py:141 — Doctor gives the same warning and fix (`run abk init to add it`) whenever the driver is not `union`, including when `.gitattributes` already sets another driver for the changelog (`CHANGELOG.md merge=ours`, `-merge`). In that state `_gitattributes_action` deliberately skips ("already has a merge setting ... left as is").
  Consequence: With `CHANGELOG.md merge=ours` in `.gitattributes`, doctor says the file "has no `merge=union` rule" and to run `abk init`. Init then changes nothing, and doctor warns again. The fix doctor prints is false for this state and cannot resolve the warning.
  Done when: In `_changelogs`, branch on `merge_attribute(...)`. `None` keeps the current warning and the `abk init` fix. Any other value warns that the changelog's merge setting is `<value>` and says to change it to `merge=union` in `.gitattributes` by hand, without suggesting `abk init`. Add a case to `tests/cli/test_doctor_union_rule.py` with `attributes="CHANGELOG.md merge=ours\n"` that asserts exactly one warning, that its detail names `ours`, and that its fix does not say `abk init`.

Optional:
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/init/scaffold.py:449 — `_block_text` gets the packaged text by calling `changelog_convention(Path("/nonexistent"), RepoConfig(path=Path("/x"), slug="example/x", ...))`. This depends on an internal detail of the loader: no AGENTS.md exists under a made-up path. The test helper `packaged()` copies the same workaround.
  Consequence: If the loader ever looks anywhere else for a section, the block silently picks up that text. A reader also has to work out why a fake worktree and repo are built.
  Done when: Expose a named function such as `packaged_convention(changelog: str) -> str` in `pipeline/changelog_convention.py`. Have `changelog_convention` use it as its fallback, and have both `_block_text` and the test helper call it.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/changelog_convention.py:25 — When the loader reads a block that init wrote, it takes everything up to the next `## ` heading. A block at the end of the file therefore reaches agents' prompts with the trailing `<!-- /abk:changelog -->` marker, along with any non-`## ` text that follows the block.
  Consequence: Build and review prompts contain a stray HTML comment, plus whatever follows the block when the next heading is not a `## `. This is cosmetic today.
  Done when: Have `_section` stop at the closing marker. Add a test that runs `write_code_repo_conventions`, then `changelog_convention(root, repo)`, and asserts the result equals the packaged text exactly.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/init/scaffold.py:428 — `merge_attribute` matches only the exact pattern text. An equivalent anchored rule such as `/CHANGELOG.md merge=union` is not recognised.
  Consequence: In a repo that already anchors its rule, doctor warns spuriously and init appends a second `CHANGELOG.md merge=union` line. This is harmless, but it is noise.
  Done when: Treat a pattern equal to the path with one leading `/` as the same path, and test that case.

units.feedback:
The clock fix landed. `_now()` now stamps history from `spans.clock`, and the tests no longer edit the store's JSON. The `after_prepare` change for owed replies with saved feedback also landed in code. But the builder said they added a test for it, `test_a_unit_with_replies_owed_and_new_feedback_is_reworked`, and factored the replies test into a helper. Neither is in commit 82badaa or the working tree. `tests/graph/test_resume_at_pull_request.py` is unchanged and has no such test, so the new branch in `after_prepare` ships untested. Point 1.3 (a host outage during event delivery) is declined: the builder cannot edit the change's design.md, and leaving `resume_thread` as it is avoids wrongly parking an in-review unit. A person should decide whether to add it as a follow-up task.

Required:
- [2.1] tests/graph/test_resume_at_pull_request.py:75 — No test covers the new rule in `after_prepare` (graph/nodes.py:1750), which says owed replies route to `open_pr` only when no feedback is saved. The test the builder reported adding is not in the commit.
  Consequence: AGENTS.md ('Tests first') says a behaviour change lands with its failing test. Reverting nodes.py:1750-1752 to `state.pushed_head and (not state.opened or state.pending_replies)` passes the whole suite. A held unit requeued with new feedback would then skip rework, post its replies and clear the feedback, and nothing would catch it.
  Done when: Add `test_a_unit_with_replies_owed_and_new_feedback_is_reworked` to tests/graph/test_resume_at_pull_request.py. Set it up like the existing replies test (pushed head, `pr=5`, a seeded `UnitRun` with `pending_replies=("Done.",)`), and also call `store.set_feedback(UNIT, "Rename the helper.")`. Assert that `claude:rework` is in `recorder.events` and comes before the pull-request step. The old condition must make this test fail. If it helps, share the seed-and-run setup with the existing replies test through a helper, as the builder described.

units.feedback:
Task 1.1 asks for the live check (every `in_review`, `running` or `held` unit has a thread) to be recorded in the planning repo's design.md. It isn't there. That file is outside this branch, so it doesn't block this PR, but a person should confirm the check was run before merging. Without the conversion, a unit in review or held with no thread never gets one.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/unit_store.py:213 — `_refuse_old_engine_fields` refuses any record where the `resume_from` key is present, even when it's empty. The release this replaces wrote `"resume_from": ""` and `"classic_run": {}` on every unit, because `_write` dumps every field with `model_dump`. So every store that release wrote fails to load. `classic_run` isn't in the refused list either, so even without the `resume_from` check it fails as an unknown key (extra=forbid).
  Consequence: The first tick after updating raises on the first unit of a normal, fully converted store and stops the pipeline entirely. The live planning store has 206 occurrences of these two keys, one pair per unit, all empty. The proposal says 'no live unit has the old fields set', meaning set to a value, and this check refuses them for merely being present.
  Done when: On read, drop `resume_from` when it is `""` and `classic_run` when it is `{}` or missing. These are the defaults the previous release wrote on every unit. Refuse with the named error, which names the unit and the field and says to finish or requeue, only when a value is non-empty. Add `classic_run` (non-empty) to the refused fields so it gets the named error instead of a generic validation error. The in-run keys (`review_rounds`, `deferred`, `pending_replies`, `person_comments`) never appeared in a store after the switch, so refusing them on presence is acceptable. Rewrite these over the network/fixture: a test that writes a store exactly as the previous release did (every unit with `"resume_from": ""` and `"classic_run": {}`) and asserts it loads, and that the next write leaves out both keys. Keep the parametrized non-empty refusal test and add a `classic_run={"review_rounds": [1]}` case to it.
- [1.2] tests/pipeline/test_old_engine_fields.py:44 — `test_an_empty_old_engine_field_is_refused_too` pins the defect above. It asserts that an empty `resume_from` (and an empty in-run key) is refused, which is exactly the shape of every store the previous release wrote.
  Consequence: The test enforces behaviour that bricks every existing installation's store, and it would fail any correct fix.
  Done when: Remove the test or invert it for `resume_from`/`classic_run`: an empty value loads and is dropped. If refusing an empty in-run key is kept, limit the parametrization to those four keys.
- [1.3] CHANGELOG.md:5 — The Breaking entry says a `units.json` that 'still holds' `resume_from` no longer loads. After the fix, only a non-empty value (or a non-empty `classic_run`) is refused, and the entry doesn't mention `classic_run` at all.
  Consequence: The entry describes the wrong trigger. Read as written, it tells every operator their store will stop loading, even though the stores the last release wrote should load untouched.
  Done when: Say that a units store whose unit still carries a value in one of the previous engine's fields (`review_rounds`, `deferred`, `pending_replies`, `person_comments`, `resume_from`, `classic_run`) no longer loads and names the unit and field. Say that the empty `resume_from`/`classic_run` written on every unit by the last release are dropped on read. Apply the same wording to the `units.json` row in docs/architecture.md (line ~756) and to docs/unit-graph.md (line ~109).

units.title: Replies and the close are kept until done
units.feedback:
The close half is mostly there. The reply half stores what the host did not take, but nothing in a round ever posts it again, so the main thing task 1.1 and the spec ask for ("the next pass posts what is left") is not delivered. All 12 new tests pass and the leak check passes.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:762 — No round re-posts a unit's owed replies. `open_pr` stores the unposted ones in the thread's `pending_replies` (nodes.py:1497-1517) and the unit then waits in `await_review`. The only code that reads `pending_replies` again is `open_pr`, which runs only after another rework. The design says "The pass's round posts a unit's pending replies when the host is reachable", and the comment at nodes.py:1496 says "for the next pass to post".
  Consequence: Take a unit in review whose reply to comment 11 the host refused. If the reviewer then approves or merges without commenting again, that reply is never posted: it stays in the thread state until merge and is lost, which is the failure the proposal set out to fix. `abk status` reports it as "waiting for the host" every pass, but nothing is retrying it. The test for this (test_the_next_pass_posts_what_is_left_once) calls `post_replies` twice by hand, so no pass is under test.
  Done when: Add a round step next to `_retry_pending_closes`, e.g. `retry_replies`. For each IN_REVIEW unit whose thread state has non-empty `pending_replies` and a known `pr`, it calls the reply poster for each owed answer and writes back only what is still owed, through the thread/checkpoint update path the graph uses so the next `open_pr` sees the reduced list. It must be safe when the unit's branch is locked or being built: skip that unit and leave it for the next pass. Tests needed: (a) a round with one IN_REVIEW unit whose thread holds an owed answer, and a working stand-in forge, posts the reply once and leaves `pending_replies == ()`; (b) the same with a refusing forge leaves the answer unchanged; (c) a second round after (a) posts nothing.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/pr_replies.py:207 — An owed reply is signed again with whatever sha the later attempt is given (`_signed(reply.body, sha)`). The existing-comment read compares the exact body, sha included. The owed JSON (`owed.model_dump_json()`) does not record the sha it was first signed with.
  Consequence: The forge layer's `post_reply`/`post_comment` are `contained` creates. When even the landed-read fails, they give up with `()`, so a reply the host did store is marked owed. The next attempt, from a later rework's `open_pr` at a new head (or the round retry above), signs it "in <new sha>". `comment_exists` then finds no match and the reply is posted a second time. The spec's "A reply SHALL NOT be posted twice" and the "A reply that landed" scenario both fail.
  Done when: Keep the sha with what is owed and sign retries with it. For example, give `Answer` an optional `sha: str = ""` field (it is `extra=forbid`, so it has to be declared), set it on the returned owed answer, and use `answer.sha or sha` when signing. Test: a reply first attempted at sha A that the host holds (a stand-in whose `comment_exists` matches only the A-signed body) is retried with `sha=B` and is not posted again; its id is recorded in own posts.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:1514 — `has_work` decides whether a tick runs at all (line 512) and ignores `close_pending`. A satisfied unit is not in `NEEDS_TICKS`.
  Consequence: If the only thing left in an installation is a satisfied unit whose close failed, every tick returns at line 512. `_retry_pending_closes` never runs and the pull request stays open indefinitely, while `abk status` says "closing is retried each pass". The same applies to the reply retry above once it exists, unless the unit is IN_REVIEW, which does keep ticks running.
  Done when: `has_work` returns True when any unit has `close_pending`. Add a test in the existing has_work tests: a store with only a SATISFIED unit carrying `ClosePending` (and its change otherwise verified) gives `has_work(...) is True`.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:221 — `retry_closes` closes `pending.pr` without checking that the unit is still SATISFIED and still owns that pull request. Nothing clears `close_pending` when the unit leaves SATISFIED (for example `abk requeue` at line 2300, or `set_state(..., PLANNED)` anywhere).
  Consequence: A satisfied unit's close fails, so #4 stays open with `close_pending=ClosePending(pr=4)`. A person then runs `abk requeue` on it and it is rebuilt. `open_pr` finds and reuses the still-open #4, the unit goes IN_REVIEW, and the next round's `retry_closes` posts the old "implemented elsewhere" reason and closes the pull request now under review.
  Done when: In `retry_closes`, act only when `unit.state == SATISFIED and unit.pr == pending.pr`; otherwise drop the record (`set_close_pending(unit.id, None)`) without closing. Test: a unit in PLANNED or IN_REVIEW that carries a `ClosePending` is not closed by `retry_closes` and has its record removed.

Optional:
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/unit_store.py:134 — `ClosePending.reason_posted` is never set or read. The implementation finds an already-posted reason through `comment_exists` in `build_close_pr`, and the docstring ("whether that reason is already there") describes a mechanism that does not exist.
  Consequence: The next reader will assume `reason_posted` guards against a duplicate reason and may rely on it. It is always False.
  Done when: Remove the field and the docstring clause, or set and use it. Removing it is simpler, since the read already covers the case.
- [1.6] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:320 — The status line counts `len(owed.pending_replies)`, which is the number of owed rework answers (JSON blobs), not the number of replies.
  Consequence: One answer with two owed replies and a summary shows as "1 waiting".
  Done when: Count the replies by parsing each owed answer (`parse_answer`) and summing `len(replies)` plus 1 for a non-empty summary, or word the line as "answers".

units.title: Per-role session_reuse setting
units.feedback:
Task group 3 is otherwise complete: the field, its default, both rejections, the docs, the skill and the changelog are all there and match the spec and design. The changelog folds into the existing session-reuse bullet as the convention asks. The rename in tests/cli/test_metric_records_tick.py (`run_claude` -> `run`) is a correct catch-up to unit 1's rename. One point blocks: the rule "a role the setting does not name is off" lives only in a helper inside the test file, so no code under test enforces it.

Required:
- [1.1] tests/test_config.py:237 — The spec rule "a role not named SHALL be off" (task 3.1) is enforced only by the test's private helper `_reuse` (`config.session_reuse.get(role, False)`), not by anything in config.py. `test_a_role_the_setting_does_not_name_is_off` and the default test therefore check the test's own lookup rule, not the code's.
  Consequence: With `session_reuse: {}`, or with only `review: false` set, the code has no defined answer for whether `build` reuses. The unit 4 resolution step will write its own lookup. If that lookup is `session_reuse[role]` (KeyError on a missing role) or `.get(role, True)` (reuse on for a missing role), every test here still passes. The shipped behaviour would then contradict the spec's "a role not named is off" with no test failing.
  Done when: Add a named accessor to `WorkspaceConfig` in src/agent_build_kit/config.py, e.g. `def reuses_session(self, role: str) -> bool: return self.session_reuse.get(role, False)`, with a docstring that states the unnamed-is-off contract. Delete the `_reuse` helper from tests/test_config.py and call `config.reuses_session(SessionRole.BUILD)` / `config.reuses_session(SessionRole.REVIEW)` in the default, empty-mapping and build-off tests, so that `reuses_session(SessionRole.BUILD)` is False for `session_reuse: {}` and True for the default. Unit 4's resolution step then reads the setting through this accessor and never indexes the dict directly.

Optional:
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/config.py:440 — `SESSION_REUSE_ROLES = ("build", "review")` repeats the values of `graph.state.SessionRole` by hand. The duplication is likely deliberate, because graph.state imports pipeline modules and config cannot import it, but nothing keeps the two lists in step.
  Consequence: If a role is added to `SessionRole` and not to `SESSION_REUSE_ROLES`, an abk.yaml naming the new role is refused as "unknown role" even though the graph records sessions under it.
  Done when: Add a test in tests/test_config.py asserting `set(SESSION_REUSE_ROLES) == {role.value for role in SessionRole}`. Alternatively, a one-line comment in config.py naming SessionRole as the source this tuple mirrors.

units.title: Resume ACP sessions behind a listing check, and attribute usage to the node that made the call
units.feedback:
Group 5 (listing-guarded `session/resume`) and group 6 (ledger keyed on unit, node and round) each match their tasks, and the touched tests pass (52 passed). The blocker comes from putting the two together: once an ACP session can be resumed, the cost the ACP runtime reports is the session's running total. The ledger now files that total under the continuing node and adds it to the node that opened the session, so the same money is counted twice.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/runtimes/acp.py:1136 — A resumed ACP call reports the session's cumulative cost as its own `cost_usd`. `_Session.cost_usd` is the last `usage_update.cost`, which the ACP schema documents as "Cumulative session cost" (`acp/schema.py` `_UsageUpdate.cost`). The fake agent says the same at tests/runtimes/acp_agent.py:62-63 and 224 ("the session's cumulative spend so far"). Before this unit, every ACP call opened a new session, so cumulative and per-call cost were the same number. Now `session/resume` continues a session, and they are not.
  Consequence: Without a gateway, take `implement` costing $0.50 in session S, then `fix_checks` resuming S and spending $0.08. The agent's last `usage_update` reports $0.58. `_spent` records `cost_usd=0.58` for `fix_checks`. The new `records_in` key keeps that record apart from `implement`'s $0.50, so the ledger, `abk report` and the breakdowns show $1.08 for $0.58 of real spend. A crash-resume of the same node is folded by addition, so it double counts the same way. docs/architecture.md:847-851 then says something false: "a resumed call ... reports that call's figures, not a running total". It is checked only against Claude Code, and it now covers ACP calls too.
  Done when: A resumed ACP call records only what was spent during that call. One acceptable approach: remember the cumulative cost seen when the prompt is sent (from any `usage_update` received during `session/resume`) and report last minus that baseline. Where no baseline was seen on a resumed session, report `cost_usd=None` / `usage_source` `none` rather than the total. A new session keeps today's behaviour. Give the fake agent's `--cost` a starting amount for a resumed session, e.g. a `--prior-cost X` that it reports from `session/resume` and adds to before the answer. Add a test in tests/runtimes/test_acp_session.py: resume a listed session whose prior cumulative cost is X, and assert that `result.cost_usd` is the increase (or None when there is no baseline), never the total. Make the architecture.md sentence name what holds for each runtime.

units.title: A unit reviewed and merged without a code host

description.summary: Adds a live acceptance test, run on Claude Code, of a unit built, reviewed in the web UI, reworked, approved and merged by a person with git, in a repo with no code host (`forge: local`).
changes: A `local_stack` test tagged `runtime_claude_code` builds a two-unit change in a scratch code repo with no remote. It checks that the unit's branch and pull request exist only locally and that the planner kept the second group as a unit of its own that depends on the first.
A comment posted through the web UI's thread endpoint sends the unit back. The test checks that the rework adds commits without rewriting earlier ones, acts on the comment and answers the thread.
Approve, recorded through the UI's decision endpoint, leaves the unit in review and its local pull request open, with the approval recorded on it.

After a person merges the branch with git, the next tick records the unit merged. The dependent is moved on: its local pull request is retargeted from the first unit's branch to main, or its branch now exists if it had not started.
docs/agent-runtimes.md describes the acceptance run and how to start it.

units.title: The diff and review API
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/serve/server.py:256 — A new thread is anchored to the branch tip at the moment of the POST, not to the commit of the diff the reviewer was looking at. `ThreadIn` has no `commit` field, and `add_thread` calls `branch_tip(repo, unit.branch)`.
  Consequence: The design says the branch is resolved to a commit once and the diff and every thread are pinned to it. Suppose a reviewer loads `/diff` at commit A, the pipeline then pushes commit B (a rework, or a restack, which moves lines), and the reviewer comments on line 3 as it was in A. The thread is stored with `commit=B`, `line=3`, so it is not marked outdated and it shows on whatever line 3 is in B. The comment is silently attached to the wrong code, and the feedback path in group 3 will send that wrong anchor to the agent.
  Done when: Add `commit: str | None = None` to `ThreadIn`. When it is given, resolve it in the unit's checkout (with `_resolve` or a named equivalent in review.py) and store the resolved sha; answer 409 or 422 if it does not resolve. Fall back to the branch tip only when it is omitted. Add a test in tests/serve/test_serve_review_store.py: take `/diff` (commit A), `advance` the branch with lines inserted above line 3, POST a thread with `commit=A` and `line=3`, then assert the stored `commit == A` and that `GET /review` returns it with `outdated` true and `line` relocated (5).

Optional:
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/serve/review.py:89 — For a restacked unit, a diff pinned to a commit from before the restack is taken against the merge-base with the *current* base. That merge-base is no longer the point where that commit left its old base.
  Consequence: This is the setup of `test_a_restacked_unit_...`, except that `?commit=` names feature/4's commit from before the rebase. merge-base(new spec/feature/2, old feature/4 commit) is main's commit, so the patch also shows `two.py`, the predecessor's pre-amend work, as if it were the unit's own. The 'diff as it was' promise holds only while the base has not been rewritten.
  Done when: Optional for this unit. Either record the base commit with each thread or pinned view and diff from that, or document that a pinned commit from before a restack is diffed against the current base's fork point.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/serve/server.py:57 — `ThreadIn` does not check the anchor. `line` may be 0 or negative, `start_line` may be greater than `line`, and `path` need not be a file in the diff.
  Consequence: A malformed anchor is stored as given. Relocation then works on nonsense (for example a range whose end comes before its start), and group 2's viewer has to defend against it.
  Done when: Use `Field(ge=1)` on `line` and `start_line`, plus a model validator that `start_line <= line`, so a bad anchor answers 422.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/serve/review.py:101 — `_moved` runs `git diff` with `check=False`. If the diff fails (for example the thread's commit is no longer in the checkout), the output is empty and the line is reported as unchanged.
  Consequence: The thread is shown as outdated but placed at its original line number, as though nothing above it changed, instead of being shown with no line.
  Done when: When the diff's returncode is non-zero, return None so the thread is outdated with no line.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/serve/review.py:147 — `_update`'s `change` parameter is untyped and it returns `object`, so both callers need `# type: ignore[return-value]`.
  Consequence: The store's write path is not type-checked. A caller returning the wrong shape is not caught.
  Done when: Make it generic: `def _update[T](self, unit_id: str, change: Callable[[Review], tuple[Review, T]]) -> T`, and drop the ignores.

units.title: Checks are one list with a status
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/pr_poller.py:120 — The snapshot keys checks by name in a dict, so two checks that share a name collapse into one. Whichever comes last wins, and a failure can be lost. Neither forge removes duplicate names: GitHub's `_rollup` returns every CheckRun, and Azure merges status contexts and policy display names into one list.
  Consequence: Two GitHub workflows can each have a job named `build`. Say the rollup lists the failing one first and the passing one second. The snapshot then records `{"build": "passed"}`. `_dispatch_terminal` and `_dispatch_changes` see no failure, and the unit stays in review with red CI and is never reworked. The old name tuples did not have this problem: the failing tuple held `build` whatever else shared the name.
  Done when: When several checks share a name, the snapshot keeps the most severe status for that name: failed over cancelled over pending over passed. Do this in `snapshot` (or a small helper beside it), not with a plain dict comprehension. Add a test in tests/pipeline/test_poller_check_statuses.py with a PR carrying two checks named `build`, one FAILED and one PASSED, in both orders (parametrised). The test asserts the poller dispatches `rework` with reason `failing checks: build`, both when the PR is first seen and on a passed→failed transition.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/forges/azure_devops.py:403 — A build-policy evaluation's Check has no url, even when the evaluation names a build. The design says the link is "the status's target or the build's link on Azure DevOps".
  Consequence: The design.md section 'Mapping, per host' says a policy check carries the build's link. As written, every policy check has `url == ""` even though the build id is known; `failed_check_logs` already builds that link (`{_HOST}/{account}/{project}/_build/results?buildId={build}`). docs/code-forges.md says `""` is used only "where it gives none", which is not true here.
  Done when: When `item.context.build_id` is set, an evaluation's Check gets `url` = the same `_build/results?buildId=` link `failed_check_logs` builds (share one private helper for it). It stays `""` when there is no build. Update test_azure_rest_parity's expected `CI build`/`slow build` checks, and add a test in test_azure_check_statuses.py asserting that a rejected evaluation with build 41 carries `.../_build/results?buildId=41` and a queued one with no build carries `""`.
- [1.3] CHANGELOG.md:9 — The entry says two things changed that did not. Unknown states 'can no longer send a unit back' and a check that finishes failing 'is noticed' both imply the old behaviour was different. Before this branch, only FAILURE/TIMED_OUT (GitHub) and failed/error (Azure) counted as failing, and a newly failing name was already noticed.
  Consequence: Readers are told a bug was fixed that never existed: that unknown check states used to rework units and that late failures used to be missed.
  Done when: Reword so it states what is true now, without implying earlier behaviour. For example: 'A check state the forge does not know counts as pending, never failed. The poller records each check's status; snapshots recorded before this are recorded afresh on the next poll without sending anything back.' Keep it one bullet.

Optional:
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/pr_poller.py:294 — Upgrading can lose a failure. Suppose a check turns red between the last poll with the old format and the first poll with the new one. That poll compares nothing and records the check as failed, so it is never news afterwards. The same thing happens if the unit is held during the upgrade: `_keep_unseen` copies the old-format snapshot forward, so failures during the hold are dropped once it is released.
  Consequence: An old snapshot has `failing_checks: []`, and the first new poll sees `CI` failed. Nothing is dispatched, and every later poll sees CI as already failed, so the unit stays red in review. The pr-polling spec scenario ('nothing is sent back') asks for exactly this, so this branch conforms. units.title: Free sessions and commits by another session
units.feedback:
Free sessions, the planning gate and the outside-commit prompt part are all in place, and the prompt tests run over a real git branch. Four things block approval. The consequences list can say something false about the next tick, because it works out 'replan' and 'needs' differently from the tick and treats a unit's number as its group number. The lease keeps counting planning files after the planning checkout is committed. A commit request naming both checkouts quietly skips the planning one. One test that task 4.4 asks for is missing.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/consequences.py:368 — Whether the plan changed is decided by comparing each group's lines with checkboxes kept, and lines outside a `## N.` group are ignored. The tick decides re-planning with `specification()` (cli/pipeline.py:1695), which strips checkbox progress and `Needs:` lines and hashes every other non-blank line of the file.
  Consequence: A free session that ticks `- [ ] 2.1` to `- [x] 2.1` is told 'The plan changed: the change is re-planned on the next tick', but the tick does not re-plan, because `specification()` strips the checkbox. In the other direction, an edit to a line above the first group (for example `Priority:` or the top `Acceptance:` line) changes the plan hash so the tick re-plans, yet the list says nothing. Either way the answer contradicts what the next tick does.
  Done when: Use the tick's own rule. Give `specification` a form that takes text (for example `specification_text(text)`, with `specification(path)` calling it) and use it on the `before` and `after` contents of tasks.md: the plan changed exactly when the two results differ. A `needs` consequence applies only when they are equal and a group's `Needs:` lines differ. Add tests: ticking a checkbox produces no `replan`; editing a line above the first group produces `replan`.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/consequences.py:380 — `_number(u)` treats the number in a unit's id as its task-group number. Units carry `groups: tuple[int, ...]` and `joined` members (units.py:124-130), so one unit can build several groups, its number need not match a group, and a unit of another change can build this change's groups. The started set also filters on `u.change == change`, which misses joined units.
  Consequence: A unit `feature/1` that builds groups (1, 2): a commit changing only group 2's `Needs:` line lists no unit (or lists `feature/2`, a different unit). A unit of another change that joined `feature`'s groups is never listed for a spec or plan change to `feature`.
  Done when: Pick out started units by `any(m.change == change for m in u.members())`, and match groups through the groups of the member whose change is `change`, not through the id. Add a test where a unit's id number differs from the group whose `Needs:` changed (for example unit `feature/1` with groups (1, 2), `Needs:` of group 2 edited) and assert that unit is listed.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/serve/chat.py:342 — `note_changes` now records `changed = files + planned`, but committing the planning checkout (`attach.commit_planning` -> `Leases.release_checkout`) only drops `planning` from `checkouts` and leaves `changed` at the old total.
  Consequence: Take a free session that edited only tasks.md: the lease is `{checkouts: [worktree, planning], changed: 1}` with a clean worktree. After a successful planning commit it becomes `{checkouts: [worktree], changed: 1}`. Closing the page does not release it (`release_all` skips `changed`), `abk status` reports the unit attached with 1 file, and once the server stops it remains a stale attachment holding 'changes' that do not exist. With both checkouts dirty, the count shown afterwards includes the files already committed.
  Done when: After the planning commit, set the lease's `changed` to what is left in the checkouts it still covers: the worktree's `changed_paths` count, or 0 when it covers none. A lease with nothing left is then removed (`release_checkout`) or released when the page closes. Add a test: a free-session lease covering both checkouts with only the planning checkout dirty, commit `checkouts: ["planning"]`, then assert `attachment(UNIT).changed == 0` and that the lease is gone after `close_tab`.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/serve/chat.py:820 — The commit endpoint commits the planning checkout only when `checkouts == ["planning"]`. Any other value, including `["worktree", "planning"]`, goes to `attach.adopt`, which commits only the worktree and then drops the whole lease (`finish` -> `drop`).
  Consequence: A free session that changed code and a task file sends `checkouts: ["worktree", "planning"]`. It gets 200 with the worktree commit, while the planning edits stay uncommitted, never go through `abk check`/`abk tags`, and are no longer on any lease. The design says a call committing both checkouts commits each with its own gate and releases the lease once at the end.
  Done when: Either commit both (the planning checkout through `commit_planning` with its gate, then `adopt` for the worktree, answering with both commits and the consequences, and releasing the lease once at the end), or reject any `checkouts` value other than `[]`, `["worktree"]` or `["planning"]` with 422. Add a test for whichever is chosen with `checkouts: ["worktree", "planning"]`.
- [1.5] tests/graph/test_outside_commits_prompt.py:675 — Task 4.4 asks for a test that 'a commit by a free session carries the adopted-from trailer'. The graph tests write the `Adopted-From` trailer by hand in `land()`. The only test of the real commit path checks the build session's trailer (tests/serve/test_chat_commit.py:139). Nothing ties a free session's lease to the trailer that `outside_commits` parses.
  Consequence: If the commit endpoint stamped a free session's commit with the build session (for example via the `held.session or recorded.session_id` fallback at chat.py:792, or a claim that recorded no session), `outside_commits` would treat the commit as the builder's own and leave it out of every prompt, and all current tests would still pass.
  Done when: Add a test that commits through POST /api/units/{unit}/commit (or `attach.adopt`) under a lease whose session is a free session different from the recorded build session. Assert that the commit message has `Adopted-From: <free session>` and that `outside_commits(tree, base, BUILD_SESSION)` returns that commit with that session.

Optional:
- [1.6] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/attach.py:130 — `planning_gate` copies `cmd_check` and the `abk tags` loop (cli/pipeline.py:2470-2500), including the error formatting, instead of sharing one function with them.
  Consequence: If `abk check` or `abk tags` later changes what it checks (another validation, a different `repos` argument), the chat gate silently drifts from the commands it says it runs.
  Done when: Pull a function out of the CLI that returns `(ok, output)` for check and for tags of a change, and have both the CLI commands and `planning_gate` call it.
- [1.7] src/agent_build_kit/serve/chat.py:338 — A free session's lease counts every uncommitted path in the whole planning checkout, so edits to other changes or to files no session made are counted too, and the same files count on every unit with a free-session lease.
  Consequence: When a person has unrelated uncommitted planning edits, every free-session lease reports them as that session's changes in `abk status` and the UI.
  Done when: Consider counting only the paths under the unit's change directory, or recording the planning paths that existed when the lease was taken.
- [1.8] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:1117 — The review context is rebuilt as `{"context": ...}`, which drops any other key `review_notes` returns.
  Consequence: None today, since `review_notes` returns only `context`. A key added there later would be lost silently whenever an outside commit exists.
  Done when: Use `{**context, "context": ...}`.

units.title: The tick keeps the environment current, and the environment cause
units.feedback:
This unit covers task groups 2 and 3. The behaviour matches the spec: the tick-level sync, check and one heal; the non-zero exit with the output; the status line; the `environment` cause at both tier 1 call sites; resuming through `requeue`; and `has_work`. The tests run `sync` and `check` as real child processes and drive `cmd_tick` and the graph, so they test the argv boundary rather than the code against itself. Two required points block approval: a failed `sync` is ignored, and its hash is recorded anyway; and the pipeline skill does not yet document the tick step, which task 2.5 asks for. Task group 4 (per-worktree environments) is for a later unit and is not expected here.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/environment.py:96 — `ensure` ignores the exit status of `sync` (`_, output = _run(environment.sync, ...)`, here and again in the heal path at line 104) and records the new inputs hash whether or not the sync succeeded.
  Consequence: The inputs change (a dependency is added to the manifest or lock) and `sync` fails, for example on a network error or a resolver failure. `check` still passes against the old environment. The hash is then recorded as if the sync had happened, so every later tick sees unchanged inputs and never runs `sync` again. The environment stays stale indefinitely while `abk status` says `environment: healthy`, until `check` happens to fail or another input changes. The failed sync's output is also dropped without being printed. This contradicts `EnvironmentState`'s own docstring ('the inputs' hash at the last sync') and the spec's intent that a changed input is synced.
  Done when: Record the new hash only when the `sync` that ran for it exited 0; after a failed sync, keep `previous.hash` so the next tick runs `sync` again. Apply this to both the changed-input sync and the heal sync. Print the failed sync's output through `say`. Add a test in tests/cli/test_tick_environment.py: change an input, make `sync` exit non-zero while `check` passes (add a switch to FakeEnvironment's `_SYNC` script, e.g. a `sync-fails` file that makes it exit 1). The first tick returns 0 and its calls are `["sync", "check"]`. After clearing the switch, the next tick's calls start with `sync` again rather than being `["check"]`.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/skills/abk-pipeline/SKILL.md:11 — Task 2.5 asks for the tick's environment step to be documented in the pipeline skill. The only edit is the `failed` row for the `environment` cause; the skill still does not say that a tick syncs and checks the environment, that an unhealthy environment makes it start nothing and exit non-zero, or that `abk status` shows the environment's state.
  Consequence: The skill is what an agent reads when asked why the pipeline is stuck. An operator who asks why `abk tick` exits 1 and starts nothing, with no unit failed, gets no answer from it. Its pass description at lines 11-12 and its `abk status` row at line 25 now leave out behaviour this unit added, and task 2.5 is unmet.
  Done when: Add the step to the pass description at lines 10-14: once a tick has work, and before its round, it runs `environment.sync` when the inputs changed, then `environment.check`, syncing once more if the check fails; if the check still fails it starts nothing and exits non-zero with the output. Add the environment's state (healthy, or unhealthy with the check output) to the `abk status` row. Say what to do: fix the environment, for which `abk doctor` runs the check, and the next tick resumes the waiting units.

Optional:
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/environment.py:346 — Optional: `ensure` runs `sync` and writes `environment.json` with no lock. Ticks are separate processes that can overlap (cli/pipeline.py line 10), so two ticks can run `sync` on the same environment at once, or one tick's heal sync can rewrite the environment while another tick's unit is in tier 1.
  Consequence: Not every package manager tolerates two concurrent syncs, and a non-atomic write of the record can race. The design does not call for a lock, so this is not required.
  Done when: Wrap the body of `ensure` in `file_lock(inst.state_dir / "environment.lock")` (pipeline.file_lock already exists), and write the record atomically (write a temporary file, then replace).
- [1.4] tests/environment_fakes.py:920 — Optional: `environment_cause()` returns `Cause("environment")`, a stand-in from before the enum member existed. The tests can now use `Cause.ENVIRONMENT` directly. Similarly, `in_progress_label` in pipeline/units.py:616 compares against the literal string "environment" instead of the enum member.
  Consequence: This is an indirection the next reader has to work through, and a rename of the enum value would not be caught by the type checker in units.py.
  Done when: Remove `environment_cause()` and use `Cause.ENVIRONMENT` in the three test files. In units.py, compare with `Cause.ENVIRONMENT` if the import does not create a cycle.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:712 — Optional: `environment.ensure` (which can run `sync`) and `_resume_environment_waiters` (which requeues units) run before the `--dry-run` check, so a dry run can install packages and move failed units to planned.
  Consequence: The skill describes `abk tick --dry-run` as reporting 'without building anything'. Installing dependencies and requeueing units goes further than the store writes the round already makes.
  Done when: Either skip the sync and the resume under `args.dry_run` (still run `check` and report what would happen), or note in the skill's `--dry-run` row that a dry run also syncs the environment and resumes the units waiting for it.

Only `cmd_status` and `_may_build` were converted.
  Consequence: The spec requirement 'The pause line is never in the past' says the line announcing a pause gives its end in local time and never earlier than the moment it is printed. Two cases break it. When a unit's run is stopped by the usage guard (`UnitOutcome.PAUSED`, then `_pause_for_usage`), the log says 'pausing until HH:MM UTC'. When the model refuses a build, the log says 'rate limited — pausing until HH:MM UTC'. Neither goes through the clamp in `pause_line`. The changelog bullet's claim 'The pause line shows local time' and the pipeline skill's 'Times are local' are false for both lines, and `_pause_for_usage` is the usage-pause path the change is about.
  Done when: Both lines are built with `pause_line(state, verb="pausing")`. In the rate-limit branch, keep the 'rate limited — ' prefix around it, or rely on the pause's reason, which already says 'rate limited during <unit>'. A test with `TZ` set to a non-UTC zone (like the `kolkata` fixture) drives at least `_pause_for_usage` through its public caller, a unit run whose outcome is PAUSED. It asserts that the logged line shows the local time and contains no 'UTC'. The same goes for the rate-limit path if a caller-level test can reach it cheaply.

Optional:
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:714 — The resume line 'resuming a pause that was to last until {paused.until:%H:%M UTC}' still prints UTC, while every pause it refers to is now announced in local time.
  Consequence: An operator reading the run log sees a pause announced as 18:30 and resumed 'until 13:00 UTC'. That is the same moment written two ways, and it is confusing. The line announces a resume, not a pause, so the spec does not strictly cover it.
  Done when: Format `paused.until` in local time, for example `paused.until.astimezone():%H:%M`, matching `pause_line`.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:694 — `_hhmm` still writes 'MM-DD HH:MM UTC' into a threshold refusal's reason. `pause_line` prints that reason right after a local time.
  Consequence: A single line reads, for example, 'paused until 18:30 — session usage at 80% (threshold 75%, ramping to 90% by 10-09 13:00 UTC, live)'. The two times are in different zones in one sentence.
  Done when: Make `_hhmm` local (`moment.astimezone():%m-%d %H:%M`), or leave it and say so in the next unit.
- [1.4] tests/pipeline/test_pause_deadline.py:213 — The cache-file test asserts only `served.source != "live"`. The spec scenario says the reading's source says it came from the cache.
  Consequence: A regression that labelled cache readings with some other wrong source, such as 'claude.json', would still pass.
  Done when: Assert `served.source == "cache"`.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:644 — A stale refusal's `resume_at` is now plus the stale-retry interval, and `pause_until` then adds `RESUME_GRACE`. The written pause therefore lasts 7 minutes by default, while the docs and changelog say 5.
  Consequence: This is harmless in practice because a usage pause is re-asked every tick. Still, the marker and the pause line show a 7-minute deadline, and the docs say five.
  Done when: Either skip the grace for a deadline that is not a window reset, or word the docs as 'about five minutes, plus the grace'. This is optional.

units.title: A failed live read is absorbed
units.feedback:
The cache, the cool-down, the retry and the order of sources in `read_live_usage` are well built, and the new tests fake the endpoint at `urllib.request.urlopen`, which is the right boundary. Five things block approval. The refresh of an expired token can no longer run. Task 2.6 is not done. The failure log is not once per tick. The rate-limit reason the spec asks for is missing. And the cool-down tests never check how long the cool-down lasts. All of these belong to task group 2, which is this unit's. `uv run pytest tests/pipeline/test_usage_read_absorbs_failures.py tests/pipeline/test_usage_guard_live.py tests/pipeline/test_usage_guard.py` passes (58).

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:550 — The new `except urllib.error.HTTPError` clause comes before `except Exception` and returns `failed(error)` for every code except 429. An expired token gets HTTP 401 from `urlopen`, so the `expired`/`refresh_login` path can no longer run for the failure it exists to fix.
  Consequence: Take the overnight case `refresh_login` was written for: the saved token has expired and the endpoint answers 401. `urlopen` raises `HTTPError(401)`, which lands in the HTTPError branch and returns the last good reading or None. No refresh happens and the read is not retried. Every tick then pauses on unknown usage until someone opens a session, which is the regression `refresh_login`'s docstring describes. `test_an_expired_token_is_refreshed_once_and_the_read_retried` (tests/pipeline/test_usage_guard_live.py:288) still passes because its fake raises `OSError("401 Unauthorized")`, which is not what the real `urlopen` raises.
  Done when: Check for an expired saved token before the 429/other HTTP split, so that a non-429 HTTPError (at least 401/403) with `given is None and (expired or token_expired)()` still runs the refresh and asks again with the fresh token. Change the expired-token test, or add one in test_usage_read_absorbs_failures.py, so the endpoint raises `urllib.error.HTTPError(USAGE_URL, 401, ...)` through the faked `urlopen`. It should assert that refresh is called once and the second call's reading is returned with source `live`.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:361 — Task 2.6 is not done: `Node.gate` still reads usage twice, once through `runner.may_start` and again through `runner.resume_at` (wiring.py `build_may_start`/`build_resume_at`, each calling `current_usage()`). The task says the gate takes one reading for both. Nothing in this diff touches nodes.py, wiring.py or stack_runner.py.
  Consequence: When the first read fails with a non-429 error and no last good reading exists (nothing is cached), the gate's second read calls the endpoint again, with another retry and sleep. One refused gate then makes up to four requests and logs the failure twice. The pause's `until` may also come from a different reading than its `reason`. The design names this double read as one of the things the change removes.
  Done when: The gate takes one `UsageReading` and derives both the allow/reason and the `until` from it. For example, a single runner callable returns the decision together with the resume time, built from one `current_usage()` call in wiring.py, and the runtime-without-usage short-circuit is kept. Add a test that drives the gate (or the wired callable) for a refused start against a counting usage source and asserts the source was read exactly once and the interrupt's `until` matches that reading's decision.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:545 — `failed()` logs a warning on every failed call, not once per tick as task 2.4 and the spec ('logged once per tick at warning level') require. Only a 429 is cached, as a cool-down, so every other failure is retried and logged again by each reader in the same tick.
  Consequence: When the endpoint answers 500 or times out across a tick that gates several units, plus the pass check and `resume_at`, there is one warning per read. That is several identical lines per tick instead of one. `test_a_repeated_failure_logs_its_exception_name_once` calls `current_usage()` only once, so it would pass with a log on every read.
  Done when: A failure's cause is logged once per tick (for example once per cause per process, or kept beside the cool-down in the cache file), and later failures in the same tick are not logged again. The test calls `current_usage()` two or three times in one tick with a timeout that keeps failing and asserts exactly one warning naming `TimeoutError`. Do the same for a non-429 HTTP status, such as `HTTP 503`.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:527 — During a cool-down, `read_live_usage` returns the last good reading labelled only `cache`, or returns None. Nothing tells the guard's reason that a rate limit is in force or when the next call will be made, which the spec scenario 'The host answers that it is rate limited' requires.
  Consequence: Take a 429 with Retry-After 900, then a unit refused on the kept reading or on the editor's. The reason reads e.g. 'session usage at 85% (..., cache)' or 'usage is unknown...'. It does not say that the endpoint is rate limited or that the next call is at HH:MM. The spec's THEN clause ('the reason names the rate limit and when the next call will be made') is unmet.
  Done when: While a cool-down is active, the reading used (or the decision for a None reading) carries the rate limit and the cool-down's end, e.g. source `cache (rate limited until HH:MM)`, and `may_start_unit`'s reason shows it. Add a test: after a 429 with Retry-After, `may_start_unit(current_usage()).reason` contains the rate-limit wording and the cool-down end time.
- [1.5] tests/pipeline/test_usage_read_absorbs_failures.py:200 — `test_a_rate_limit_answer_is_not_retried_and_starts_a_cool_down` is parametrized on Retry-After '900' and None, but both cases make the same assertions. No test checks how long the cool-down lasts, or that a call is made again once it ends.
  Consequence: Task 2.2 asks for 'a cool-down of the time the answer names, or the default'. Ignoring Retry-After and always using the five-minute default, or writing a cool-down that never expires, would still pass every test.
  Done when: Assert the cool-down's length. For Retry-After 900, `cooldown_until` in the cache file is about now+15 min, and with no header about now+`DEFAULT_COOLDOWN`. Alternatively, rewrite the cache's `cooldown_until` into the past and assert that the next `current_usage()` calls the endpoint.

Optional:
- [1.6] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:523 — `last_good()` checks only the fallback age, not `_past_reset`. During a failure or cool-down, a kept reading whose window has reset since it was taken is still used.
  Consequence: The spec says a reading SHALL NOT be kept past its window's reset. Take a reading at 95% taken 10 minutes before the reset, and a failing endpoint after the reset. The guard refuses on the old 95% instead of falling to the editor's reading. This is conservative (it refuses rather than overspends), so it is optional.
  Done when: `last_good()` also returns None when `_past_reset(kept, now)`, with a test.
- [1.7] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:571 — The retry branch retries any non-HTTP Exception, including a ValueError from a malformed JSON body, not only a timeout or connection error as the spec says.
  Consequence: A body that cannot be parsed is fetched twice, with a sleep, for every reader. This is minor.
  Done when: Retry only on `TimeoutError`/`urllib.error.URLError`/`ConnectionError` (OSError subclasses), and fail at once on anything else.

units.title: State files are written by one function
units.feedback:
The move is complete and correct. I found every temporary-then-replace copy in src/ (fifteen call sites across the fourteen listed writers) on atomic_write_text. The only one left is runtimes/policy_apply.py, which is mkstemp-based and keeps the file mode, and the guard exempts it with a stated reason. The shared function takes the safest variant (a per-process name, the temporary removed on BaseException, the parent made, the replace last). The two locking writers (local forge, review store) still take their lock around the call. One thing blocks: the guard misses the other spelling of the same idiom (rename).

Required:
- [1.1] tests/test_atomic_write_guard.py:31 — The guard only matches a call named `replace`. `Path.rename(target)` and `os.rename(src, dst)` replace over the target just as atomically on POSIX, and the guard lets both through.
  Consequence: Task 2.5 asks for a guard that fails when the same kind of duplicate is added again. A future writer spelling the idiom as `partial.rename(path)` or `os.rename(scratch, path)` adds a sixteenth copy and the guard passes, so the cleanup can quietly regress through the most common alternative spelling.
  Done when: In `replacements`, treat `rename` like `replace`: flag `os.rename(...)`, and `<side-named receiver>.rename(<one arg>)`, as well as the existing `replace` cases. Update the docstring and the failure message to match. The guard should still pass on the current tree, since no src module uses rename for this.

Optional:
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/wait_log.py:137 — The decision-log trim used to write raw bytes. It now decodes them as UTF-8 and writes text in the locale's encoding, which changes behaviour in a group the design calls behaviour-preserving.
  Consequence: The log is written with json.dumps (ASCII), so in practice nothing changes. Under a non-UTF-8 locale, though, `write_text` can raise UnicodeEncodeError on the U+FFFD that `decode(errors="replace")` inserts. That error is not an OSError, so the `except OSError` no longer contains it, and a diagnostic trim that used to be best-effort would raise. The existing test had to be rewritten (write_bytes to write_text) to follow the change.
  Done when: Either keep the bytes path by giving the shared module a bytes variant that shares the same temporary/replace/cleanup body, or catch `(OSError, UnicodeError)` here. If the decode stays, keep the changelog sentence that already describes it.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/runtimes/policy_check.py:65 — Trimming the comment left a fragment: "# So a doctor and an init running at once never read half a file." It also drops the old leading-dot hidden temporary name, which is harmless.
  Consequence: A reader meets a comment that starts mid-sentence.
  Done when: Reword it to a full sentence, e.g. "# Written whole, so a doctor and an init running at once never read half a file."
- [1.4] tests/pipeline/test_atomic_write.py:97 — The two-writers test runs the writes one after another with a faked pid. It mostly restates the f-string, and it says nothing about two threads in one process, which share a pid and so share the temporary name.
  Consequence: None today: every writer that can run on two threads at once takes the file lock, and the old copies were no better. A future unlocked writer called from threads (for example in `abk serve`) would share a temporary unnoticed.
  Done when: Optionally document in atomic_write_text's docstring that concurrent writers within one process must hold the file lock, or add the thread id to the temporary name.

description.summary: Every state file that is written by writing a temporary file and then replacing the real one now goes through a single shared function, `atomic_write_text`, and a guard test stops new copies of that pattern from being added.
changes: Writers that each had their own write-a-temporary-then-replace code now call `atomic_write_text` in pipeline/file_lock.py. It creates the parent directory, writes to a temporary named after the current process, replaces the real file last, and deletes the temporary if anything goes wrong, so the old file is kept.

The writers that hold a file lock (the local forge and the review store) still take it around the shared call. The function's docstring says that two threads of the same process share the temporary name, so they must hold the lock.
Trimming the decision log is still best-effort: the `except` around the trim now catches both `OSError` and `UnicodeError`, so an error in either stops the trim without raising.

A new guard test, tests/test_atomic_write_guard.py, fails when any source module other than the shared one calls `os.replace` or `os.rename`, or calls `.replace(target)` or `.rename(target)` on a path with a temporary, scratch or partial name. The mkstemp-based policy writer, which keeps the file's mode, is exempt, with the reason given in the test.

units.title: Test helpers live in one place
units.feedback:
The helper moves are correct. I ran the touched tests (tracks, restack, gate, commit order, no-remote, events, artifacts, profile-owned paths, scaffold, init) together with the leak guard and the ecosystem-names guard: 566 passed. Callers of the merged sha-returning `commit` (test_no_remote, test_events_base_tip) do not depend on the old content, `git add <name>` or the 'add' message, so moving them to the shared helper is safe. The only assertion that changed is `protected_branches=("trunk",)` in test_runner_runtime. That follows from the shared `make_installation` activating the installation, and the comment explains it, so it is fine. Task 4.2 also lists 'the write_change copies that write the same tasks file'. I compared every `write_change` and no two are identical (test_cli_pipeline and test_round differ in `exist_ok` and in what they return), so there was nothing to merge and the guard's COPIED entry covers future copies. Two required fixes remain, both small and both in the new test files.

Required:
- [1.1] tests/test_test_helpers_defined_once.py:522 — The guard does not cover two of the helpers this change merged: `commit_files` (moved from test_commit_order and test_gate) and `commit_unit_work` (moved from test_artifacts_worktree_and_commit and test_profile_owned_paths). Neither name is in MERGED or COPIED. And because each old copy was called `commit` locally, its body is never compared with the shared `commit_files` or `commit_unit_work`.
  Consequence: Spec code-reuse 'A helper defined twice' requires that a merged helper defined again fails the guard. Paste the old `def commit(repo, message, files)` back into tests/pipeline/test_gate.py, or add `def commit_files(...)` with the same body there, and all three guard tests still pass. That is exactly the copy this change removed.
  Done when: The guard flags any top-level helper outside the shared modules whose body and arguments (the `shape` that `helpers()` already computes) equal any top-level helper defined in tests/factories.py or tests/conftest.py, whatever its name. Exclude tests/factories.py and tests/conftest.py themselves. I ran that check against the current tree and it reports nothing, so it can be added as is. Add `commit_files` and `commit_unit_work` to MERGED as well. Pasting the old local `commit(repo, message, files)` body into a test file must then make the guard fail.
- [1.2] tests/test_shared_commit_helper.py:469 — Task 4.1 asks for a test that the shared commit helper 'returns what a caller needs'. None of the three tests checks what `commit` returns, yet test_no_remote (`newer = commit(repo, "b.txt")`) and test_events_base_tip rely on it being the new commit's sha.
  Consequence: If `commit` returned nothing or the wrong sha (for example `rev-parse HEAD~1`), this file would still pass. The failure would show up only indirectly in callers, and the test the task asked for would not exist.
  Done when: Add an assertion to test_commit_writes_the_file_and_commits_it_with_the_name_in_the_message, or a new test: `sha = commit(repo, "markers.py", ...)` followed by `assert sha == git(repo, "rev-parse", "HEAD")`.

Optional:
- [1.3] tests/test_test_helpers_defined_once.py:508 — The module docstring says 'no two top-level helpers anywhere share a name and a body', but the third test only checks the names in MERGED and COPIED. Over the whole tests/ tree about 50 same-name, same-body pairs exist today (for example `committed_files` in test_artifacts_worktree_and_commit, test_environment_locks and test_profile_owned_paths; `count` and `branch_of` in tracks/test_runner_planning_repo and test_runner_propose_commit; `row_of` in three usage tests).
  Consequence: A reader who trusts the docstring will believe every duplicated helper is guarded, when only the listed names are.
  Done when: Reword the docstring to say what is checked: the merged helpers are defined only in the shared modules, no test file repeats a shared helper's body, and the listed names (`commit`, `write_change`) are not copied with the same body. Whether to extend the guard to every helper is a scope decision for a person (see follow_ups).
- [1.4] tests/tracks/test_runner_rows.py:19 — `described_installation` goes through the shared `make_installation`, which already calls `installation.activate()`. So the `installation.activate()` lines in the `inst` fixtures of test_runner_rows.py and test_runner_track_settings.py now do nothing.
  Consequence: None in behaviour. A reader may think `described_installation` does not activate.
  Done when: Return `described_installation(...)` directly from both fixtures.

description.summary: Tier 1 now runs the tests a unit added or changed several more times under the load of the full run, and fails the unit if any of those runs fails, so flaky new tests are caught before review.
changes: After a passing tier 1 run, the tests the unit added or edited are found by comparing against the base ref (deleted tests are left out) and run again `limits.tier1_repeat_runs` times. Any failure fails tier 1.

Repeats select exact test identifiers (`file::Class::test`), not name patterns. Each test command gets only the ids under the paths it runs, so a workspace member's test is never run in another member's environment or in the root tests environment.
Only files the toolchain counts as test files contribute ids, so a `test_*` method in a source module is not repeated.

Profiles opt in through a new `RepeatsTests` protocol (`repeat_command`). The python-uv profile keeps the run's workers and markers and replaces its paths with the ids. A profile without the hook, a repeat count of 0, or a base ref that can't be read skips the check and the pass stands.
A repeat that collects nothing stops early only when the profile's no-tests-collected status is non-zero, so a node-shaped profile whose status is 0 still repeats every run.
