units.title: The interval adapts
units.feedback:
The adaptation does what the change asks. Each refusal doubles the time up to the maximum. A longer Retry-After holds the time while it lasts, and the cool-down in read_live_usage already stops calls during it. Each quiet stretch of the current time halves it, never below the configured value. The status line names the time and what set it. The tests go through read_live_usage and cmd_status with the real record format, and each one would fail if its rule were missing (no doubling, no halving, or halving below the configured value). The usage tests (295) and the leak check pass. One required point is left: two descriptions still say the cache time is fixed.

Required:
- [1.1] docs/architecture.md:754 — Two descriptions still say a good reading is kept for exactly `usage_cache_minutes`. The time now adapts between that value and `usage_cache_max_minutes`. The same fixed-time wording is in the storage table at docs/architecture.md:952 and in the `read_live_usage` docstring at src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:524 ("for `ttl` (the configured cache time)").
  Consequence: After a refusal, the reading is kept for 30–60 minutes, and longer while a Retry-After lasts. This makes "kept in `usage-cache.json` for `usage_cache_minutes`, fifteen by default" false. Anyone reading architecture.md or the docstring to work out why the endpoint was not asked for 40 minutes gets the wrong answer.
  Done when: Reword architecture.md:754 so the reading is kept for an adaptive time. It starts at `usage_cache_minutes` (fifteen by default). Each refusal doubles it up to `usage_cache_max_minutes` (an hour by default), and a longer retry time is respected. Each quiet stretch of that time halves it, never below the configured value. `abk status` shows the time in use. The reading is still never kept past a window's reset. In the table at line 952, write `(usage_cache_minutes to usage_cache_max_minutes)` or similar. In the docstring at usage_guard.py:524, say `ttl` defaults to the adaptive cache time from `current_cache_interval`, not the configured one.

Optional:
- [1.2] CHANGELOG.md:9 — This unit adds a second Unreleased bullet for the usage-api-observability change, beside the bullet unit 1 added.
  Consequence: The changelog convention in AGENTS.md says one change is one bullet, even across several pull requests. The repo's checks pass, so this is optional.
  Done when: Fold the adaptive-interval sentence into the existing bullet about usage-calls.jsonl.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:534 — Every `read_live_usage` call, cache hits included, now reads and parses the whole week-long `usage-calls.jsonl` to work out the time. `record_call` already reads and rewrites that file on every call.
  Consequence: The cost of one read grows with how many calls were made in the week. It doubles the file I/O the record already costs on every read. This is acceptable today, so it is optional.
  Done when: Optionally, read the record once per `read_live_usage` and use it both for the time and in `record_call`. Or, if the file grows, cache the computed time alongside `usage-cache.json`.

units.title: The parked unit's thread and the readers of the derived names
units.feedback:
Not approved: two required fixes and one missing test. The rest of the work matches the change. `UPSTREAM_CHANGED` is in `EventKind`, with its handler in `on_event`. The pass is now a `run_round` step after `_refresh`, beside `gate_sent_back` and `release_gated`. `why_branch_is_changing` sits beside `build_upstream_incomplete`. The server summary and the `abk.units` gauge read the stored state. The chat's `running()` already read it on main, and the new test pins that. The docs and the skill were updated. The fixtures under `web/src/test/recorded` were reformatted by re-recording, but `.prettierignore` excludes that folder, so this costs nothing.

Required:
- [1.1] CHANGELOG.md:9 — The entry says a parked unit 'resumes when released instead of starting a fresh run'. The code does not do that: the release still starts a fresh run.
  Consequence: On release the unit goes through `_evaluate` → `build_unit` → `run_unit` (graph/unit.py). There `interrupted = bool(where.next) and not set(where.next) & WAITS` is False for a thread at `await_review`, so `run_thread` gets a new `UnitRun` and the run starts from the beginning, just as it did before this branch. The design also says the release is unchanged. The bullet's sentence is false.
  Done when: Reword the bullet to describe what changed. The move is now delivered to the unit's thread as an event, so the thread records it and stays waiting for review instead of believing it is still in review. The release itself is unchanged. Keep the sentences about `state`/`status` and the gauge. Check that docs/architecture.md ("keeps waiting at `await_review` for the release") makes no stronger claim than that.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:1801 — The new path drops a safety check. The old store-only path re-read the unit under its claim and skipped it unless it was still `in_review` (wiring.py:2051–2054). The `deliver` path has no such check, and the `upstream_changed` handler sets `planned` whatever the stored state. `UPSTREAM_CHANGED` is also missing from the guard at the top of `on_event` that stops automatic events touching a unit a person holds (`REWORK, HOLD, BASE_MOVED`).
  Consequence: The pass reads the unit as `in_review` from its snapshot. Before delivery, a person holds it: the HOLD event moves the thread to the HELD wait with `RunStatus.HELD` and the store to `held`. `resume_thread` then delivers `upstream_changed` to that wait, and the handler overwrites the hold with `planned`/`upstream_went_back`. The scheduler can later build a unit a person had held. The old path would have skipped it.
  Done when: Add `EventKind.UPSTREAM_CHANGED` to the tuple in the `state.status is RunStatus.HELD` guard. In the `UPSTREAM_CHANGED` branch, set `planned` only when `r.store.get(unit.id).state == IN_REVIEW`; otherwise return `{"event": None}`. Add a graph test in tests/graph/test_await_review.py: tick to review, deliver a HOLD, then deliver `UPSTREAM_CHANGED`. Assert the store stays `held` and the thread's next node is still `HELD`.
- [1.3] tests/pipeline/test_follow_predecessors.py:91 — Nothing tests that the pass hands the move to the thread. The `follow` helper never passes `deliver`. The round test monkeypatches `follow_predecessors` away. The graph test sends the event directly. So nothing exercises `follow_predecessors(deliver=...)` or the `deliver=` wiring in `cli._follow_predecessors`.
  Consequence: If `deliver=deliver` is deleted from `_follow_predecessors`, or `follow_predecessors` ignores `deliver`, the pass goes back to writing the store only. That is the exact gap task 3.4 and the group-2 follow-up asked to close, and every test would still pass.
  Done when: (a) In test_follow_predecessors.py, pass a fake `deliver` that records `(unit.id, note)` and returns True. Assert it was called once with the dependent and a note naming the predecessor, the pass did not write the store itself (the dependent's state is whatever the fake left, still `in_review`), and the returned ids include the dependent. A second test has `deliver` return False and asserts the store fallback sets `planned` with `upstream_went_back`. (b) A test of `cli._follow_predecessors(inst, store)`: the dependent has a real thread at `await_review` (as the graph_driver/tick tests build one), and the same-repo predecessor's branch is changing. Assert the thread's recorded event kind is `upstream_changed` (e.g. `position(...).state.event.kind`), the store reads `planned`/`upstream_went_back`, and the next node is still `AWAIT_REVIEW`.

Optional:
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:1704 — `deliver` returns `resume_thread(...) is not None`. A delivery that raised returns `Resumed(raised=True)` after recording the unit as failed, so it still counts as delivered.
  Consequence: A handler error marks the unit `failed`, yet `follow_predecessors` logs '<id>: set back to planned' and includes the unit in its moved ids.
  Done when: Return `resumed is not None and not resumed.raised`. The fallback then re-reads the unit, finds it is not `in_review` and skips it, so it is not logged as parked.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/serve/server.py:254 — `related()` still puts the derived name under `state`, while `summary()` now uses `state` for the stored state and `status` for the derived name.
  Consequence: In the same unit response, `state` means the stored state at the top level and the display name inside `depends_on`/`merge_gates`. That will mislead the next reader of the API.

units.title: A blocked unit gives its place to the unit blocking it
units.feedback:
1.2 and 1.3 are done: `blocked()` is now only `waiting_on`, the stale-cause fallback is gone, and the three docs describe the new rule accurately. 1.1 is fixed for the case it named, because an interrupted build whose dependencies had merged now resumes at the limit. But the replacement signal (the stored cause is still `gated`/`upstream_went_back`) misses the most ordinary way a paused build becomes blocked, so the spec's 'freshly unblocked unit at the limit' scenario still fails for it. That is the one required finding below. It is new in this rework, which introduced the cause-based signal.

Required:
- [2.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/units.py:651 — `_waits_for_room` sees a unit as 'was blocked' only when the cause on its record is `gated` or `upstream_went_back`. A paused build gets blocked because its same-repo predecessor went back after the build stopped, and nothing writes a cause on it, so the unit resumes past the limit once the predecessor returns.
  Consequence: I ran this on HEAD. The unit `u/1` is planned with branch `spec/u/1`, cause None (a tick ended), and depends on `p/1`. `p/1` is sent back for rework (PLANNED, pr=3, feedback): `blocked(u/1)` is True and u/1 is not counted. Then `p/1` returns to IN_REVIEW with `a/1` and `b/1` also in review, so 3 units are in progress at limit 3. `ready_units(..., max_units_in_progress=3)` returns ['u/1'], which makes 4 in progress. Nothing sets a cause on u/1 meanwhile: `follow_predecessors` only moves IN_REVIEW units, and `upstream_incomplete` only fires inside a running build. This breaks the spec requirement 'A planned unit that was blocked and no longer is ... SHALL start only while the number of other units in progress is below the limit' and its scenario 'A freshly unblocked unit at the limit → it stays planned'. The same happens for a paused unit whose predecessor failed or was held and later came back. The tests do not catch it, because `unblocked_graph` gives its unit `upstream_went_back` by hand, and on a cross-repo merged dependency, a combination the pipeline never writes: `upstream_went_back` is only set for same-repo parents.
  Done when: A planned unit with work and no PR that was blocked at any point since its last run must wait for room, whatever its stored cause. Interrupted builds whose parents stayed reviewed or merged throughout (cause None, `host_unavailable`, `released`, `usage`) must still resume at the limit. Two acceptable ways: (a) derive it from history, so the unit waits when a unit it depends on (`through_satisfied` / `depends_on`) has a state-change entry later than the unit's own last entry that put it outside REVIEWED/merged; or (b) have the tick write `upstream_went_back` (or `gated` for a merge gate) on every planned, worked unit it finds `blocked`, so the stored cause the current check reads is always present. Add a test built the way the pipeline really gets there: a worked planned unit with no cause depends on a same-repo `p/1` whose history shows it went PLANNED (rework) after the unit's last entry and is now IN_REVIEW again, with two other units in review at limit 3. Assert `chosen(graph, limit=3) == []`, and that it becomes `['u/1']` when one of the busy units merges. Keep `test_an_interrupted_build_whose_dependencies_had_merged_resumes_at_the_limit` passing. Under (a), also change `unblocked_graph` to use a same-repo predecessor that went back and returned, rather than a hand-set cause on a cross-repo merged dependency.

units.title: The Python profile selects by coverage, falls back to the failed tests, and each run is measured

description.summary: With `checks.affected.mode: profile`, a fix round in a Python repo now runs only the tests the fix affects, chosen by coverage data that earlier full runs record. If there is no such data it runs the failed tests, and every selected run is measured in the usage ledger.
changes: Full test runs in a unit's worktree record coverage data through pytest-testmon without deselecting anything. The data is stored at `<project>/.abk/affected`, a path git already excludes, so a commit never contains it.

In a fix round, a selected run uses that data when it exists. Otherwise it runs only the failed tests named in the previous output, and with no test named it runs the full suite. A full run still confirms any selected pass before the unit goes green.

If a command run with the plugin fails without producing any pytest result (for example, uv cannot install the plugin), it is run again plainly, and a selection falls back to the full suite. A one-line log names the program. When the plugin run collects no tests, the selection counts as a pass, not as the plugin being unavailable.
The repo's root `extras` are passed to the profile's selection commands, so the selected tests run with the same extra packages as the full run.
Each selected run writes an `affected` line to the usage ledger. It records the number of tests selected and in total, the estimated seconds saved, and whether the confirming full run agreed.

Windows toasts, the init prompt, the doctor check and the docs
units.feedback:
Task 2.7 (the hand-run toast) is a person's task and does not block this review. The required points are task 2.6 (docs), the version pin from task 2.5, a re-run of init that asks the question and then drops the answer, an Install-Module call whose prompts the operator never sees, and a quoting test that only checks the code against a copy of itself.

Required:
- [1.1] docs/configuration.md:1 — Task 2.6 is not done. Apart from the changelog, nothing in docs/ or src/agent_build_kit/skills mentions notifications (a grep for 'notif' and 'BurntToast' finds nothing relevant).
  Consequence: Task 2.6 requires docs/configuration.md (the `notifications` section and its defaults: off, 30, 10, the command templates), docs/architecture.md (the reconciliation step and the state table row for notifications.json), docs/init.md, docs/cli.md and the abk-config skill. AGENTS.md also says a new config field must be documented in the abk-config skill and docs/configuration.md. Today `notifications` appears in neither.
  Done when: Each of the five files describes its part. configuration.md and the abk-config skill list provider/command/delay_minutes/remind_after_minutes with their defaults, the windows provider, and the pinned BurntToast version. architecture.md has the reconcile step in run_round and a state-table row for notifications.json. init.md covers the WSL/Windows question and the install command. cli.md covers the doctor `notifications` check. Add the follow-up's 1.7 line too: 'no rework pending' is feedback == "", 'needs a person' is HeldBy.REVIEW/TOOLCHAIN or Cause.NEEDS_HUMAN, and there is no person-activity signal yet.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/notify/windows.py:256 — The BurntToast version is not pinned anywhere. Task 2.5 says 'the module version pinned in the script', and the design says it is pinned in the provider's script and the docs because the cmdlet names changed between versions.
  Consequence: Install-Module without -RequiredVersion installs whatever PSGallery has as latest. BurntToast 1.x renamed and reshaped the cmdlets that show() and clear() call (New-BurntToastNotification -UniqueIdentifier, Remove-BTNotification -Tag, New-BTButton -Arguments). A fresh install can therefore make every show fail. Doctor would still pass, because it only checks that some BurntToast is listed.
  Done when: Add one constant, e.g. BURNTTOAST_VERSION = "0.8.5" (the release whose cmdlets the scripts use). Use it in three places. (1) INSTALL_COMMAND adds `-RequiredVersion <v>`. (2) The show and clear scripts start with `Import-Module BurntToast -RequiredVersion <v>;`. (3) Doctor fails when the listing does not contain that version, with the install command as the fix. Tests: the windows-provider test asserts the import line is in the script; the doctor test with a listing of a different version fails; tests/cli/test_init.py INSTALL/INSTALL_TEXT carry the version.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/cli/init.py:404 — On a re-run where abk.yaml already exists (`keeps`, no --force), init still asks the notifications question and may run the install. The answer is then thrown away: write_planning_repo keeps abk.yaml, and fill_missing_environment fills only `environment`.
  Consequence: On WSL, `abk init <planning>` against an existing planning repo goes like this: the operator answers y and y, BurntToast is installed, and the run prints 'kept abk.yaml'. notifications.provider stays off, no toast ever appears, and nothing says the choice was dropped.
  Done when: When `keeps` is true, either ask nothing about notifications, or add a `notifications` block to the kept file when it has none and print 'filled notifications in abk.yaml' (the same way fill_missing_environment adds a missing block). Add a test in tests/cli/test_init.py: an existing abk.yaml on Host.WSL, answers y/y. Assert either that no notification prompt was asked, or that load(abk.yaml).notifications.provider is WINDOWS.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/cli/init.py:148 — The install runs `Install-Module BurntToast -Scope CurrentUser` with capture_output=True. On a stock Windows PowerShell 5.1 it stops at interactive prompts (bootstrapping the NuGet provider, and trusting the 'untrusted repository' PSGallery). The operator cannot see those prompts because the output is captured. On failure, stderr is also dropped.
  Consequence: On a fresh Windows/WSL machine, `abk init` appears to hang after 'install it now? y', waiting on a prompt the operator never sees. If the install fails, the message gives only the exit code, unlike the policy_fix path just above it, which prints stderr.
  Done when: Do one of two things. (a) Run the install without capturing output, so its prompts reach the terminal. (b) Make the command non-interactive (`-Force`, plus `-RequiredVersion` from the pin finding), and print result.stderr in the failure message as _offer_policy_fix does. Whichever you choose, the command printed before the question, the one run, and doctor's fix are the same INSTALL_COMMAND. The init test asserts the printed text equals what was run.
- [1.5] tests/notify/test_windows_provider.py:695 — The quoting tests copy `_literal` into the test (`literal`) and assert the copy's output appears in the Python argv. They never check what powershell.exe actually receives. The script also goes through the Windows command line (WSL interop or list2cmdline), where embedded double quotes, backticks and non-ASCII text in unit.title/unit.note are parsed again.
  Consequence: Suppose a unit title or note contains `"` or a backtick, which is common in tasks.md titles. If the command-line conversion re-splits or strips quotes, PowerShell runs a different script and every show for that unit fails. The test still passes, because it checks the code against its own helper, not the boundary.
  Done when: Pass the script as `powershell.exe -NoProfile -EncodedCommand <base64 of the script in UTF-16LE>`, so no command-line quoting is involved. Keep `_literal` for the PowerShell-level string quoting. The test decodes argv[-1] (base64, then UTF-16LE), the same decoding powershell.exe does, and asserts the decoded script contains the single-quoted literal of AWKWARD_TITLE and of a title with a non-ASCII character. It should not use a copy of the implementation's helper.

Optional:
- [1.6] src/agent_build_kit/notify/windows.py:285 — `New-BTButton -Arguments` with an empty link fails BurntToast's parameter validation. The notifications/1 follow-up proposes an empty link as the fallback for a unit whose repo has left abk.yaml.
  Consequence: If that follow-up lands as 'empty link', every show for that unit raises a ProviderError on every tick.
  Done when: Add the button only when link is non-empty, and test that a show with link="" builds a script without New-BTButton.

units.title: Wait reasons, the decision log, timestamps, spans and samples

description.summary: Every unit that is not running gets a recorded reason for waiting, and a decision log, readiness and human-activity timestamps, wait spans and slot samples are added to the pipeline's ledger.
changes: Each tick works out a wait reason for every unit not in flight: blocked, queue full, slot, usage pause, lease, backoff, waiting for review, needs a person, or ready. It appends a reason to `runs/decisions.jsonl` only when the reason changes, and leaves units excluded by `--only` open.

Waits for a full queue, a lease, a backoff or a person that end are written as spans in the usage ledger. A running pass adds `sample` rows and sets the `abk.slots.free` and `abk.slots.idle_with_ready` gauges.

Units gain `ready_at`, set the first time a unit is judged ready, slot-bound or usage-paused even on ticks that start nothing. They also gain `first_human_activity_at`, set when the PR poller first sees a person's new comment or review.
A unit started during a pass that later ends in review, held or failed is judged by its stored state in that same pass, so its review or person wait is dated from when it began.

A stored `running` unit that no run holds while a pause is in force is shown as `paused` in status, the graph, labels and the web UI. This is documented in the architecture and unit-graph docs and in the abk-pipeline skill.
Rework and adapt ledger spans record why they ran (review, check or conflict). The configuration docs name `decisions.jsonl` as a gitignored file in the state directory.

units.title: Filled summaries and abk report --waits
units.feedback:
All nine earlier points were reworked, and the related tests pass (32 in test_wait_report, test_wait_summary and test_report_waits_command). The changelog is clean. The unit_size.measured/Kind.label extraction, the _READY allowlist, the Sample parse and the single history walk are all good. Two problems remain. Both come from this round's rework. They are new because in round 1 the rounds came out of the in_review budget and the review remainder stayed under in-review. Moving rounds into running time and the remainder into running_checks created them. Separately, earlier findings 1.1 and 1.2 contradict each other: rounds lie outside the review stretch, so they cannot also be a part of it. Finding 1 below resolves that, and the design text decides it.

Still open from earlier rounds:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_report.py:1004 (reported open) — Review-round spans are taken out of the unit's `in_review` stretches, but a round never runs while the unit is in review. The round nodes are REWORK, FIX_CHECKS and ADAPT (graph/nodes.py:234-255). They run while the unit is RUNNING: the build's own reviewer loop runs before the PR is in review at all, and a rework a review asked for moves the unit to RUNNING (nodes.py:1824) or PLANNED (events.py:1308) first. `_unit_waits` subtracts `_round_spans` from the review budget, and `_review_entry` (line 1131) subtracts their sum from the review stretch.
  Consequence: Example: a unit runs 4 h, including one 1 h internal rework round (span node=rework, cause=review, before any review), then waits 3 h in review and nobody answers. `abk report --waits` gives in_review_person 2 h and in_review_round 1 h, but the person's wait was 3 h and the round's hour is also counted inside the running stretch. The archived summary gives review_person 3 h, review_round 1 h, review_checks 0, which is 4 h against review_wait_ms 3 h. Every unit with an internal review round, which is most units, gets its person time understated in the report and an inconsistent summary. The fixtures hide this: wait_fixture.py and test_wait_summary.py write the round span with node="review" (not a round node) and stamp it inside the in_review stretch, which is the implementation's assumption rather than the shape the pipeline writes.
  Done when: Attribute each round span to where it actually lies, using its `started`/`ended`. A round counts as in-review-round only if it falls after the unit first entered review (`review_requested_at`), and its time comes out of the stretch it lies in (running or planned after review entry), never out of an in_review stretch. A round before the first review entry is running time. Apply the same rule in the roll-up's `review_round_ms`. Fixtures write rounds as the pipeline does (node rework/fix_checks/adapt, with started/ended), and add one test: history running → in_review → running (rework) → in_review → merged, with an internal round before the first review. Assert the internal round adds nothing to in_review_round, the post-review round does, and in_review_person equals the in_review stretches minus nothing.

Required:
- [2.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_report.py:1176 — The table's 'in review' and 'running' totals are no longer the time spent in those states. `in_review_ms` is person + round. The review stretch's remainder (the time after a person answered) is now added to running_checks_ms, and post-review rounds, which lie in running stretches, are added to in-review. The worked-example fixture had its `first_human_activity_at` and its round spans removed so that the pinned 172 h still holds.
  Consequence: I ran the worked example with every unit answered 30 minutes after entering review, with nothing else changed. The headline went from 'in review 172.0, running 93.0' to 'in review 36.0, running 229.0'. For a real installation, where people do answer, the line therefore misstates both state times that task 2.1 and the design's table ('time in `in_review`', 'time in `running`') name. Today the 2.1 test passes only because its fixture leaves out the data that breaks it.
  Done when: The planned / in review / running totals on the table and in the JSON total are the time in each state from the units' histories (in_review stretches, running stretches, planned stretches), independent of how the causes divide that time. Restore `first_human_activity_at` on the worked example's units, and give some units a review-round span after their review entry, the way the pipeline writes it (node rework/fix_checks/adapt, cause, started/ended, in a running stretch after review). test_the_worked_example_reproduces_the_analysis, test_the_table_shows_the_analysis_figures and test_the_table_is_the_default_and_shows_the_analysis must still give planned 1343.0, in review 172.0, running 93.0 (agent 11.6) with that data. The causes must still sum to each unit's wall time.
- [2.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_report.py:1015 — `_review_split` makes room for the post-review rounds by shrinking a person's time (`person = min(person, stretch - round_ms)`). But those rounds lie in running/planned stretches, outside the review stretch. A person's in-review time is cut by time that passed elsewhere, and the report books the cut hours of the review stretch as running_checks_ms.
  Consequence: Example: 3 h in review, nobody answers, and a 1 h check-fix or restack round runs after the review entry. The report gives in_review_person 2 h, running_checks 1 h (from the review stretch) and in_review_round 1 h. A person held it the full 3 h. design.md:97 says person is 'all of the stretch when nobody answered'. test_a_review_nobody_answered_is_all_the_persons now pins 5 h of a 6 h unanswered stretch, which contradicts that sentence and its own test name. Check and conflict rounds after review entry with nobody answering are common: restacks and check fixes during a long review.
  Done when: person = from the first review entry to `first_human_activity_at`, clipped to the review stretch, or the whole stretch when nobody answered. checks = stretch - person. round = the post-review round time, which lies outside the stretch and is not clipped to it or subtracted from person. In the summary, review_person_ms + review_checks_ms == review_wait_ms. review_round_ms is recorded beside them, not as a part of review_wait_ms. Say so in docs/cli.md, replacing 'which sum to `review_wait_ms`' and '(all of it when nobody answered, less the rounds)'. test_a_review_nobody_answered_is_all_the_persons asserts review_person_ms == review_wait_ms == 6 h, review_checks_ms == 0, review_round_ms == 1 h. test_the_reports_person_time_is_the_summarys still holds.

Optional:
- [2.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_report.py:1039 — A post-review round's agent calls are counted twice: the round's whole span is booked as in_review_round_ms, and the same calls also come out of the remaining running budget as running_agent_ms. running_other_ms absorbs the difference.
  Consequence: For a unit with a 1 h rework round of which 50 min is agent calls, running_other is understated by 50 min and agent time includes round work. The wall-time sum still holds because of the clamping. The spec does not set a precedence between overlapping causes.
  Done when: Either subtract a round's own agent and check time from the round (or the reverse), or document which cause wins when a round's calls overlap it.
- [2.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_report.py:1039 — For a unit with no ready stamp, `_unit_waits` skips every planned stretch, including one after review that holds a rework round. `_review_split`, used for the summary, counts that round. For such a unit, the report's in_review_round is less than the summary's review_round_ms.
  Consequence: Only older units without `ready_at` or a decision-log ready reason are affected.
  Done when: Skip only the planned_blocked/planned_ready split for such a stretch and still book its round time, or document the difference.
- [2.5] docs/cli.md:63 — One line of the --waits paragraph is about 140 characters long and is not re-wrapped like the rest of the paragraph.
  Consequence: Cosmetic only.
  Done when: Re-wrap the paragraph.

description.summary: Adds `abk report --waits`, which splits each unit's wall time into causes and shows idle hours and estimate ratios, and makes each change's archived summary carry its slot, pause and review waits.
changes: `abk report --waits` splits each unit's time, from its state history, into planned-blocked, planned-ready, running (agent, checks, other), in review (a person's, or rounds), paused and failed, grouped by unit or by day. The causes sum to the wall time, a cause never recorded prints as `-`, and asking for any grouping other than unit or day exits 2.

The report's planned, in review and running totals are the time spent in each state, taken straight from the history, so they do not depend on how the causes divide that time. The JSON output carries them as well.

A review round (a rework, check-fix or adapt round that began after the unit first entered review) is counted as in-review-round, and its time comes out of the running or planned stretch it lies in. A round before the first review counts as ordinary running time.
Time in review is split into a person's (from entering review until the first human activity, or all of it when nobody answered) and the checks' (the rest).

Under the table, the report shows the sampled hours in which nothing ran, split into hours with a full queue and hours with room, and the estimate ratio (actual over estimated lines) for each unit kind, labelled with the new shared `Kind.label`.

At archive, each unit's summary records `slot_wait_ms`, `pause_wait_ms` and `review_wait_ms`. The review wait is split into `review_person_ms` and `review_checks_ms`, with `review_round_ms` recorded beside them. `abk usage backfill-costs --apply` now passes the store's units, so re-rolled summaries get these fields too.

units.title: Ledger completeness and retention
units.feedback:
All four required points from round 1 are fixed. The four touched test files pass (74 tests). One new test, added for optional point 1.6, passes whatever the code does, so it blocks approval. The fix is small.

Required:
- [2.1] tests/pipeline/test_log_retention.py:160 — test_the_ledger_is_not_read_while_no_log_is_old_enough passes whether or not the ledger is read. The test makes the ledger path a directory, so `ledger.read_text()` raises IsADirectoryError. That is an OSError, and `remove_old_logs` catches it in `except OSError: return` (run_log.py:142-145). The function then returns quietly. The only log is also within the age limit, so `recent.exists()` holds on both paths.
  Consequence: Delete the early `if not (candidates := ...): return` in `remove_old_logs`. The ledger is then read every round again, which is what point 1.6 removed, and this test still passes. It claims to pin behaviour it does not check.
  Done when: Make reading the ledger fail the test instead of being swallowed. For example, monkeypatch `Path.read_text` (or use a ledger object) to raise AssertionError('the ledger was read'), which is not an OSError. Then assert that `remove_old_logs` returns and the recent log still exists. Without the early return, the test must fail. Alternatively, delete the test, since 1.6 was optional.

Optional:
- [2.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/run_log.py:154 — The rework took away the per-file `try/except OSError` around stat and unlink in `remove_old_logs`. Two effects follow. A stat that fails on one file aborts the whole pass: for example, a log another process prunes between `iterdir` and `stat`. An unlink that fails with PermissionError raises out to `_step`, so the old logs after it are not removed in that round.
  Consequence: One unreadable or undeletable log stops all age-based removal for as long as it stays that way. `_step` logs 'bounding the logs failed' each round, so nothing is silently wrong.
  Done when: Guard each file separately: skip a file whose stat or unlink raises OSError, and carry on with the rest, as the previous version did.

description.summary: Bounds the pipeline's on-disk logs: the decision log is capped by size and old unit run logs are removed once their unit's summary is in the usage ledger. The branch also adds tests that a killed agent call that is retried still records exactly one ledger row.
changes: Each pipeline round now starts with a guarded 'bounding the logs' step. If it fails, the rest of the round still runs, including marking units ready.

When the decision log grows past `retention.decision_log_mb` (default 50), it is trimmed to 80% of that limit, keeping the newest lines. The rewrite goes through a scratch file, and if the write fails the log is left as it was.

A unit's run log last written more than `retention.unit_log_days` days ago (default 30) is removed, but only when the usage ledger has a summary line for that unit. The ledger is read only when some log is old enough to go. A log that cannot be removed is skipped and the others are still removed.
run_log.py now parses unit-log file names with one shared pattern, used for archive-time removal, age-based removal and listing.
The new `retention` settings are documented in docs/configuration.md and the abk-config skill.
New tests: a killed agent call that is retried resumes the same session and records exactly one ledger row, and a round-level test shows retention applies the configured settings.

units.title: The usage module is the only authority
units.feedback:
Predecessor check: `usage-read-on-decision/1` is now on main as 40e7987, and this branch sits on main (deba67b). In tests/cli/test_tick_scheduling.py the conflict resolution only appends `test_a_rate_limit_pause_ends_at_its_deadline_within_the_pass` and its `json` import. The predecessor's tests are untouched and none is duplicated. Each new test still checks behaviour the predecessor leaves in place: the tick-outcome test would get 'paused' from main's `_tick`; the deadline test would hit main's sticky `stopping` flag; the lock, counter and editor-reset tests have no counterpart on main. The new and related tests pass locally (25 passed, with DeprecationWarning raised as an error, so the fork-based process test is clean). No test needs removing. What blocks approval is the missing documentation task (4.9) and two gaps in the 'not used past its window / served the last good reading' rule.

Required:
- [1.1] docs/architecture.md:815 — Task 4.9 is not done. The branch changes no doc and not the pipeline skill: docs/architecture.md, docs/configuration.md and src/agent_build_kit/skills/abk-pipeline/SKILL.md are all untouched.
  Consequence: The docs now describe behaviour the code no longer has. SKILL.md:237 says of a usage pause that 'a tick before that time exits without work', but a tick now asks the guard and starts work when it allows, and only a `rate_limit` marker makes a tick 'paused'. SKILL.md:51 says `runs/paused.json` is 'present while the pipeline is paused for usage', which presents the marker as an authority. The usage-guard paragraph in architecture.md (around 815-857) and the state table row for `usage-cache.json` (around 1028) do not mention the refresh lock, the `usage-cache.json.lock` file, the last good reading served to a process that finds the lock held, or the `abk.usage.cache` counters. The task list requires all of this (4.9), and AGENTS.md says docs describing code a change builds land with that change.
  Done when: 1. docs/architecture.md, usage-guard paragraph: say that every run (tick, pass round, gate, tracks, status) asks the usage module and the module alone decides whether to call. Say one process refreshes under a non-blocking lock on `usage-cache.json.lock`, any other asker is served the last good reading and does not call, and the file is written whole. Say the pause marker is a record, and only a `rate_limit` marker stops a pass or makes a tick 'paused', until its deadline, worked out again each round. Say a step that began under the threshold finishes and the next gate refuses. Name the `abk.usage.cache` counter with its `event` values hit/miss/expiry/wait.
2. docs/architecture.md, state table: add a row for the lock file.
3. docs/configuration.md: note that the cache time is shared through the lock, beside `usage_cache_minutes`.
4. SKILL.md: correct line 237 (a usage pause does not stop a tick: the next tick asks the guard again; only a model refusal's `rate_limit` pause holds starts until its deadline) and lines 51-52 to match.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:703 — A process that finds the refresh lock held returns `last_good()`, and `last_good()` drops the kept reading once it is older than `usage_fallback_minutes` (30 by default). The cache time adapts up to `usage_cache_max_minutes` (60), so at expiry the kept reading can already be older than the fallback age.
  Consequence: Example: the cache time has stretched to 40 minutes after refusals, and the kept reading is 40 minutes old. Two askers arrive at its expiry (the pass's round and a gate in a build thread, or two ticks). One takes the lock and calls. The other gets None from `read_live_usage`. `current_usage` then falls back to the editor's reading, or to None, and `may_start_unit(None)` refuses with 'usage is unknown' and writes a usage pause for UNKNOWN_RETRY. Before this change both askers would have called and both started. The spec scenario says 'the others are served the last good reading', and design.md says the waiter 'serves the last good reading'. It does not do that here.
  Done when: In the `not taken` branch, serve the kept reading whenever it exists and its window has not reset (for example `kept if kept is not None and not _past_reset(kept, now) else None`), labelled `cache` as now, and do not gate it on the fallback age. That age is about covering a failed call; here the call is being made. Add a test in tests/pipeline/test_usage_one_authority.py. Set it up with ttl (or `usage_cache_minutes`) at 40 and a kept reading 35 minutes old. Make the lock held by taking `try_file_lock` on `usage-cache.json.lock` in the test. Assert that `read_live_usage()` returns that reading with source `cache`, that no call is made, and that a `wait` is counted.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/usage_guard.py:793 — `held_usage` now filters the editor's reading through `_unspent`, but it returns the cache file's kept reading unfiltered, even after the reset of a window it describes.
  Consequence: The requirement 'A reading is not used past its window' covers a cached reading 'within the cache time, kept as the last good reading or taken from the editor'. With a kept reading of session 90% whose window reset ten minutes ago, `abk status` (`_status_reading`), `refreshed_usage` when the interval refuses a call, and the `RateLimited` branch of `build_unit` (cli/pipeline.py:2641) all still use it. Status shows 90% for a window that has reset, and the rate-limit pause takes a reset time already in the past. The editor's reading is dropped in the same situation, so `held_usage` applies the rule to one source and not the other.
  Done when: Make line 793 `_noted(_unspent(_kept_reading(_load_cache(_cache_file()))) or _unspent(read_cached_usage()))`. Add a test: `host.keep_reading` with a session reset 10 minutes ago plus a current editor reading whose window has not reset, then assert `held_usage()` returns the editor's reading (source `claude.json`). With no editor reading, assert it returns None.

Optional:
- [1.4] tests/cli/test_tick_scheduling.py:1829 — The deadline test asserts only that `later/1` started at some point. It never checks that the pass was held before the 0.5 s deadline.
  Consequence: On its own the test would pass if the pass ignored `rate_limit` markers entirely (`stopping = failed`). It would also pass if the round never saw the marker in force. `test_a_rate_limit_pause_still_stops_new_builds_for_the_pass` covers the stop, so this is not a gap in coverage, but this test does not show 'a pass stopped by a rate_limit pause' as its scenario says.
  Done when: Record when `later/1` is started (for example a script for it that notes `datetime.now(UTC)`), and assert that time is at or after the marker's `until`.
- [1.5] tests/pipeline/test_usage_one_authority.py:616 — The thread test asserts that every loser was served `("cache", 14)`. A loser that arrives after the winner has written the file and released the lock gets the fresh reading as `("cache", 33)`.
  Consequence: The test fails on a slow worker when one thread is scheduled more than CALL_SECONDS after the barrier. This is a flake risk, not a correctness gap.
  Done when: Assert as the process test does: exactly one call, one `("live", 33)` answer, and every other answer has source `cache` with a session in {14, 33}.

units.title: The environment's lock files are the pipeline's
units.feedback:
The new and touched tests pass locally (35 passed), and so does the scrub check. Four things block approval: the commit step compares against the wrong base for stacked units, the adopt path still commits through the old rules, task 1.7's docs update is missing, and one test has an assertion that is always true.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/wiring.py:2171 — The commit step decides whether the unit changed a dependency by comparing against the trunk (`local_ref(repo.default_branch)`), which `build_runner` fixes once. It does not compare against the unit's own base. The environment preparation (`nodes.py:808`, `self.ref(state)`) and the restack both use the unit's base.
  Consequence: Take unit B stacked on unit A's branch, where A bumped `manifest.toml` and committed the matching lock. If the sync rewrites the tracked lock while B is built (a newer tool reformats it), B's commit computes `merge-base(main, HEAD)`, which is before A's work. It sees the manifest as changed and commits the noise lock rewrite into B's diff. The spec says this lock must be restored, because B changed no dependency against the point its branch left its base. A rewrite in the other direction behaves the same way once the base moves onto a parent.
  Done when: Base the commit step's lock rule on the unit's current base, the same `local_ref(state.base or self.base, repo=...)` that `worktree_fault` uses. For example, the commit callable could take `base=` per call from the graph nodes' `r.commit(...)` sites, or the runner could resolve it. Add a test in `tests/pipeline/test_environment_locks.py` with a parent branch that changes the manifest and a child branch built on it. The test commits in the child with the lock rewritten and no manifest change, using the child's base. It asserts the lock is not in the commit and is back to the branch's version.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/attach.py:110 — `adopt` commits a unit's worktree with `build_commit(unit_id=..., fix=..., adopted_from=...)` and passes no `repo` or base. That path still runs a plain `git add -A`, so none of the new lock rules apply to it.
  Consequence: A unit's worktree in a repository that does not track its lock has the untracked lock its sync created. A person attaches and adopts their changes. The lock is swept into the adopted commit, which breaks the requirement that a lock the branch does not track is never committed. A tracked lock rewritten with no dependency change is committed the same way.
  Done when: Pass the unit's repository configuration (`inst.config.repos[unit.repo]` or its equivalent) and the unit's base into `build_commit` in `adopt`. Add a test that adopts over a worktree holding an untracked lock named in the lock inputs plus one other change, and asserts that only the other change is in the commit and the lock stays in the worktree.
- [1.3] docs/architecture.md:1160 — Task 1.7 asks for `docs/architecture.md` to be updated where it describes the dirty-worktree rule (around lines 1160–1172) and the environment sync (around lines 26–35). The branch does not touch `docs/` at all.
  Consequence: The architecture doc still says any uncommitted path holds the unit as `dirty_worktree`. That is now false for paths named in `environment.inputs.lock`, and the doc says nothing about the commit step restoring a lock or leaving one out, or about the restack restoring one. The tasks put this docs edit in the same change so the doc and the code land together.
  Done when: In the dirty-worktree section, say that paths named in the repository's `environment.inputs.lock` belong to the pipeline: they never hold a unit and are never listed as leftovers. In the environment section, add the commit rules: a tracked lock is committed when the unit changed a dependency input against its base, otherwise it is restored, and an untracked lock is never committed. Also note that a restack restores an unchanged tracked lock before it moves the branch.
- [1.4] tests/pipeline/test_environment_locks.py:206 — `assert local_ref("main") != "main" or True` is always true and checks nothing. The `local_ref` import exists only for this line.
  Consequence: It looks like a check of the restack's base, but it passes whatever the code does, and the next reader is left asking what it was meant to pin.
  Done when: Delete the line and the now-unused `local_ref` import.

Optional:
- [1.5] tests/pipeline/test_environment_locks.py:617 — The two-repository test and the no-environment test pass `locks=` straight to `workspaces.prepare_worktree`. Neither goes through `lock_paths(repo)` and `build_worktree(..., repo=config)`, so the claim that the lock comes from the configuration is never tested end to end, and neither is `lock_paths` itself (its path normalisation, and an empty result when there is no environment section).
  Consequence: If `build_worktree` or `lock_paths` derived the wrong paths for a repository with no environment section, or for a lock input written as `./deps.lock`, these tests would still pass.
  Done when: Drive these two cases through `build_worktree({...}, root=..., repo=repo_config(root, env_or_None))`. One case uses an environment with no lock entry, and one has a lock input written with a `./` prefix.

units.title: The environment is drafted through the toolchain profile
units.feedback:
The registry walk, the node draft and moving the Python detection into its profile are sound, and the 190 tests in tests/init, tests/profiles and the two guards pass. But group 3 is only partly built. Tasks 3.6, 3.7 and 3.8 are missing: these are the drift-checked draft for a repository with path sources, and the remedy added to the deprecation message. The committed fixture pins the very shape 3.7 replaces. The group's 'Done when' line says 'a repository with path sources gets a drift-checked draft that lists nothing outside it', so this is not a follow-up.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/profiles/python_uv.py:147 — Tasks 3.6–3.8 are not built. When the manifest has path sources, `detect_environment` still adds each path-source checkout's `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` to `inputs`, and keeps the plain import check. The deprecation message in `config.py`'s `EnvironmentInputs` validator was not extended either.
  Consequence: This breaks the spec requirement 'A drafted environment never lists a path outside the repository'. For a manifest with path sources, init should draft `check` as `[sh, -c, "uv lock --check && uv sync --check && <import check>"]` with inputs holding only the repository's own manifest and lock. Instead `abk init` writes `vendor/lib/pyproject.toml` and `vendor/lib/uv.lock` into inputs and no drift check. `tests/fixtures/init/python_environment.yaml` pins that wrong shape for both keys, and the 'The warning names the remedy' scenario is not met.
  Done when: Implement 3.7 in the Python profile. When `_path_sources(root)` is non-empty: `inputs.dependencies == ['pyproject.toml']`, `inputs.lock == ['uv.lock']` (when present), and `check == ['sh', '-c', 'uv lock --check && uv sync --check && uv run --no-sync python -c "import agent_build_kit"']` with framework, or ending in the plain `... -c pass` check without. The draft carries the explanatory comment the task asks for, wherever init writes it.

Implement 3.8: add 'use `check` to detect drift' to the existing deprecation message, keeping its current text, and update its test.

Add the 3.6 tests: no input leaves the repository; inputs are only the repository's own manifest and lock; the draft loads through `EnvironmentConfig.model_validate` with no deprecation warning (assert with `caplog` or `warnings`, whichever the validator uses); `check` differs from the plain check and holds `uv lock --check`, `uv sync --check` and the import check in that order; a node-shaped profile's draft is unchanged; the comment is present.

Update `docs/init.md` and `docs/configuration.md` per 3.8. Fold the drift check into the existing changelog bullet: 'A Python repository gets the section it always did' becomes false for one with path sources.
- [1.2] tests/init/test_environment_drafting.py:24 — The 3.1 pin uses `python_repo`, which has two path sources (`vendor/lib` and `../outside`). Task 3.1 asks to pin a repository with a manifest and a lock file and no path source, and no test covers that case.
  Consequence: The case the spec promises stays identical ('A Python repository is written as before', 'A repository without path sources') is not pinned. A regression in the no-path-source draft would pass unnoticed, and once 3.7 lands the current fixture keys are wrong.
  Done when: Add a fixture repository with only `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`, with `plain` and `framework` keys in `python_environment.yaml` pinning `sync: [uv, sync]`, the `-c pass` and `-c 'import agent_build_kit'` checks, `dependencies: [pyproject.toml]`, `lock: [uv.lock]`, and `artifacts: []`. Give the path-source repository its own expected entries under 3.6/3.7.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/profiles/base.py:31 — Task 3.4 says 'Add the optional hook to the profile protocol', but `ToolchainProfile` in base.py is unchanged. The hook exists only as a `getattr` in `profiles.detect_environment`, plus a row in docs/toolchain-profiles.md.
  Consequence: The protocol is where a profile author looks for the contract, and the type checker sees no signature for the hook. A profile whose hook has the wrong signature (no `framework` keyword, say) is accepted silently and fails at `abk init` time with a TypeError.
  Done when: Declare the hook in `profiles/base.py`, for example a `@runtime_checkable` `EnvironmentDrafting` Protocol with `detect_environment(self, root: Path, *, framework: bool) -> EnvironmentConfig | None` and a docstring saying it is optional and None means 'cannot say'. Have the walk in `profiles/__init__.py` select on it instead of a bare `getattr`. The existing hookless-profile test keeps passing.
- [1.4] tests/init/test_environment_drafting.py:70 — The `register` fixture does `monkeypatch.setattr(profiles, "_REGISTRY", {})`, which reaches a private name from a test.
  Consequence: This breaks the AGENTS.md convention 'Tests reach a public surface. A test imports no private name.' It also couples the test to the registry being a module-level dict called `_REGISTRY`.
  Done when: Give `profiles` a public way to register a profile temporarily and remove it, such as an `unregister(name)` beside `register`, or a `registered(profile)` context manager, documented in its docstring. Use it in the fixture so no test touches `_REGISTRY`.

Optional:
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/profiles/node_environment.py:53 — Task 3.4 says the argv lists are UNVERIFIED and must be confirmed against each manager's documentation, and nothing in the diff records that confirmation. For a `check` to be useful it must exit non-zero when dependencies are not installed. `npm ls` does, but it is not established that `pnpm ls --depth 0`, `yarn list --depth=0` or `yarn info --name-only` do: the last reads project metadata, not the install state. A modern-line yarn repository with no `packageManager` field (`yarn.lock` plus `.yarnrc.yml`) also gets the classic-line `yarn list`.
  Consequence: If a check passes on a fresh worktree with no `node_modules`, the tick's check-fail-then-sync loop never fires for that manager, and only an inputs hash change triggers a sync.
  Done when: Confirm each check's exit status with dependencies missing and record it in docs/toolchain-profiles.md, or in a comment beside `_check`. Replace any check that does not fail. Consider treating `.yarnrc.yml` as a sign of the modern line when `packageManager` is absent.

units.feedback:
Required:
- [2.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/environment.py:267 — This rework also changed `repo_artifacts`, which round 1 did not ask for and no test covers. It now passes `inst.checkouts.get(name)` as the root, so in a repository without dependency inputs the profile's created files (python-uv's lock file) count as artifacts in `attach.changes_of`, `attach.discard`, `serve/server.py:319` and `serve/chat.py:331`.
  Consequence: Before this commit, a person who ran discard on a unit in a python-uv repository with no environment section had the untracked lock file cleaned away, and the serve and chat views counted it as a changed file. Now discard keeps the file and the views stop counting it. The change's design.md says the human-driven discard in attach.py "is left that way: a person asked for it", so this contradicts a recorded decision. The AGENTS.md rule "a behaviour change lands with its failing test" is also broken: no test touches `repo_artifacts`, `changes_of` or `discard`, so the change could be dropped or broken without anything failing.
  Done when: Prefer reverting the line to `return artifact_patterns(inst.config.repos.get(name))` so attach and serve behave as before, which is what the design records. If the builder keeps the change instead, they must add a test under tests/pipeline/ with a fake profile from tests/created_files_fakes.py and a repo with no environment section. It asserts that `changes_of` leaves the untracked created file out and that `discard` keeps it. The design.md bullet on attach.py must then be revised in the planning repo to say so.

Optional:
- [2.2] tests/profiles/test_created_files_hook.py:10 — Both tests call `created_files` through `# type: ignore[attr-defined]`. They could assert `isinstance(profiles.get(...), CreatedFiles)` and call the hook through that type, which would also show that the built-in profiles satisfy the new protocol.
  Consequence: If either built-in profile's `created_files` signature drifted from the `CreatedFiles` protocol, pyrefly would not catch it here, and these tests could still pass.
  Done when: In each test, narrow with `assert isinstance(profile, CreatedFiles)` before the call and drop the type-ignore comments.

description.summary: A toolchain profile can now name the files its own commands create or rewrite in a worktree, such as an uncommitted lock file, and the pipeline treats them as its own instead of holding a unit for them or committing them.
changes: Adds an optional `CreatedFiles` protocol to profiles/base.py whose `created_files(repo)` hook returns repo-relative paths. A profile without the hook counts as naming none, and absolute paths, paths containing `..` and paths naming `.git` are dropped.
The python-uv profile names its lock file and the node-npm profile names none.

The worktree dirty check counts a profile's created files as lock files when the repository declares dependency inputs. Otherwise it counts them as untracked-only artifacts, so a unit is not held because a profile command rewrote a file.
The commit step unstages created files that are untracked, so the agent never commits a lock file the repository does not track.
The restack restores tracked created files only where the repository declares dependency inputs.
Human-driven discard and the serve and chat change views are unchanged: they still use only the configured artifact patterns.

description.summary: The tests prompt no longer pins functions that already exist, the authoring skill tells authors to describe behaviour rather than names, and the prompt-text helpers the tests used now live in one shared module.
changes: The tests-step prompt has a paragraph telling the agent not to pin, by a test or a stub, a function that already exists. Only the tests prompt carries it: the other build prompts and every continuation prompt do not.

description.summary: Adds acceptance tests on Claude Code for record-and-replay of a unit build: a live pass is promoted to cassettes, an unchanged rerun replays and is labelled, and an edited task sends only the changed calls live. changes: New e2e acceptance scenarios in tests/integration/test_replay_unit.py, tagged runtime_claude_code and excused in CLAUDE_ONLY_REASONS. In record mode a live pass becomes cassettes; an unchanged rerun replays its deterministic calls and is labelled as replayed; an edited task sends exactly the changed calls live.

The replay hit-rate report counts a recorded call as replayed only when a request asked for it and it was fresh enough to answer it. Recorded calls nobody asked for, and matches too old to answer, are left out.

The replay proxy outlives a long-running child: a request after the default limit would have fired is still answered, and when a limit ends the wait the child is gone before the proxy stops.

The inner unit build runs in a runtime_scratch Claude Code installation, is collected under the driver's command and carries the e2e marker. The docs gap list in agent-runtimes.md no longer lists the scenarios excused in CLAUDE_ONLY_REASONS.
