The planner is given the ceiling in its own terms, recent evidence and a split to make
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/planner.py:653 — _calibration_section only enforces SECTION_MAXIMUM by dropping examples. When the section is still over 2000 characters with no examples, the loop ends and the oversized text is returned anyway, so the maximum is not a fixed bound.
  Consequence: calibration_kinds_listed has no upper limit (Field(ge=1) only). With `calibration_kinds_listed: 25` and 25 calibrated kinds such as `repository-NN tier1`, the section is 2656 characters; I measured this with build_prompt on the branch. The spec says the added text SHALL be bounded by "a fixed maximum size", and docs/architecture.md now says "and at most 2000 characters". Both are false for that configuration, and the prompt grows with the number of kinds.
  Done when: After examples are down to 0, if the text is still over SECTION_MAXIMUM, drop listed kinds from the end (fewest samples first). Count each dropped kind into the existing "(N more kinds left out)" line, so the section never exceeds SECTION_MAXIMUM. Add a test in tests/pipeline/test_planner_calibration_prompt.py: set calibration_kinds_listed to 25 with 25 kinds above 1, and assert len(section) <= 2000, that the left-out line gives the true number left out, and that the kinds kept are the ones with the most samples.

Optional:
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:2439 — Examples are built with a separate store.all() call for every kind in `ratios`. Each call re-reads and re-parses units.json, and the ratios on the line above come from another read.
  Consequence: The design says the examples are computed once per round from the store in hand, and the comment above says the plan check, prompt and figures use one set. With K kinds that is K extra file reads, and a store written between reads would give examples from a different snapshot than the ratios.
  Done when: Read `units = store.all()` once before `ratios = calibrations(units)` and pass `units` to both calibrations and recent_examples. Optionally build examples only for kinds above 1.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/unit_size.py:137 — largest_raw uses float floor division, so a ratio that is not exact in binary can come out one below floor(limit / ratio). Its docstring claims more than the function gives.
  Consequence: largest_raw(110, 1.1) returns 99, but floor(110/1.1) is 100 and round(100*1.1)=110 passes the ceiling check. It is also only a lower bound against the round()-based check: for ceiling 750 and ratio 1.51, 497 also passes. So 'the largest raw estimate whose calibrated figure stays within limit' is not exact. The error is always on the safe side.
  Done when: Either compute it exactly, for example with a small epsilon or Fraction, or change the docstring to say it is floor(limit / ratio), the figure the spec defines.
- [1.4] CHANGELOG.md:258 — 'a rejection for size names that figure and how many groups to split by' reads as if the message gives a number of units to split into. It actually states how many groups the unit carries and says to split by group.
  Consequence: Someone using the tool expects the message to suggest a target split count, which it does not give.
  Done when: Reword to something like 'a rejection for size names that figure and how many groups the unit carries, and says to split it by group'.
- [1.5] tests/pipeline/test_planner_calibration_prompt.py:29 — The test sets its own MAXIMUM = 2000 instead of importing planner.SECTION_MAXIMUM, which is a public name.
  Consequence: Two copies of the bound must change together. If the constant changes, the test keeps checking the old figure.
  Done when: Import SECTION_MAXIMUM from agent_build_kit.pipeline.planner and assert against it.

description.summary: The planner now gets the unit-size ceiling in terms of its own raw estimates for each calibrated kind, plus recent merged examples, and a rejection for size tells it to split the unit by group.
changes: For each calibrated kind with a ratio above 1, the planning prompt lists the ratio, the sample count and the largest raw estimate (floor(ceiling / ratio)) a unit of that kind may carry.

Each listed kind shows its few most recent merged units with their estimated and landed lines. `limits.calibration_examples` and `limits.calibration_kinds_listed` control how many examples and kinds appear.
The calibration section stays within a fixed maximum of 2000 characters. Examples are removed first, then the kinds with the fewest samples, and a line says how many kinds were left out.
The text joining the ceiling and the calibration states the largest raw estimate of each listed kind.
When a unit is rejected for size, the message gives that figure and how many task groups the unit carries, and tells the planner to split it by group.
A plan round reads the unit store once and uses that one read for the plan check's ratios and the prompt's examples.

units.title: abk tags says what to pass when given nothing
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] tests/cli/test_tags_usage_error.py:61 — Task 1.3 asks for a test that `abk tags <change>` for a change with no tasks file still reports that file as missing. No test does this. Nothing in tests/ asserts the `no tasks.md for change ...` line, and the new file covers only the two refusals and the help text.
  Consequence: The new guard sits on the same `args.change` path that a missing change takes. A later edit could widen it, for example to refuse a change whose directory does not exist, or reorder it so a missing change is refused with exit 2 instead of reporting its missing tasks file with exit 1, and the suite would still pass. That breaks the spec scenario 'A change or `--all` alone … reports as before' and leaves the test task 1.3 lists unwritten.
  Done when: Add a test to tests/cli/test_tags_usage_error.py that calls `cli.cmd_tags(argparse.Namespace(change="absent", all=False), installation)` on an installation with no `absent` change. It should assert status 1, that stdout contains `no tasks.md for change 'absent'` and `1 problem(s) in absent`, and that stderr is empty. Optionally, beside it, add one case each for `--all` over the tagged `feature` (status 0, stdout has `feature: 1 task group(s), all tagged`) and for `change="feature"` alone (same line, status 0), so the file pins all four cases the design lists.

Optional:
- [1.2] tests/cli/test_tags_usage_error.py:30 — The two refusal tests build the Namespace by hand. They do not run `abk tags` through the parser, so they never show that bare `abk tags` and `abk tags feature --all` really parse to those namespaces and reach the guard.
  Consequence: Suppose the parser changed, for example `change` got a default of `""` or `--all` became a store_const. The hand-built namespaces would still pass while the real command line behaved differently.
  Done when: Run at least the neither case through `main(["--config", str(abk_yaml), "tags"])` (as tests/integration/test_init_end_to_end.py:98 does for `--all`), or through `build_parser().parse_args(["tags"])` fed to `cmd_tags`, and assert exit 2 and the stderr line.

description.summary: `abk tags` now refuses a call with no change and no `--all`, or with both, by printing one line saying what to pass and exiting 2, where it used to crash.
changes: `abk tags` with neither a change nor `--all` prints `abk tags: name a change, or pass --all for every change` on stderr and exits 2. It no longer fails with a traceback.
`abk tags <change> --all` prints `abk tags: give a change or --all, not both` on stderr and exits 2 without checking anything.
The `tags` help and description now say to name a change or pass `--all`, and the positional `change` argument has its own help text.

`abk tags <change>` and `abk tags --all` behave as before, including reporting a missing tasks.md with exit 1. New tests in tests/cli/test_tags_usage_error.py pin all four cases through the real parser.
The changelog has an Unreleased bullet for the change.

units.title: The acceptance agent gets a scratch home and the first step proves its session is listed
units.feedback:
This branch adds the helper, its tier-1 tests and a changelog bullet. The task group asks for more than that: the helper has to be wired into the acceptance fixtures (1.10), the precondition called in every acceptance test that resumes a session (1.11), and the variables documented (1.13). None of those is on the branch, so the group's 'Done when' is not met: the acceptance fixtures do not start the agent with a scratch home, and no resuming test fails at its first step. 1.14 (a live run) cannot be done offline. Say so in the PR description instead of leaving it out silently. 1.8 and 1.12 are optional and may stay undone.

Required:
- [1.1] tests/integration/test_acp_build_unit.py:1 — Task 1.10 is not done. No acceptance fixture uses `agent_home`. The module-scoped `scratch` fixtures in `tests/integration/test_acp_build_unit.py` and `tests/integration/test_graph_acp_unit.py` still build the environment for `abk tick` and `abk report` without `home.env`.
  Consequence: An installation that sets the three `verify.env` entries gets no scratch home in the tier-2 acceptance runs, so the agent still refuses its session store and the resume steps still fail. The spec requirement says the scratch home's variable SHALL be added to the environment of every process that may start the agent. Nothing on the branch does this.
  Done when: Add a module-scoped call `home = agent_home(tmp_path_factory)` in each `scratch` fixture, merge `**home.env` into the env dict passed to `abk tick` and `abk report`, and apply `home.env` to `os.environ` for the module (pytest.MonkeyPatch context) so `can_resume_session` sees it too. Where `tests/scratch_stack.py` exists, call it there as well.
- [1.2] tests/integration/test_graph_acp_unit.py:1 — Task 1.11 is not done. `assert_session_listed` is called nowhere outside its own unit test. No acceptance test that resumes a session (the chat turn on a build session, the adopt and commit flows, session reuse) checks the precondition after its first agent step.
  Consequence: A resuming acceptance test can still pass by falling back to a fresh prompt, or fail at its last step without saying why. That is the exact problem the design says the check exists to stop ('The check is skipped nowhere').
  Done when: In each acceptance test that later resumes a session, call `assert_session_listed(AcpRuntime(), <session id from the run's agent record>, <the step's cwd>)` right after the first agent step.
- [1.3] docs/agent-runtimes.md:1 — Task 1.13 is not done. `docs/agent-runtimes.md` does not document `<redacted>`, `<redacted>` or `<redacted>`, the bypass fallback, or the hazards.
  Consequence: The changelog sends readers to three `verify.env` entries that no user-facing doc explains. The task asks for them in the acceptance paragraph beside `<redacted>`.
  Done when: Add to that paragraph: the three variables (with `~` expansion and comma-separated plain file names), the bypass fallback and its cost, and the hazards (credentials rewritten through links, retention under pytest's tmp dir, 0700, a missing file shows up as the agent failing to start).
- [1.4] CHANGELOG.md:5 — The changelog bullet says the acceptance tests 'can now give it a scratch home … so an agent … still keeps the sessions a later step resumes'. On this branch no acceptance test uses the helper.
  Consequence: The claim is false for the code as it stands: setting the three entries changes nothing in any acceptance run.
  Done when: Once 1.10 and 1.11 land the bullet is true as written. It should also mention that a resuming test now fails at its first step, naming the variables to check.
- [1.5] tests/test_agent_home.py:91 — `test_the_real_home_is_never_the_scratch_home` passes for the wrong reason. It points `REAL_HOME` at `alias` (pointing to the empty `scratch` dir) but keeps `HOME_FILES=<redacted>` from `configured`. `_refuse_name` then fails with '<redacted> is listed … but is missing' before the same-directory check runs, and the bare `pytest.raises(AssertionError)` accepts that.
  Consequence: Deleting the check `fresh != real` in `agent_home` would leave this test green, so task 1.2's 'a real home that resolves to the scratch directory fails' is not pinned.
  Done when: Write the listed files into `scratch` before calling the helper (so the real home holds them), and assert the specific failure: `pytest.raises(AssertionError, match="is, or is inside, the real home")`. Add the same `match=` to `test_a_real_home_that_contains_the_scratch_home_is_refused`.
- [1.6] tests/test_agent_home.py:145 — In `test_a_directory_a_path_or_the_state_database_is_refused`, the separator cases `a/b` and `../<redacted>` name paths that do not exist (`real/a/b`, `tmp_path/<redacted>`), so the missing-file assertion would also reject them. The bare `pytest.raises(AssertionError)` cannot tell which check fired.
  Consequence: Removing the separator check from `_refuse_name` leaves the test green, so task 1.4's 'a name that has a separator is refused' is not pinned.
  Done when: Parametrize the expected message: 'not a plain file name' for `a/b` and `../<redacted>`, 'is a directory' for `subdir`, and 'looks like the agent's state database' for the three `state.db*` names. Assert it with `match=`. Optionally make `real/a/b` exist so only the separator check can refuse it.

Optional:
- [1.7] tests/agent_home.py:67 — `agent_home(tmp_path_factory: Any)` and `assert_session_listed(runtime: Any, ...)` take `Any`. A small Protocol (`mktemp(basename) -> Path`; `can_resume_session(session_id, cwd) -> bool`) or `pytest.TempPathFactory`/`AcpRuntime` would let pyrefly check the callers.
  Consequence: A caller passing the wrong object is only caught at runtime.
  Done when: Type the parameters with `pytest.TempPathFactory` (or a Protocol the test `_Factory` satisfies) and with a Protocol that has `can_resume_session`.

units.title: Record an edit to started groups without asking the planner

description.summary: When an edit to a change's tasks.md leaves no group for the planner to claim, plan_all now records the new hash without calling the planner, and refuses edits that would contradict units that have already started.
changes: plan_all skips the planner for a change when every group is taken, either by a started unit (in flight, failed, held, merged or satisfied) or by another change's planned unit. It records the edited tasks.md hash as planned and logs why. `abk replan` prints that nothing was asked of the planner.

An edit that changes the repo or tier tag of a group a started unit carries, its own or joined, is refused with no planner call and no record, and with a report naming the unit and the group. The flag is also compared when the stored flag is non-empty. The report suggests `abk requeue --restart` only for failed or held units.
An edit that deletes or renumbers a group a started unit carries is refused with no planner call, and the log names the missing group.
On the record-only path, an unstarted unit that carries one of the change's groups gets its priority recomputed from the edited tasks.md. The planning path uses the same shared helpers to do this.
A tick no longer asks the planner, or checks the usage limit for it, about a change whose groups are all taken.
A requeued failed or held unit keeps its groups, repo and tier; the next plan is skipped, and the unit reads the edited tasks.md when it builds.

units.title: Tell the planner which groups are taken and keep why a plan was refused

description.summary: The planner is told which task groups started units already build, and a refused plan keeps why it was refused and which unit ids the planner returned.
changes: The change text given to the planner marks each group heading that a started unit builds with `(built by <unit id>)`, and the prompt says never to claim those groups. Headings are matched with the same `GROUP_NUMBER` grammar the validator uses, so extra whitespace after `##` is handled too.

Every PlannerError now carries the unit ids read from the planner's reply, including ids read before a refusal partway through reading the units (unknown repo, unknown tier, duplicate id, missing fields).
A refused plan's record in the plan store keeps `units` and `reason` for every planner refusal, including GroupTooLarge, which spends every attempt at once. A later successful plan clears them.
A bare `abk replan` listing shows the stored refusal reason beside the plan state (`failing n/m` or `given up`), so a person can see which group to split or what the planner got wrong.
The docs (architecture, cli) and the changelog describe the built-group marking and the kept refusal reason.

units.title: Make the rate-limit pause deadline test deterministic
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] tests/factories.py:176 — The diagnosis is correct. The old test wrote the marker in place, so a round's unlocked `is_paused` could read a truncated file as 'not paused' and submit later/1 early. But the fix adds `write_rate_limit_marker`, a test-side second copy of `pause.pause_until`'s marker format (the until/reason/kind/at keys) and its write-aside-and-rename (src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/pause.py:118-137). The copy also drops the real one's cleanup of the partial file on failure. The new file tests/cli/test_pause_marker_written_whole.py exists only to pin that copy, and its first test checks how the copy is written (no `Path.write_text` on the marker), not what it does. A helper that wrote in place through `open()` would still pass it.
  Consequence: Two copies of the marker's on-disk shape and its whole-write must now change together. A change to the format or write in pause.py leaves the scheduling test exercising a marker the pipeline never writes. The prior-art rule makes a duplicate the change introduces a required finding. The atomicity this test needs is already pinned for the real writer at tests/pipeline/test_pause.py:151-169.
  Done when: Delete `write_rate_limit_marker` from tests/factories.py, along with its `__all__` entry and the `json`, `os`, `UTC` and `datetime` imports it added. Delete tests/cli/test_pause_marker_written_whole.py. In `test_a_rate_limit_pause_ends_at_its_deadline_within_the_pass`, write the pause with the real writer and drop only the grace: `monkeypatch.setattr(pause, "resume_deadline", lambda until, **_: until)`, then in `refused_by_the_model` call `pause.pause_until(ends[0], reason="the model refused", marker=marker, kind="rate_limit")`. `pause_until` looks up `resume_deadline` through the module, so the patch takes effect. Patch `resume_deadline`, not `RESUME_GRACE`: `resume_deadline` turns an `until` that a descheduled thread has already passed into now+30min, which would bring back a load-dependent failure. Update the comment above the write to say the real writer is used with the grace removed. The test then still passes under `poe test` and the repeat check, and `git grep write_rate_limit_marker` finds nothing.

Optional:
- [1.2] tests/cli/test_tick_scheduling.py:1845 — The test still sets a 0.5 s wall-clock deadline and waits through `eventually` and `REFRESH_SECONDS` polling. The design says the fix leaves nothing to wait on by the clock. With a whole marker the only remaining failure is not starting later/1 within WAIT=30 s, so this is safe in practice, but it is not clock-free.
  Consequence: None observed: with the torn read gone, load can only delay later/1, and a delayed start still satisfies `submitted[0] >= ends[0]`.
  Done when: Optionally inject the clock `is_paused` reads, or let the deadline be passed by a step the test drives, so the test does not sleep through the 0.5 s.

description.summary: Makes the rate-limit pause deadline scheduling test deterministic by writing its pause through the real pause writer instead of overwriting the marker in place.
changes: `test_a_rate_limit_pause_ends_at_its_deadline_within_the_pass` records its pause with `pause.pause_until`. The marker is written aside and renamed into place, so a round's unlocked `is_paused` can no longer read a half-written file as 'not paused' and start later/1 early.

The test patches `pause.resume_deadline` to return `until` unchanged. This removes only the resume grace, so the 0.5 s pause ends within the test, and an `until` that has already passed is not turned into the default retry.
The test file's unused `json` import is removed.

units.title: Wait for the tier 2 lock without a deadline, and say who holds it
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/tier2.py:112 — The new `process_alive` is a copy of `_process_alive` in src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/workspaces.py:54. Both have the same body: `os.kill(pid, 0)`, with ProcessLookupError meaning dead and PermissionError meaning alive.
  Consequence: The pipeline now has two definitions of 'is this recorded process still alive', one for branch locks and one for the tier 2 lock. A fix to one, such as handling a zombie or a pid of 0 or below, has to be repeated in the other or the two lock kinds will disagree about the same pid. The review rules say a duplicate the change introduces must be removed.
  Done when: Keep one public function with a docstring and have both callers use it. Either `workspaces.lock_holder_gone` and line 100 call `tier2.process_alive`, or the function moves to a small shared module that both import. `workspaces._process_alive` is deleted. The existing workspaces tests and the new tier 2 tests still pass.
- [1.2] tests/tier2_lock_fakes.py:701 — `SleepingTime` and `Foreign` repeat the fakes already in tests/pipeline/test_tier2_lock_wait_setting.py:35-66. `SleepingTime` copies `WaitClock` (monotonic, a sleep that moves the clock, strftime) and `Foreign` copies `held` (an `flock` taken on another open of the lock file). Both copies keep a `strftime` that nothing calls now, because `stack_lock` writes `spans.clock.now().isoformat()` and no longer uses `time.strftime`.
  Consequence: Two fake `time` modules and two 'lock held by someone else' helpers now cover the same `stack_lock`. The next change to how `stack_lock` reads time, for example the sleep or clock it calls, has to update both or one test file stops faking what the code reads.
  Done when: Make test_tier2_lock_wait_setting.py use `tests.tier2_lock_fakes` (`install_clock` for its `clock` fixture and `Foreign`, or a context-manager wrapper over it, for `held`). Delete `WaitClock` and `held` there. Remove the dead `strftime` from `SleepingTime`. The setting tests pass unchanged in what they assert.
- [1.3] tests/pipeline/test_tier2_lock_holds_the_unit.py:505 — The test for task 1.3 only checks that each wait line contains the text 'held for'. It never checks the age itself. The three lines are told apart only by their 'waited' part, so the test still passes if `_held_for` always returns 0 or ignores the record's `since`.
  Consequence: Task 1.3 and the spec scenario 'The wait is logged' require the log to say how long the holder has held the lock. Logging 'held for 0m 0s' on every line, for example after a timezone or parse error that falls back to 0.0, would pass this test.
  Done when: Assert the ages from the fake clock. With `Foreign(..., age=40*60)` and lines at 0, 300 and 600 seconds, the lines contain 'held for 40m 0s', 'held for 45m 0s' and 'held for 50m 0s' in that order. Also assert each line's waited part: '0m 0s', '5m 0s', '10m 0s'.

Optional:
- [1.4] tests/tier2_lock_fakes.py:736 — `dead_pid()` relies on the pid of a child that has exited not being reused before the test reads it. Under a heavy parallel suite another process can be given that pid, and the record then looks alive.
  Consequence: This is rare. If the pid is reused, test_a_free_lock_with_a_dead_holders_record_is_logged_stale_and_overwritten finds no stale line, and test_a_held_lock_whose_recorded_process_is_gone_is_not_broken finds no 'gone' line. Both fail only under load.
  Done when: Make liveness deterministic in these tests. Either monkeypatch the shared liveness function so it reports the chosen pid as dead, or use a pid above /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max.
- [1.5] tests/pipeline/test_tier2_lock_holds_the_unit.py:429 — `Ran.at` is set to None and never read.
  Consequence: The next reader may think timing is being captured. This is dead code only.
  Done when: Remove the attribute.

description.summary: A unit waiting for the tier 2 lock now waits for as long as the holder runs instead of timing out. The wait is logged with who holds the lock and for how long, and it is recorded as a span.
changes: The tier 2 step's `stack_lock` waits without a deadline when given no timeout. A unit is no longer failed for queueing behind another tier 2 run.
While held, the lock file holds a JSON record of the holder: its unit, process id and start time. The file is emptied on release.

A waiting unit logs a line when the wait begins and every five minutes. The line names the holding unit, how long it has held the lock and how long this unit has waited, and says when the recorded holder's process is gone but the lock is still held.
When a unit takes the lock and finds a record left by a process that no longer exists, it reports the record as stale and overwrites it. A lock that is still held is never broken.
A wait that ends is recorded as one `tier2_lock` span. `limits.tier2_lock_wait_seconds` now bounds only post-merge verification, which writes `verify <change>` as the holder.
Branch locks and the tier 2 lock share one `workspaces.process_alive` check for whether a recorded process is still alive.

units.title: Show the holder and its age in abk status

description.summary: `abk status` now shows who holds the tier 2 lock and for how long, by briefly probing the lock without ever changing it, and every caller gets the lock's path from one accessor.
changes: `abk status` prints `tier 2: held by <unit> for <age> (since <time>)` while the tier 2 lock is held. It works the age out from the record the holder wrote into the lock file.

A record left on a free lock is shown as a stale record, not as a holder. A held lock whose recorded process is gone is shown as held, with a note that the process is gone. A free lock with no record, or no lock file, prints no tier 2 line.

The probe takes a shared, non-blocking `flock` on a separate open and releases it at once, so it never creates, changes or keeps holding the lock file, and a unit asking for the lock right afterwards gets it.
The `runs/tier2.lock` path now comes from one `Installation.tier2_lock` property, which the tier 2 runner, post-merge verification and the status line all use.
`docs/cli.md`, `docs/architecture.md` and the existing changelog bullet for the tier 2 lock describe the new status line.

units.title: Split a tier 2 test's time by agent role, checks and the rest
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] tests/integration/test_acp_build_unit.py:112 — Nothing requests the new `scratch_ledger` fixture. Every test in the module takes `built` (built from `scratch`), and no test, fixture or autouse takes `scratch_ledger`. So it is never in a test's fixture closure, `item.funcargs` never holds it, and `tests/time_split.py::_ledger` returns None for every live test.
  Consequence: On a real `pytest -m local_stack` run no test prints an `ABK-TIME` line, so the tier 2 result shows a dash in Agent/Checks/Other for every entry. Group 2's done-when ("a tier 2 test using the scratch installation prints, per phase, its agent time by role, checks time and remainder") and task 2.5 ("the `scratch_ledger` fixture for the live scratch-installation tests") are not met. The pytester tests pass because their generated tests request the fixture directly, so they don't show the gap.
  Done when: Put `scratch_ledger` in the closure of every test in the module. The simplest fix is to have `built` take it as a parameter (`def built(scratch: Scratch, scratch_ledger: Path)`). Module-level `autouse=True` on `scratch_ledger` also works. Either way the tick in `built`'s setup lands in the first test's setup line, and later tests get their own lines. A unit-level check (for example, collect the module with `--collect-only` and assert that every item's `fixturenames` contains `scratch_ledger`) keeps it wired, since the live run isn't part of the default suite.

description.summary: Tier 2 tests that drive a scratch installation now print, per test and phase, how their wall time splits into agent time by role, check commands and the remainder. The tier 2 result shows that split beside each entry.
changes: A pytest plugin (tests/time_split.py) reads the scratch installation's usage ledger around each setup, call and teardown phase. At session end it prints one `ABK-TIME` JSON line per phase with agent milliseconds and calls by role, `checks_ms`, `other_ms` (never negative) and an `overlap` flag.

units.title: The probe, the known-agent table and the runtime hooks

description.summary: Runtimes can now say which agents are installed on this machine, what they ask during setup, and which models they offer, all without sending the agent a prompt. A runtime entry in abk.yaml can also record that its policy check was skipped.
changes: A table of the protocol agents abk knows how to start, in `runtimes/known_agents.py`, which does not import the protocol library. A probe checks each one: is the program on the path, is the extra installed, and for agents whose start flag varies by version, which spelling `--help` shows (five-second limit). Each comes back usable, or unusable with the reason.

`runtimes.candidates(which, run)` collects what every registered runtime finds on this machine. Where the protocol extra is missing, the known agents are still listed, each unusable with a reason naming the extra.

Optional runtime hooks `detect`, `setup_questions` and `list_models`, with `candidates_of`, `questions_of` and `models_of` helpers, plus the `Candidate`, `Question` and `ModelList` models. Claude Code reports `claude` on the path and its documented model aliases. The protocol runtime asks for its start command and reads the models the agent advertises when a session opens in a temporary directory; it sends no prompt and gives up after 20 seconds.
`runtimes.<name>.policy: unchecked` is accepted in abk.yaml, and only that value. A file without the key loads as before. Documented in the abk-config skill, docs/configuration.md and the changelog.
The host-probe aliases `Which` and `Run` now live only in `runtimes/base.py`, and `abk doctor` imports them from there.

units.title: abk init asks which runtime and records the choice

description.summary: `abk init` asks which agent runtime to use, records the choice and its start command in abk.yaml, and runs research and propose on that runtime.
changes: Before research and propose run, init lists the agent runtimes this machine can run, usable ones first and each unusable one with its reason, plus a configure-your-own option. --runtime and --agent-command answer it ahead of time, and with --yes init picks the only usable runtime or exits 2 without writing anything.

A kept abk.yaml's runtime changes only after you confirm, or with --force. When a kept file stays as it is but --agent-command was given, init prints that the runtime and command were left as they are.

Recording an answer into abk.yaml replaces a runtime's start command (an argv) outright, while other lists such as names still only gain what they lack. Choice.applied_to and record_in_file share this rule.
A runtime question's own default is used whenever no candidate supplies a command, so --yes with a runtime whose program is missing fails naming the missing program.
A usable runtime is offered as a fallback only when it is not already configured under runtimes:, with a kept file's contents laid over the drafted config.

claude_call.runtime_for decides which runtime a step runs on: a stand-in RunClaude replaces a Claude Code runtime that was handed in, and any other runtime is used as given, so cli/init.py no longer names the Claude Code class.

units.title: Setup questions and models, the other routes and the confirmation

description.summary: `abk init` now asks about a chosen agent's prerequisites and which models to use (without ever calling a model), accepts every answer non-interactively through `--set` and `--runtime-config`, and writes the runtime choice only after showing it and getting a yes.

A models question follows the runtime's setup questions. Claude Code offers a 1/2/3 menu over its documented aliases (defaults, per role, typed). A protocol agent's advertised models are listed with its current one first and marked default. An agent that lists none says so and takes typed names. The choice is written under `models:`.

New repeatable `--set key=value` and `--runtime-config FILE` give any answer by its abk.yaml key. They preset the matching setup questions, are checked by the same validators, and an unknown key exits 2 naming it, also when abk.yaml is kept.

Before writing, interactive init prints the abk.yaml fragment it will record and asks `write it and proceed? [Y/n]`. A no prints `nothing written` and exits 1 with no file changed. The runtime choice now runs before `--dry-run`, so a dry run prints it too.
The y/yes reply checks across init are folded into one `yes()` helper with an optional Enter default.
docs/cli.md, docs/init.md (a new 'Choose the runtime' step), docs/agent-runtimes.md ('Adding an agent' and what the models question can know) and the changelog describe the new flow.

units.title: The server starts its agents in the environment it is given

description.summary: Code that starts the web UI's server can now give a complete environment for the agents the server starts, so a test's own variables no longer reach those agents; `abk serve` does not pass one and works as before.
