units.title: abk usage replay re-runs the estimator over the recorded history
units.feedback:
The replay works and all 11 of its tests pass (`pytest tests/cli/test_usage_replay.py`: 11 passed). The walk-forward test tells apart calibrating from earlier gaps only, from all gaps, and from earlier gaps plus the current one. The fixtures write real `UsageCall` and `UsageRecord` shapes through the normal writers. The abk-pipeline skill lists no usage commands, so it needs no change. Four things need fixing before approval: the replay keeps its own copy of the guard's estimate and refusal rule, it re-implements an existing reader of the calls file, the tests add a second copy of an existing fixture helper, and the replay prints less than the design asks for.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/cli/usage_cmd.py:314 — The replay writes out the guard's estimate (`pair.before + allowance * pair.units`) and refusal rule (`estimate + margin < threshold`) again instead of using the guard's own `WindowEstimate` (`pipeline/usage_guard.py:1030-1046`, whose `estimate` and `ample` hold exactly these rules). Task 2.5 says the command is built on the estimate of group 1.
  Consequence: There are now two copies of the rule that decides a pause. If the guard's rule changes (`<` becomes `<=`, or `estimate` gains a term), the replay keeps judging gaps by the old rule. Its false-pause and false-allow counts would then describe a guard that no longer exists, which defeats the command's purpose: measuring what the guard would have done.
  Done when: Build `WindowEstimate(name=window, read_pct=pair.before, spent_pct=allowance * pair.units, threshold=threshold, margin=margin)` for each gap and take `estimate` and `ample` from it. `cmd_usage_replay` keeps no arithmetic or comparison of its own for these two. The existing count tests pass unchanged.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/cli/usage_cmd.py:292 — `try: parse_calls((inst.state_dir / CALLS_NAME).read_text()) except FileNotFoundError: calls = []` re-implements `read_calls` in `pipeline/usage_calls.py:85`. That function already returns [] when the file cannot be read and is what `_estimates` uses.
  Consequence: This is a second copy of how the calls record is read, so the two must change together. It is also weaker than the original: a calls file that exists but cannot be read (for example, a permission error) makes the replay crash with a traceback instead of treating it as having no readings. A read-only diagnostic command should not crash that way.
  Done when: Use `calls = read_calls(inst.state_dir / CALLS_NAME)` and drop the `parse_calls` import if nothing else in the module uses it. `refresh_allowances` stays as it is, because it deliberately leaves the stored result alone on errors other than a missing file.
- [1.3] tests/usage_allowance_records.py:52 — The test commit adds `gaps`, which repeats the loop of `segments` (lines 39-49) line for line. The only difference is that `segments` fixes the earlier figure at 10 and takes a `gap` argument.
  Consequence: There are now two fixture builders with the same layout: readings `STEP` apart, a pair `GAP` apart, and spend at the midpoint. A change to the layout must be made in both. If one is missed, the replay tests and the calibration tests quietly fixture different record shapes.
  Done when: Keep one loop. Give `gaps` a `gap: timedelta = GAP` keyword and have `segments` return `gaps(window, [(10, 10 + gain, units) for gain, units in spent], start=start, gap=gap)`, or the reverse. The tests of both units still pass.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/cli/usage_cmd.py:326 — The design's output for `abk usage replay` lists the mean overshoot as one of the per-window figures: estimate minus actual, averaged over the gaps where the estimate was above the actual, 'so a person sees the cost of caution'. It also says the output ends with the `usage allowances:` line the settings would give today, and says when there are too few pairs to judge. The command prints only the four counts and the threshold line.
  Consequence: The overshoot is the headline figure of the analysis this command replaces: the weekly allowance overshot by 4.3 points on average, which is what caused the false pause. Without it, a person comparing `--weekly-allowance 2` with `1` sees no false pauses on a quiet record and cannot see how much caution each setting costs. The CHANGELOG and docs/cli.md describe a command that makes the by-hand analysis repeatable, and they are true only in part.
  Done when: End each window's counts line with `mean overshoot <x>` (one decimal; 0 or `none` when no gap overshot). After both windows, print the line `allowances_line(calibrated_allowances(calls, ledger, limits=limits, now=now), limits)` gives, and when a window has fewer than `usage_allowance_min_pairs` usable gaps, say there is not enough to judge. Add a test: in the five-gap weekly fixture the overshoots are 1 and 1, so the mean overshoot is 1.0. Add another test that the last line starts with `usage allowances:`. Update the docs/cli.md section to match.

Optional:
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/cli/usage_cmd.py:1 — The module docstring ('one-time repairs of the usage ledger') and the parser help `repairs of the usage ledger` (line 341) no longer describe `abk usage`, which now also holds a permanent, read-only replay.
  Consequence: `abk usage --help` describes the group as ledger repairs, which hides the replay and suggests it writes.
  Done when: Reword both, for example 'the usage ledger and readings: a one-time cost backfill and a read-only replay of the estimate'.
- [1.6] src/agent_build_kit/cli/usage_cmd.py:353 — `--session-allowance`, `--weekly-allowance` and `--margin` accept negative numbers, which the configuration refuses for the same settings.
  Consequence: `--margin -3` runs and prints counts for a setting no installation could load.
  Done when: Use a non-negative int type for all three that names the value when it refuses one, and add `help=` text to each, as `--since` has.
- [1.7] src/agent_build_kit/cli/usage_cmd.py:322 — A row does not print the allowance it used. The design's row also has the gap length and the difference (actual minus estimate).
  Consequence: In a walk-forward run, a person cannot see where calibration took over from the default without dividing estimate minus before by units.
  Done when: Add `allowance=<n>` (and optionally `gap=` and `diff=`) to each row.

description.summary: Adds `abk usage replay`, a read-only command that re-runs the usage guard's estimate over the recorded readings and ledger, so a person can see how a given allowance and margin would have judged each past gap.
changes: `abk usage replay` prints one row per usable gap: the figures before and after, the units spent, the allowance used, the estimate, and actual minus estimate. Each gap's allowance is the one calibration would have given from the earlier gaps only.

For each window it prints the number of underestimates, misses beyond the margin, false pauses and false allows, plus the mean overshoot (the cost of caution). A window with too few gaps says there is not enough to judge.
The estimate and the pause rule come from the guard's own `WindowEstimate`, so the replay judges gaps exactly as the guard would.

`--since`, `--session-allowance`, `--weekly-allowance` and `--margin` let a person try other settings. Negative values are refused with the value named. The output ends with the `usage allowances:` line today's settings give.
The command writes nothing and calls neither the model nor the usage endpoint. docs/cli.md and the `abk usage` help describe it.

units.title: A unit waits for all but one unrelated open parent
units.feedback:
Spec issue for a person, not something to send back to the builder: the planner gives the group after an `Independent:` group only one parent, the last group before the independent one (units.py:228 `depends_on = (tail,)`, and the planner prompt at planner.py:527 says the same). So the spec's second warning shape, "an `Independent:` group followed by a later group of its repo", describes a unit that never gets two open parents. The builder followed the spec, so it is reported as an optional finding below. The change's spec and design should drop that shape, or restate it as the acceptance/narrow case.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/units.py:423 — `base_of` now uses the new rule (deepest unrelated open parent, ties to the later in plan order) for units that have already started too, so a started unit's base can move to a different sibling with nothing merging.
  Consequence: The spec says a started unit SHALL keep the branch it started on and SHALL NOT be moved off it (task 1.6: it 'keeps its base_of'). I checked on this branch. A started unit (branch `spec/kid/1`) with `depends_on=("p2/1","p1/1")`, both siblings in review: the old `candidates[-1]` gave `spec/p1/1`, the new code gives `spec/p2/1`. With `depends_on=("p1/1","p2/1")` where p1 sits on an open root: the old code gave `spec/p2/1`, the new gives `spec/p1/1`. A unit running when this lands therefore trips `wiring.build_base_moved` (wiring.py:2695, `Cause.BASE_CHANGED`, 'its base moved from … to …'). Its build stops and a later restack moves it onto the other sibling. Depth also changes as roots merge, so even after the upgrade a started unit's base can flip between siblings without either of them merging. `test_a_started_unit_keeps_the_base_it_has_today` passes only because its `depends_on` order happens to match plan order, and its docstring ('the last open dependency in the order listed') describes code that no longer exists. The changelog line 'Started units are untouched' is false for these cases.
  Done when: In `base_of` (or `_stack_base`), when `_worked_on(unit)` is true, return the old choice: the last same-repo `IN_REVIEW` dependency in `through_satisfied` order. Use the new maximal/deepest choice only for a unit that has not started. Parametrize `test_a_started_unit_keeps_the_base_it_has_today` with two more cases, `depends_on=("p2/1","p1/1")` (expects `spec/p1/1`) and a deeper p1 listed first with `depends_on=("p1/1","p2/1")` (expects `spec/p2/1`), each asserting the base the old rule gave. Update the `base_of` docstring to say a started unit keeps the last-listed choice.
- [1.2] tests/pipeline/test_open_parents.py:847 — Task 1.2 asks for the closed-sibling case, but the readiness test is parametrized only over MERGED and SATISFIED, and docs/unit-graph.md says the unit waits for the rest 'to merge, close or land'.
  Consequence: When a sibling is CLOSED, `waiting_on` still returns it through the existing same-repo rule (`state not in REVIEWED`). I checked: p1 closed, p2 in review, the never-started kid gives `waiting_on` = `['p1/1']`, so the kid is not ready. The doc sentence 'waits for the rest to merge, close or land' tells a reader that closing a sibling releases the unit, and it does not. No test pins either answer.
  Done when: Add the CLOSED case beside MERGED/SATISFIED. It should assert that the second-open-parent wait ends (`unrelated` == ["p2/1"], and `second_parent_wait` is "" through the status/diagram) and that the kid still waits for the closed parent through the ordinary dependency rule, as it did before this change. Change docs/unit-graph.md's 'to merge, close or land' to 'to merge or land (a closed parent still holds it as any closed dependency does)'. Also note the gap from the spec's 'is closed → ready' scenario in the PR, so the spec can be corrected. Changing `waiting_on` for closed dependencies is outside this change.

Optional:
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/work_graph.py:561 — `_group_parents` claims to chain groups 'as the planner chains them' but gives the group after an `Independent:` group both the independent group and the one before it. The planner gives it only the last group before the independent one. This is a third copy of the group-edge rule, after `units.plan_units` and `cycles.needs_cycle`, and it disagrees with both.
  Consequence: For groups `1, 2 (Independent:), 3` in one repo, `abk tags` warns that group 3's unit 'can wait for a second open parent'. Under plan_units, unit 3 depends only on unit 1, so the warning is a false positive and the abk-authoring skill tells the author to reorder for nothing. The spec asks for this shape, so the fix needs the spec revised first (see feedback).
  Done when: Once the spec is settled: the group after an `Independent:` group gets only the last non-independent group as its parent, matching units.py:222-228, with the edge rule kept in one place shared with `plan_units`. Rewrite or remove the 'Independent: followed by a later group' shape and its test to match.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/work_graph.py:584 — `_reaches` (work_graph.py) and `_builds_on` (units.py) are the same transitive-closure walk with a seen set, written twice over different maps.
  Consequence: The two walks have to change together if the cycle handling changes. Minor.
  Done when: Optionally use one small helper that takes a successor function.

description.summary: A planned unit that has never started and has two or more unrelated open parents in its own repo now builds on the deepest of them and waits for the others to merge, instead of stacking on whichever dependency happens to be listed last.
changes: A never-started unit's base is its deepest unrelated open same-repo parent. A tie goes to the later one in plan order, and the newest unit of a chain wins whatever order `depends_on` lists it in.
Such a unit is not ready while any other unrelated open parent is unmerged. `abk status` shows 'waiting for <parent> to merge (second open parent)' and the graph draws the unit blocked.
A unit that has already started keeps the base it had before: the last open same-repo dependency in the order listed. It is never held by the new rule, so no running build has its base moved.
A closed parent ends the second-parent wait, but it still holds the unit through the ordinary closed-dependency rule.

`abk tags` and `abk check` warn about task-group shapes that produce a unit with two unrelated open parents. A shared `reachable` walk in units.py now serves both the unit graph and this group-graph check.
docs/unit-graph.md and the changelog describe the rule.

units.title: Hold the repo's turn per phase of a restack; temporary worktree for units with none
units.feedback:
Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:982 — In a run, a branch that moves a second time while the resolver works fails the unit. Task 1.4 says it should be held `planned` with `restack_deferred`.
  Consequence: `build_restack_onto` (wiring.py:2336) wraps the move in `retried_once`, but nothing on the in-run path catches the second `BranchMoved`. It reaches `prepare`'s generic `except Exception` (nodes.py:982-991), which calls `self.stop(why)`. `after_prepare` then routes to `Node.FAILED`, and `failed` records `Cause.FAILED`. So a unit whose branch was moved twice by another writer during the conflict resolution is failed, when it should be left `planned` with cause `restack_deferred` and a note naming the branch and both heads. The CHANGELOG bullet ('then the unit is left planned with the heads named') is false for this path. Only the handler path catches `BranchMoved`.
  Done when: In `prepare`, add `except BranchMoved as error:` before the generic `except Exception`. It returns `self.hold(PLANNED, note, detail, cause=Cause.RESTACK_DEFERRED)`, where the note names `error.branch`, `error.expected[:12]` and `error.found[:12]`. It must not go through `self.rebase()`, so the once-per-run hold is not consumed. Add a test (for example in tests/graph/) that drives `prepare` with a `restack_onto` raising `BranchMoved` twice, or a resolver that moves the ref on both attempts. It asserts the unit is stored `planned`, with cause `restack_deferred`, the branch and both heads in the note, nothing pushed, and the run's once-per-run restack flag (`state.restack`/`rebased`) unchanged.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/events.py:1604 — When the unit has no worktree, the handler now runs tier 1 in the operator's checkout, which is no longer on the moved branch, and then pushes.
  Consequence: `cwd = worktree if worktree.exists() else repo` (events.py:1413) is still used for tier 1. Before this change, the rebase in `repo` checked the branch out there, so tier 1 at `cwd=repo` tested the moved branch. Now the move happens in a temporary worktree that is removed in `move_in_temporary_worktree`'s `finally`, and `repo` stays on whatever branch and tree the operator has. Example: a child with no worktree, an approved head, and a clean move whose diff is unchanged (`unchanged` true). Tier 1 runs against the operator's checkout, not the moved branch, and on a pass `push` sends the moved head with checks that never ran on it. That breaks the order the docstring calls 'the guarantee' (checks run on the rebased head before the push). No test reaches this path: the `Rig` child is never approved, so every test ends at `planned` before tier 1.
  Done when: When the unit has no worktree, tier 1 must run on a checkout at the moved head. Either keep the temporary tree until tier 1 has run (remove it under the turn afterwards), or make a detached temporary tree at `moved.sha` for tier 1. `tier1_of` already recognises a path under `worktree_root/<repo>/`. Add a test with a `Rig`-like handler: the child is approved at its head, has no worktree, and the move is clean. The repo's checkout is on `main` with an edit. The fake `tier1` records `cwd` and `git rev-parse HEAD` there. Assert the HEAD it saw equals the branch's new head, that `cwd` is not the repo's checkout, and that the temporary tree is gone afterwards.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/restack.py:352 — In detached mode, `started` is read from the branch ref in a later turn than the one that created the temporary tree. The compare-and-swap can therefore land a rebase of an older head over commits added in between.
  Consequence: `move_in_temporary_worktree` creates the tree at `_branch_head(repo, branch)` in one turn (line ~503), then releases the turn. `move_branch_onto` then reads `started = _branch_head(repo, branch)` in a new turn and rebases the tree's detached HEAD. Suppose another writer moves the branch from H0 to H1 between those two turns. The tree rebases H0, `started` is H1, the phase-3 check `found == started` passes (both H1), and `update-ref refs/heads/<branch> <rebased H0> H1` succeeds. The branch silently loses the commits in H1. This is the lost update the compare-and-swap was meant to prevent (design: 'made at the branch head under the turn ... an explicit compare-and-swap').
  Done when: With `detached`, take `started` from the tree's own HEAD (`git(repo, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD')`) before the rebase, not from the branch ref. The phase-3 compare and the `update-ref` old value then both refer to the head that was actually rebased, and a moved ref becomes `BranchMoved`. In `_land_detached`, compare `_branch_head` with `started` and raise `BranchMoved` before `update-ref`, so a clean detached move whose ref moved is retried rather than surfacing as a `CalledProcessError`. Test: wrap `prepare_detached` (or the turn factory) so the branch ref moves to a new commit right after the tree is made. Assert the final branch contains that commit (the retry rebased it), or that the unit is held, and never that the branch equals a rebase of the old head.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/restack.py:478 — `temporary_tree` copies `worktree_path`'s branch-to-directory-name rule (`re.sub(r'[^A-Za-z0-9]', '_', branch)`, workspaces.py:125).
  Consequence: There are now two copies of the rule that maps a branch to its directory name under `<root>/<repo>/`, and they must change together. The docstring says the temporary name exists so that 'the test for a unit's own worktree never mistakes it for one'. If one copy changes alone, that guarantee silently drifts.
  Done when: Derive it from the existing function: `own = worktree_path(repo, branch, root); return own.parent / f"restack-{own.name}"`.
- [1.5] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/wiring.py:2784 — The comment above `unit_repo_turn` says only worktree add and push take the turn. That is now false.
  Consequence: The comment reads: 'Adding a worktree and pushing both take git's own locks there ... so those two steps take turns per repo. Everything else happens inside the unit's own worktree and needs no turn-taking.' This change passes `unit_repo_turn` to `build_restack_onto` (line 2859), so the in-run restack's rebase start, continue/abort and rerere writes take the turn too.
  Done when: Reword it to name the restack's git phases (rebase start; continue or abort and the rerere writes) among the steps that take the turn, and say the resolver's edits do not.
- [1.6] tests/pipeline/test_restack_turn_phases.py:284 — Task 1.4's last clause has no test: a remote that moved is still a `StaleRemote` from the push's lease and is not retried.
  Consequence: If someone later widens `retried_once` (or the handler's except list) to catch `StaleRemote`, a remote moved by another writer would be rebased and pushed again, and nothing would fail.
  Done when: Add a handler test (with the `Rig`, or `build_restack` with a fake `push`) where the move succeeds and `push` raises `StaleRemote`. Assert the move ran exactly once (one resolver call or one `move` call) and the push was attempted once. Also assert the outcome the handler already gives a `StaleRemote` (raised or held as today), unchanged.
- [1.7] tests/pipeline/test_restack_turn_phases.py:230 — The in-run test builds `build_restack_onto` with a turn itself. It would still pass if `build_runner` stopped passing `unit_repo_turn`.
  Consequence: Task 1.3 asks that 'a unit's own `restack_onto` in a run takes it' (and 1.9 that `build_runner` passes `unit_repo_turn`). The only test injects `turn=partial(file_lock, lock)` directly. If the wiring line at wiring.py:2859 were reverted to `build_restack_onto(store, repo=repo)`, every test would still pass, and the in-run rebase would be back to taking no turn.
  Done when: Add a test through the real wiring. tests/pipeline/test_worktree_in_turn.py's `wired_runner` already builds `build_runner` over a real repo. Use it to call `runner.restack_onto` on a conflicting tree, with a resolver that records `lock_is_held(<state>/locks/repo-app.lock)`. Assert that `rebase --onto` and `rebase --continue` ran with the repo lock held and the resolver ran without it.

Optional:
- [1.8] tests/pipeline/test_restack_turn_phases.py:87 — The concurrency test never checks that the move it blocked actually finished.
  Consequence: `mover` runs `move(...)` in a daemon thread whose result and exceptions are dropped. If the continue phase deadlocked or raised after `release.set()`, the test would still pass. The move-side behaviour is shown by other tests, so this is not blocking.
  Done when: Run the mover through a wrapper that stores its outcome (as `run_bounded` does). After `mover.join(60)`, assert it is no longer alive and returned a `Moved` with `resolved == ('markers.py',)`.

description.summary: A restack holds the repository's turn only for its git phases, never while the conflict resolver works, and moves a branch with no worktree in a temporary detached worktree using compare-and-swap.
changes: Moving a branch onto a new base takes the repo's turn for the rebase start and again for the continue or abort, the rerere writes and the branch update. The agent resolving a conflict runs without it, so other units can add worktrees and push meanwhile.

A branch with no worktree is rebased in a temporary detached worktree beside where its own would be, so the operator's checkout is never switched. The branch is updated by compare-and-swap against the head that was actually rebased.

If another writer moves the branch during a move, the move is retried once. If it moves again, the unit is left `planned` with cause `restack_deferred` and a note naming the branch and both heads, both in the merge handler and in a unit's own run (`prepare`), instead of being failed.
Tier 1 for a moved branch with no worktree runs on a temporary checkout at the moved head, so the push only sends a head whose checks ran on it.
`build_runner` passes the unit's repo turn to the in-run restack. A remote that moved is still refused by the push's lease (`StaleRemote`) and is not retried.

units.title: Resolve a conflict in one session, smallest change first, recorded as restack
units.feedback:
Group 2 is mostly in place and its tests pass: 93 restack/guard tests and 663 graph/wiring/agent-call-guard tests passed locally. The order prompt, the two-call ladder with checks between the calls, the rejected replay that fails its check instead of aborting, the wider `Moved.resolved`, `restack` in the node enum and SESSION_ROLES, and one ledger row per call are all there. Two things block approval. First, in a run the resolution calls run with the build agent's full tool grant instead of the resolver's narrow one. Second, one test that task 2.6 asks for is missing.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:1085 — `restack_resolver` calls `self.agent(self.runner.run, ...)`. `runner.run` is `build_run`'s `run_agent`, which always sends `allowed_tools=allowed_tools or BASE_TOOLS` (`Read Edit Write Grep Glob Bash(git *)` plus the toolchain's tools) with `permission_mode="edit"`. So in a run, the steps that are meant to touch only the conflict get git and shell access in a worktree paused mid-rebase. The design gives them the resolver's tools: `RESOLVER_TOOLS = "Read Edit Write Grep Glob"`, `allowed_tools_only` (design.md, UNVERIFIED 3: the resolver steps run with the resolver's tools, only the port with the build tools). The handler's `claude_resolver` still uses that narrow grant.
  Consequence: With the rebase stopped in the unit's worktree, a resolving agent can run `git add`, `git rebase --continue`, `git commit` or `git rerere`. Any of these writes shared state (the branch ref, the rerere cache) outside the repository's turn, which group 1 holds only around the pipeline's own git commands. It also gets past the pipeline's checks. If the agent continues the rebase itself, `move_branch_onto` then reads a branch head different from `started` and raises `BranchMoved`, which gets one retry and then leaves the unit planned. Otherwise the pipeline's own `rebase --continue` fails and the move is aborted, even when the agent's resolution was right. No test notices, because the fakes in `test_restack_step_in_prepare.py` never look at the request's tools.
  Done when: The run's restack calls go out with `allowed_tools=RESOLVER_TOOLS` and `permission_mode="allowed_tools_only"`, as `claude_resolver` does. For example, give `build_run`'s `run_agent` optional `allowed_tools`/`permission_mode` overrides and have `restack_resolver` pass them through `self.agent`'s `**inputs`. Use the existing `RESOLVER_TOOLS` constant, not a copy. Add a test in `tests/graph/test_restack_step_in_prepare.py` asserting that every restack request's `allowed_tools == RESOLVER_TOOLS` and that the next build node's request (fix_checks or adapt) still carries the build tools.
- [1.2] tests/graph/test_restack_step_in_prepare.py:206 — Task 2.6 and the spec scenario 'A usage pause and a clean move' ask for a test that a clean move in the same pause still proceeds. Only the conflicting half is tested. `test_a_usage_pause_defers_the_step_and_the_unit_is_not_failed` covers the conflicting move and nothing else.
  Consequence: Suppose a later change gates `prepare` or the restack as a whole on the usage guard, for instance by adding PREPARE to AGENT_NODES or checking `may_start` before `restack_onto`. Clean moves would then also be held during a pause, which breaks restack-conflicts' 'a move that applies cleanly in the same pause SHALL proceed', and every test would still pass.
  Done when: Add a test with a usage pause in effect: `may_start` returns False, or the runtime is rate-limited for every call. Use a `restack_onto` that applies cleanly, asks no resolver and returns a moved result with nothing resolved. Assert that the move was made (`restack_onto` was called with the resolver and returned), that no agent request was sent for it, and that the unit waits at the next agent node's gate rather than being failed or held with a conflict. Optionally, run it beside a conflicting unit, which waits.

Optional:
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/restack.py:389 — The marker failure text, '... still has conflict markers after resolution — left for a human, since staging a conflict is worse than not moving.', is now also the `{failure}` that CONTINUE_PROMPT hands to the agent on the second call. So the agent is told the conflict was left for a human in the same message that asks it to keep going.
  Consequence: A rejected replay or a first try that left a marker gets a second call that contradicts itself, and the agent may simply stop and leave the markers. The step then ends in `RestackConflict` when the second call could have settled it.
  Done when: Have `_failed_check` return a neutral reason, such as '<files> still have conflict markers'. Add the 'left for a human …' tail only to the final `_abort` message on the second failure.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/restack.py:950 — `except SessionUnavailable: result = ask(prompt, session="")` also runs when the call that failed was already a fresh one (`resumed` false), so that call is sent a second time.
  Consequence: A runtime that raises SessionUnavailable on a fresh call gets the same request twice, and the ledger gets an extra row.
  Done when: Re-raise when `resumed` is false: `except SessionUnavailable: if not resumed: raise; result = ask(prompt, session="")`.
- [1.5] tests/pipeline/test_restack_ledger_row.py:374 — The spec's ledger requirement says each row records whether the call ran in a stack move or in a run. Neither test asserts the field that tells them apart (today, implicitly, `role` is `implement` with `tier` filled in a run, and `generic` in a handler).
  Consequence: A change that makes both paths write the same role or tier would drop the distinction the spec asks for, and these tests would still pass.
  Done when: In each test, assert the field (or fields) that marks a row as from a run or from a stack move.

description.summary: A conflict found while moving a unit's branch is now resolved by the unit's own build session in at most two narrow-tooled calls, with the pipeline's checks between them, and each call is recorded as the `restack` node.
changes: When a branch is moved onto its base and conflicts, the resolver is asked at most twice. Between the two calls the pipeline checks for conflict markers and for lost content. The second call is told what failed. If the second call also fails, the rebase is aborted and the branch is left where it was, marked as left for a human.

A replayed rerere resolution that the check rejects is forgotten, and the conflict goes to the resolver instead of aborting the move. That way the next branch to hit the same conflict is not offered the bad entry.

In a run, the resolution calls continue the unit's build session on the rework model. They are granted only the resolver's tools (Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob, no git or shell) in allowed-tools-only mode. The pipeline alone moves the rebase, and the next build node keeps the full build tools.

Each resolution call writes one ledger row under the `restack` node. That node is now a valid graph node and session role. A run's rows carry the implement role and the unit's tier, and a stack move's rows carry the generic role.
During a usage pause, a move that applies cleanly still goes ahead. A conflicting move is deferred instead of failing the unit. The unit waits at the next agent node's gate.

units.title: Port as the last step of the same session; update documentation
units.feedback:
The code side of task 3.4 is right. `RestackConflict.tried` is filled from both failed checks, `build_restack_onto` copies it into `Restacked.tried`, and `adapt` adds `TRIED_NOTE` to both `ADAPT_PROMPT` and `ADAPT_CONTINUATION` without changing the prompt when it is empty. Since `restack` and `adapt` are both build-role nodes, the port continues the steps' session. The changelog bullet is folded into the existing conflict bullet and its claims match the code. Four things block approval. First, the `tried` chain is tested only through a fake that supplies `tried` itself. Second, the handler half of task 3.3 has no test. Third, task 3.2's unreachable-head case has no test. Fourth, three of the documents that task 3.5 lists were left stale.

Required:
- [1.1] tests/graph/test_adapt_in_the_restack_session.py:44 — The only test of the 'what was tried' text uses a fake `restack_onto` that hands `tried=TRIED` straight to `Restacked`. Nothing tests that `move_branch_onto` fills `RestackConflict.tried` or that `build_restack_onto` (wiring.py:2439) copies it into `Restacked.tried`.

- [1.2] tests/graph/test_restack_step_in_prepare.py:302 — Task 3.3's first half has no test: 'the stack-move handler leaves a conflict its first two steps cannot settle planned with cause restack_conflict'. The new test sets PLANNED/RESTACK_CONFLICT on the unit by hand. The closest existing test, tests/pipeline/test_satisfied_release.py:263, runs with no resolver, so neither step is ever attempted.

Assert the resolver was called twice, the child is PLANNED with `Cause.RESTACK_CONFLICT`, its branch head is unchanged, and no port or `keep|adapt|retire` prompt was asked.
- [1.3] tests/graph/test_adapt_in_the_restack_session.py:315 — Task 3.2 names two ways a session cannot be continued: 'the runtime cannot resume, the recorded head is unreachable'. Only the first (`Sessions(refuses=...)`) is tested.
  Consequence: If the port continued a session whose recorded head is unreachable (nodes.py:663 `head_reachable`), the continuation prompt would point at history the session cannot read. No test pins that the port then falls back to a new session with the full prompt.

- [1.4] docs/architecture.md:772 — The Restack paragraph, which task 3.5 lists, still describes the old resolver. It says the resolver 'may edit only the conflict', that planting a marker in a replayed file 'rejects the replay — which aborts the move', and that a failed check means 'the rebase is aborted and left for a person'.

A conflict neither step settles goes to the `adapt` port in a run, or is left `planned` with `restack_conflict` by the handler.

description.summary: A restack conflict the resolver's two steps cannot settle is handed to the adapt port, as the last step of the same build session, and the port is told which steps were tried and what their checks said.
changes: When the conflict resolver fails a step's check, the move records it: each failed step and its check text are collected on `RestackConflict.tried`, including when the resolver crashes or `rebase --continue` fails after an earlier failed step.

`build_restack_onto` copies that record into `Restacked.tried`. The `adapt` port adds a note naming the steps tried and their checks to its first prompt and to its continuation, and leaves the prompt unchanged when nothing was tried.

The port runs in the session the restack steps used. When that session cannot be continued (the runtime refuses, or the recorded head is unreachable), it starts a new session with the full prompt, which still includes what was tried.

The stack-move handler leaves a conflict its two steps cannot settle `planned` with cause `restack_conflict`, without porting it. Its note says the unit's next run resolves the conflict in its build session.

architecture.md, unit-graph.md and agent-runtimes.md now describe the resolver's order (conflicting hunks, then dependent files, then a port). They also cover the `restack` node as a build-session node on the rework model and the fact that `verify_base` makes no agent call. The changelog bullet for the conflict work now includes the port step.

units.title: A clean move is scoped by a rule, with a setting and a log line

description.summary: When a unit's branch moves cleanly onto a base that has changed, tier 1 is now told which base the branch left. It decides whether the move can be checked by only what the move can affect, and logs that decision. A new setting chooses between scoping the check and always running the full suite.
changes: A new `limits.restack_check` setting takes `affected` (the default) or `full`. Any other value is refused, and so is an unquoted YAML boolean. The setting is documented in docs/configuration.md and the abk-config skill.

A new rule in `pipeline/moved_base.py` lists the files that differ between the old base and the new one and compares them with the files the unit changes. The move can be scoped only when the two lists share no file. It falls back to the full suite when the setting is `full`, the unit produced nothing, the move has no old base, or git cannot list the files, and it gives the reason in each case.

Before a push, `verify_base` records the base the branch left (`moved_from`) only when the move was clean. The `tier1` node passes it to the tier 1 runner. A reset clears it, and a move that hit a conflict or needed resolution never passes it on.

When a merge releases a dependent unit, the merge handler passes its old base to tier 1 after a clean move. The CLI's `tier1_of` hands the pipeline log to the runner, so the decision appears in the log.
Tier 1 logs one `moved base:` line saying whether the move could be scoped and why. For now the whole suite still runs either way, as the changelog and docs/architecture.md say.

history.note: rework requested: merge conflict with its base

units.title: A scoped move runs the unit's own tests and the tests the profile names

description.summary: When a unit's branch is moved onto a newer base, tier 1 now runs only the unit's own tests and the tests the toolchain profile says the move can affect, unless it can't safely limit the run, in which case it runs the full suite.
changes: After a move onto a new base, tier 1 runs lint, then the unit's own touched tests, then the tests the profile selects as affected by the unit's files and the files the move brought in. It logs a `moved base: ran N[ of T] tests (own a, affected b)` line.

The full suite runs instead, with the reason in the log line, in these cases: the profile cannot say what is affected, `checks.affected` is off and so no selection data was kept, or the move brought in a non-document file outside the unit's projects. For the Python profile, the profile cannot say when a lock or configuration file, a conftest.py or a shared test helper changed.
A passing scoped move writes an `affected` line to the usage ledger with outcome `moved` and the selected and total test counts. No full run confirms that line.
The moved-base own run selects test ids with the same `_ids_for` helper the full run uses, so the two runs pick the same tests.
The shared moved-repo test fixtures (`commit`, `moved`) now live in tests/moved_base_fakes.py.
docs/architecture.md, docs/toolchain-profiles.md, docs/configuration.md and the changelog now describe the scoped run, its fallbacks and that it depends on `checks.affected`.

units.title: A failure in a scoped run is isolated, and a flake does not hold the unit
units.feedback:
The structure is sound: `FlakeFound.scoped`, `wait` on `on_flake`/`wait_on_fix`, and the unit's own ids passed into `isolate`. The main problem is that a scoped flake raised partway through the selected run ends the run early, and the callers then treat that as a pass. Three smaller gaps remain: the fix change's own unit is excused, the default `on_flake` breaks with the new keyword, and the log line is misleading. Task 3.3's tier 2 assertion is also missing.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/wiring.py:1217 — A scoped flake raised by `isolate` inside `run_selection` stops the moved-base run at that command. `nodes.py:1645` and `events.py:1963` then treat the unit as passed, so whatever was left of the plan never runs.
  Consequence: Take a moved-base plan of [lint, own repeat, affected A, affected B] in one project, or two projects. If A fails once and passes alone, `FlakeFound(scoped=True)` comes out of `run_selection`. Command B never runs, and nor do the other projects' commands or `root_checks` (the profile's `extra_checks` and each project's `project_checks`, called at the end of `moved_run`). `record_selected` and the `moved base: ran N of M` line are skipped too. The unit is still pushed as 'tier 1 passed'. A semantic conflict that B or a root check would have caught, which is exactly what this change exists to catch, goes through. On a full run, stopping early was harmless because the unit parks and runs again. On a scoped run it is not.
  Done when: On a scoped run (`own` given), `run_selection` collects the `FlakeFound` from `isolate` and goes on to the remaining commands and projects. `moved_run` then records the figures, logs the line and runs `root_checks`. Only when all of that passes does it raise `FlakeFound(collected, scoped=True)`. Any other failure returns that failure, so the unit is held. Add tests in `tests/pipeline/test_moved_base_flake.py`: (a) a plan whose first affected command flakes and whose second command fails returns `passed=False` naming the second command, with no `FlakeFound`; (b) a flake followed by a failing `extra_checks` command holds the unit; (c) a flake followed by passing commands still raises the scoped flake, and every later command appears in `runner.ran`.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/graph/nodes.py:1645 — On a scoped flake, both callers ignore what `on_flake` returns. For a unit of the flake's own fix change, `wait_on_fix` returns None, and the unit still passes. The same happens at `events.py:1963`.
  Consequence: A unit building `fix-flaky-<test>` moves onto a new base, and that same test fails once and passes alone in the scoped run. The unit is pushed as passing, even though the flake is evidence its fix did not work. The full path's rule (`wait_for_fix` docstring, `nodes.py:1288`) says that for the fix unit 'the flake is then a tier 1 failure the unit's agent is told of'. The scoped path drops that.
  Done when: In both callers, if `on_flake(..., wait=False)` returns None for any flake, treat the result as a failure: `ok, output = False, found.flakes[0].output` in the node, and the existing `RuntimeError` in the merge handler. Add a test in `test_moved_base_flake.py` where `Told` returns None and the unit is sent to `fix_checks`/`rebase`, not pushed. Add a handler test where the child is a unit of the fix change and the handler raises without pushing.
- [1.3] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/stack_runner.py:1301 — The default `on_flake = lambda unit, flake: None` does not accept the new `wait` keyword that `nodes.py:1646` now passes. The comment above it still says the callable 'has the unit wait on its fix'.
  Consequence: Any `StackRunner` built without `on_flake` (the default exists for that case) raises `TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'wait'` the first time a scoped flake reaches the `tier1` node, instead of recording it.
  Done when: Make the default `lambda unit, flake, *, wait=True: None`. Update the comment: with `wait` false the flake is recorded and its change ensured, but no `Needs:` line is added.
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/wiring.py:1312 — `build_on_flake` logs `<unit>: flaky test <t> — waits for <fix>` even when `wait=False`. Its docstring still says it 'make[s] the unit wait'.
  Consequence: On every scoped flake, the tick log says the unit waits for the fix change even though it got no `Needs:` line and went on to its push. Someone reading the log to find out why the unit moved on is told the opposite of what happened.
  Done when: Log `recorded as <fix>, no wait` (or similar) when `wait` is false, and keep `waits for <fix>` only when it is true. Update the docstring to describe `wait`. In `test_on_flake_wait.py`, assert the logged line for both cases using a list-appending `log`.
- [1.5] tests/pipeline/test_moved_base_flake.py:251 — Task 3.3 asks for an assertion that a tier 2 command is never isolated or repeated. The tier 2 test here only checks the order tier1 < tier2 < push.

  Done when: Add a test where tier 2 fails once after a scoped tier 1 flake (for example with a fake tier 2 that fails on its first call). Assert that the tier 2 command ran exactly once (no serial rerun), that `on_flake` was told only of the tier 1 flake, and that the unit is not pushed.

description.summary: When a unit's tier 1 run after a moved base is scoped and meets a flaky test, the flake is recorded and the rest of the scoped plan still runs. The unit goes on to its push without waiting for the fix, unless it is building that fix itself.
changes: When a test in the unit's own or affected selection fails and then passes alone in a scoped moved-base run, it is isolated as a flake (`FlakeFound` with `scoped=True`). The full suite does not stand in for it.

A scoped flake no longer cuts the run short. The remaining commands, other projects and the repo-wide checks still run, the figures are recorded, and the flake is raised only if all of them pass. Any other failure holds the unit.

In both the graph's tier1 node and the merge handler's restack, a scoped flake is recorded through `on_flake(..., wait=False)`: its fix change is made sure to exist, no `Needs:` line is added, and the unit goes on to its push.
A unit of the flake's own fix change, which has no fix to wait on, treats a scoped flake as a tier 1 failure. The graph sends it to a fix round, and the merge handler raises without pushing.
`OnFlake` is now a typed protocol with a `wait` keyword, and the default `on_flake` accepts it. The log line reads `recorded as <fix>, no wait` or `waits for <fix>`, depending on `wait`.
Tier 2 is never isolated or excused as a flake: a tier 2 failure after a scoped tier 1 flake sends the unit to a fix round before any push.

units.title: A restack runs in its own lane, takes no slot, and starts when it is seen

description.summary: Restacks now run in their own lane, separate from the build slots. A unit whose branch no longer holds its base is restacked as soon as a tick sees it, and it never takes a build slot or adds to the in-progress limit.
changes: A new restack lane (pipeline/restack_lane.py) has its own small pool of workers and a queue that holds each unit at most once, in the order units were first seen. A unit whose branch exists but does not contain its base is handed to the lane at every scan, and the tick waits for the lane to finish before it ends.

A restack attempt that leaves the unit as it was is not retried within the same tick. The lane records the unit's branch head and base head after each attempt and tries again only when one of them moves, or at the next tick.

When a merge or a released depth hold moves a child onto a new base, the child is handed to the lane. The child is read fresh from the store, so its base is current. The merged branch is kept until the child's move has run to the end.

A unit that needs a restack stays in the graph for counting and wait reasons, but it is never offered a build slot. It shows as `ready` in `wait_reasons` and in the decision log, even when no slot is free or the in-progress limit is reached.

A parked unit whose own worktree has the branch checked out is not sent to the conflict resolver. It is marked to be restacked by its own run. A unit without a worktree is still moved in a temporary worktree.
`wiring.is_ancestor` is now public and is the single check for whether a branch holds its base, used by both `prepare` and the lane.

units.title: The lane honours the usage guard, moves a parked thread, and shows itself
units.feedback:
Restacks that the merge and conflict handlers hand to the lane skip the usage gate, which is the main point of group 2. The scan path is gated and well tested. Separately, the guard refusal's `resume_at` is not kept as task 2.7 asks, task 2.3's second scenario has no test, and one doc paragraph and one changelog claim are now false. The 24 new tests pass locally.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:3277 — `_dispatch(inst, store, lane=lane)` builds its moves with `build_stack_moves(store, inst, lane=lane)`, where `gated` defaults to False. So every restack the poll's handlers hand to the lane runs with an ungated `ConflictSession`: `release_children`'s `moved_off` (events.py:346-357), which calls the dispatch's `restack`, and `on_conflict`'s lane `work` (events.py:1448-1457) when no pause marker stands at hand-over. Only the scan path (`build_restack_lane` → `move_unit`) uses `gated=True`.
  Consequence: A parent merges while the guard would refuse (for example a fresh read at 95% before the tick has written a pause marker). `on_merged` → `release_children` hands the conflicting child to the lane, and the lane worker calls `claude_resolver` without asking `build_may_start`. That breaks task 2.7 and design §5 ('before each resolver call the lane worker calls build_may_start()'). It also makes the changelog sentence 'The lane asks the usage guard before each conflict-resolving agent call' false for the most common restack, the one after a merge. The tests drive only `lane.scan`, so none of them catches it.
  Done when: Gate the moves the dispatch builds whenever a lane is given, e.g. `build_stack_moves(store, inst, lane=lane, gated=lane is not None)` in `_dispatch`, or make the lane own the gated move so no hand-over path can carry an ungated one. Add a test that drives a merge through the handler with a lane, e.g. `poll_all`/`_dispatch(inst, store, lane=lane)("merged", ...)` over the conflicting `tracked_rig` repo with the guard refusing. It should assert that `asked_of_the_guard` recorded one refusing decision, that the agent got no request, that the child's branch is at its old head with no rebase in progress, and that the child is `planned`/`restack_deferred`.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/restack_lane.py:183 — The refusal's `resume_at` is not kept. Task 2.7 says to 'keep the refusal's resume_at in memory so a scan does not retry before it'. Instead, retry depends on `scan` itself having seen the pause marker in force (`_was_paused`) and then seeing it gone. The guard does not write the marker (usage_guard.py has no `pause_until`); only the tick's pass does. So a refusal that comes with no marker leaves the unit's stamp in `_tried`, and no later scan in the tick ever retries it.
  Consequence: The lane's resolver is refused by `decide_start` on a fresh read while no pause marker exists (for example no pass ran a gate this tick). The unit becomes `restack_deferred` and `_tried[unit]` holds its stamp. Every later scan skips it because the stamp is unchanged and `_was_paused` never became True, even long after the refusal's `resets_at`. It waits for the next tick, contrary to 'when the pause ends the next scan moves the unit'. In the other direction, nothing stops a retry before `resume_at` once the marker clears early.
  Done when: Have the lane remember, per unit, the `resets_at` of the refusal that deferred it. For example, `gated_resolver` reports the refusal (unit, `resume_at()`) to the lane through a callback, or the lane reads it from the `AgentRateLimited` that `build_restack` turns into a deferral. A scan then hands the unit over again only once `spans.clock.now() >= resume_at` (or the pause marker it saw has cleared), whether or not a marker was ever observed. Test with an injected clock: guard refuses with no pause marker → scan before `resume_at` does not ask the guard again → advance the clock past `resume_at` → the next scan asks the guard again and moves the unit.
- [1.3] tests/graph/test_restack_second_hold.py:36 — Task 2.3 names two scenarios and only the first is tested, and only partly: the test never fills the build slots, though the task says the lane moves it 'at once, with no build slot free'. The second scenario, 'a run that settles the first conflict in the same run is not held and starts no lane work', has no test.
  Consequence: A regression in which a run that settled its first conflict is still held `base_changed`, or hands the unit to the lane, would pass. So would one in which the lane's move after a second hold waits for a free build worker. Both are behaviours task 2.3 asks a test to pin.
  Done when: Add to `tests/graph/test_restack_second_hold.py`: (a) the same second-hold scene with `max_concurrent_stacks` slots all held by blocking builds, asserting the lane moves the unit, and its resolver runs on a `restack` thread, before any build slot frees; (b) a run whose `Moves` resolves the first conflict in the same run, asserting the unit is not left `planned`/`base_changed` and that no restack thread ran (the lane's `running`/`waiting` stayed empty and the guard was never asked from a `restack` thread).
- [1.4] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:3822 — `advance_thread_through_prepare` copies `resume_thread`'s setup (pipeline.py:3892-3905): `graph = store.all()`, `base = base_of(...)`, the `say` closure, and `build_runner(..., record_merge=lambda repo, pr: _dispatch(inst, store)("merged", pr, repo=repo), log=say)`. That runner construction now exists in three places (3620, 3830, 3903). Task 2.8 asks to reuse `resume_thread`'s delivery. The function also checks the thread's position with `thread_position` (3824) and then `advance_through_prepare` checks it again (unit.py:301-303).
  Consequence: Two copies of the off-slot thread runner setup must change together. A change to how a thread's runner records merges or logs, made in `resume_thread`, silently misses the lane's `prepare` path.
  Done when: Extract one helper (e.g. `_thread_runner(inst, unit, store) -> tuple[UnitRunner, str, list[StoredUnit]]`) used by both `resume_thread` and `advance_thread_through_prepare`. Drop the outer `thread_position` check, since `advance_through_prepare` already returns None for a thread not parked at `prepare`.
- [1.5] docs/unit-graph.md:372 — The new paragraph at line 127 contradicts the delivery paragraph at 372-378, which still says the routed thread runs 'in a slot like any thread with work to do. No event handler, poll or `abk requeue` runs an agent, a check or a push outside a slot, so `max_concurrent_stacks` holds.' The lane now runs `prepare`, and with it the resolver agent, outside a slot. Task 2.10 also asks for the base-moved and `prepare` rows to be updated. Row 365 (`base_moved` → `prepare`), row 368 ('handled by the handler itself (restacked, …)') and the `prepare` row at 224 are unchanged.
  Consequence: The doc's sentence 'No event handler, poll … runs an agent … outside a slot' is now false, and the rows still describe handler-inline restacks and a slot for `prepare`.
  Done when: Rewrite 372-378 to say a `base_moved` delivery leaves the thread at `prepare` for the restack lane, which runs `prepare` (and its resolver, under the usage gate) outside the build slots and then leaves the thread at the next node for a worker. Amend row 365 to name the lane running `prepare`. Amend row 368 so other children are handed to the restack lane, not restacked by the handler. Note in the `prepare` row (224) that for a unit told its base moved it runs in the lane.
- [1.6] CHANGELOG.md:33 — '`abk status` and the graph page show `restacks: N running, M waiting` and each unit restacking onto its base' claims the graph page shows the count line. `render_mermaid` only relabels each unit `restacking onto <base>` (diagram.py:123-124); the page has no `restacks:` line.
  Consequence: A reader looks for a restack count on the graph page that is never written there.
  Done when: Say that `abk status` prints `restacks: N running, M waiting` and that both `abk status` and the graph page show each unit as restacking onto its base.

Optional:
- [1.7] src/agent_build_kit/cli/pipeline.py:509 — While any pause stands, `_restack_lines` labels every owed unit the lane does not hold as `restack waiting: <unit> — usage pause until …`. That includes a unit whose move would be clean, and a clean move proceeds during a pause. It also re-derives the pause-end formatting of `pause.pause_line` (pause.py:154-156: `max(pause.until, now).astimezone()` and `%H:%M`), and for a network pause it prints 'network pause until HH:MM', which `pause_line` deliberately avoids.
  Consequence: Minor: status can blame a pause for a restack the pause does not block, and the time format lives in two places.
  Done when: Optionally label only units the lane recorded as deferred by a refusal (see the `resume_at` finding), and share the end-time formatting with `pause_line`.

description.summary: Conflicting restacks run in a separate restack lane outside the build slots, ask the usage guard before every conflict-resolving agent call, and are retried when the guard's refusal expires.
changes: Every restack the lane runs asks the usage guard before calling the conflict resolver. That covers moves found by the lane's scan and children the merge and conflict handlers hand over (also the satisfied path's dependent release). A refusal aborts the rebase and leaves the unit planned with cause restack_deferred.

The lane remembers the reset time each refusal comes with. A scan does not retry the unit before that time and retries it once the time has passed, whether or not a pause marker was ever written; a pause ending still clears all deferrals.

An in-review unit told its base moved is run through `prepare` by the lane, outside the build slots, and then waits at its next node for a worker. The setup for running a thread outside a slot is now shared by `resume_thread` and the lane through one helper, and `advance_through_prepare` builds a runner only for a thread actually parked at `prepare`.

`abk status` shows a `restacks: N running, M waiting` line. Each owed unit appears as restacking onto its base, or as waiting out a pause when a pause deferred it; the graph page shows the restacking label too.
docs/unit-graph.md and the changelog now say the moved-base delivery runs in the lane outside `max_concurrent_stacks`, and that other children of a merged unit are handed to the lane.

units.title: The recording helper, the restack node and the guard

description.summary: Records the cost of each restack conflict-resolver call in the usage ledger, and adds a guard test so a new agent call cannot skip recording.
changes: Each call `claude_resolver` makes is written to the usage ledger as a row under node `restack`, with the unit being moved and its change and repository. `move_branch_onto` sets a private context variable around the resolve step to supply them.

A shared `recorded(...)` helper in pipeline/call_record.py attaches recording to an `AgentRequest`. Its rows go through the ledger's writer, which keeps `unit` and `node` as written and redacts secrets in free-text fields such as `outcome`.
The ledger's reader keeps each resolver row as its own call. A row with no unit never counts toward the per-unit usage estimate or its calibration.

A new AST guard (tests/agent_call_sites.py, tests/test_agent_call_guard.py) fails on any agent request that is not built through `recorded`, passed to it by name, or given `on_result`. Sites that later units of this change will convert sit on an allowlist that shrinks over time.
The changelog describes the resolver's ledger rows and the guard, and lists the call sites still to be recorded.

units.title: A unit about to run a full tier 2 run waits on the open fix change of a base failure

description.summary: Before running a full tier 2 run, a unit now waits while its repo has an open fix change for a test that already fails on the base, instead of spending the run to hit the same failure.
changes: Before tier 2, the build node asks whether this run will execute the whole marker. It uses the same scope decision tier 2 itself uses, through the new `Tier2Session.scope`. Only for such a run does it ask the new `on_tier2_gate` hook which open fix changes hold the unit.

`untouched_failures.holding_fixes` picks the recorded base failures whose latest fix change is open, was recorded by a unit of the same repo, is not the unit's own change, and is not already named in a `Needs:` line of a group the unit owns. Each one found gets a `Needs:` line, and the unit is parked before the stack lock and before any test runs.
`FailureRecord.latest_with_change` is now the one rule for which change fixes a test; `counts()` uses it as well.
In `abk status`, each `pre-existing:` line now ends with how many units are waiting on that test's fix.

The changelog, docs/architecture.md and the abk-pipeline skill describe the new wait. New tests cover the gate in the graph, the real `build_runner` wiring over a git repo, the failure records and the status count.

units.title: The poller offers a conflict that persists after the unit's own push, and says how fresh its answer is

description.summary: The PR poller now records when it last read a definite mergeability answer and since when a PR has conflicted, and on every poll it offers a new `conflict` event for a conflict still standing after the unit's own push. Nothing handles that event yet.
changes: Each PR snapshot records `mergeable_at` (when the poll read the last definite answer) and `conflict_since` (when the current conflict began). An undetermined answer keeps the last definite value and both times. A definite mergeable answer clears the conflict's start.
On every poll, a PR whose unit is in review and whose definite conflicting answer was read after the unit's last push gets a `conflict` event, even when the recorded answer did not change.

An answer read before the push, an undetermined answer, a snapshot recorded before the times were kept, a PR with no unit, and a unit not in review offer no conflict event. The existing transition and first-sight conflict reworks are unchanged.
The poller takes a `unit_of` lookup, which `poll_all` binds to the unit store. The pipeline's dispatch returns 'not taken' for `conflict` until a later unit adds its handler.
A shared test rig (`tests/pr_poller_fakes.py`) drives a poller with a fake clock and a fake unit lookup, and two new test modules pin the timing and conflict-offer rules.

units.title: A conflicting unit's first attempt is the stack move, any other is the conflict rework, and no head and base tip is attempted twice

description.summary: A pull request that is still conflicting after a unit's own push is now acted on again on each poll: first by moving its branch onto the trunk, then by the conflict rework. No pushed head at one base tip is attempted twice.
changes: The conflict event handler counts attempts against the unit's pushed head and its base's tip. A trunk-based unit's first attempt is the stack move; any later attempt, a stacked unit, or a move that cannot settle goes to the conflict rework. A new base tip, or a definite read that the pull request merges, starts the count again.

When a restack lane is present, the stack move for a conflict runs there under the lane's branch claim, so a resolver session no longer blocks the poll. Without a lane it runs inline. Either way the same outcome is recorded.
The move replays from where the unit's own work begins (`own_work_starts_after`), so a unit whose parent was squash-merged does not re-apply the parent's commits.

The resolver and the predecessor note are told the unit moves onto a stand-in named for the trunk, not onto itself. The lane's restack builds that stand-in with the same `moving_onto` function in pipeline/wiring.py.
Under a usage pause a clean move still goes through, and one that needs the resolver waits in review, uncounted. A busy branch defers the move without counting it.

The written change holds fixed text: a proposal, a design, `.openspec.yaml` with `skip_specs: true`, and `tasks.md` with `Acceptance: none` and its reason. units.title: The check reads the agent's configuration and judges every probe command with the kit's matcher

description.summary: The policy check for the protocol runtime no longer starts the agent. It reads the deny list from the agent's own configuration and judges every probe command with abk's own matcher.
changes: `policy_check.check_policy` reads a known agent's configuration through the policy applier's own reader. It judges each `PROBE_CLASSES` command with `recommended_policy.matches` and records the first pattern that refused it (`SpellingResult.by`). It starts no agent and keeps no answer.
The classes the recommendation leaves to the person are marked `by_design`. They never fail the check and are left out of `unenforced`, `describe` and `unrefused`.

A missing configuration, an unreadable one, or an agent abk has no policy for gives a non-passing report with a `cannot_check` reason: the path and the variable that would point elsewhere, the applier's own parse error, or that abk has no policy for the agent. Runtimes other than the protocol one keep their own answer and read no configuration.
`AcpRuntime.check_policy` no longer runs the live probe in a throwaway worktree. It returns a `cannot_check` report, and the probe-driving code is removed.
`PolicyReport` gains `source` and `cannot_check`, and `SpellingResult` gains `by` and `by_design`, all with defaults so reports stored earlier still load.
The restack lane writes its record through the shared `atomic_write_text`, so the repository's atomic-write guard passes.

units.title: Doctor, init and abk policy check use it, and ask nothing

description.summary: Doctor, `abk init` and `abk policy check` now use one shared, static policy check that reads the agent's own configuration. None of them starts the agent or asks it anything.
changes: `abk doctor` reports the runtime policy from the configuration-reading check. It says how many probe commands are refused and labels the answer as read from the configuration, not observed from the agent. When a class is open, it names the class and its spellings.
`abk init` runs the same check without prompting the agent. It prints the rendered report before saying what is not refused. When abk has no policy for the agent, it gives the same hint as doctor.

`abk init` no longer offers to continue without a check, and never records `policy: unchecked`. When no fix is known, the person can rely on abk's own layer or supply a fix command. Doctor still warns about a marker recorded earlier.

`abk policy check --agent NAME` checks the named agent's configuration whatever runtime is selected. An unknown runtime or agent name exits 2 through one shared usage check (`_entry_for`) that `abk policy show` and `apply` also use.
`policy_check` gains `summary` (refused count and source) and `NO_POLICY_FIX` (the hint for agents without a policy), shared by doctor and init.

units.title: A test harness drives an agent over the probe commands, bounded and cleaned up
units.feedback:
Group 4 is not complete yet. The harness rebuilds the protocol runtime's connection helper when task 4.6 asks it to be built on that helper. Its 'reached' test only passes because the fake agent sends exactly the command string the harness expects, so a real agent that spells the terminal request differently would be recorded as refusing, and group 6 could then pass without testing anything. Task 4.7 (record the real agent's refusal signal in docs/agent-runtimes.md, or say there that it could not be run) is missing. Two of the new tests can fail under load because they depend on the fake agent starting within the deadline.

Required:
- [1.1] tests/runtimes/policy_agent_harness.py:149 — A command counts as reached only when a terminal request's joined `command + args` equals the probe text exactly. The fake agent always sends `command=line, args=[]`, so the test matches the code rather than how real agents send terminal requests.
  Consequence: A real agent that wraps the command (for example `command='bash', args=['-c', line]`, or a `cd … &&` prefix) actually reaches the client's terminal, but the harness records it as refused. In group 6, such a false 'refused' agrees with a static verdict of 'refused', so the acceptance test passes for every covered command whatever the agent does. test_a_command_refused_without_a_terminal_request_is_refused_and_one_run_is_reached cannot catch this because the fake's wire shape is the one the harness assumes.
  Done when: Judge a turn reached when any terminal request was made during that turn. Each turn names one command, so `len(client.requested) > before` is enough. Alternatively, accept a request whose joined text contains the command. Add a fake-agent option (e.g. `--shell`) that sends `create_terminal(command='sh', args=['-c', line])`. Add a test asserting that a command sent that way is observed as reached and appears in `requested`.
- [1.2] tests/runtimes/policy_agent_harness.py:162 — The harness re-implements the protocol runtime's connection helper instead of building on it, as task 4.6 asks. It has its own spawn with start_new_session, its own stderr drain loop, `initialize` call, `_kill_group` and env merge.
  Consequence: Each of these has a counterpart in src/agent_build_kit/runtimes/acp.py: `_bare_connection` (1673), `_Drained` (1714), `_kill_group` (1742), `_initialize` (1698), `_exited`/`_ended` (1751/1764), and `child_environment` in runtimes/base.py:137. They now have to change together. For example, the harness uses `process.wait()`, which `_exited`'s docstring says can hang on pipes held by leftover processes. Group 6 would also check the agent through a connection path different from the one the product uses.
  Done when: Give acp.py one public, documented helper that opens a connection to an agent command with a caller-supplied client and environment, and that ends the agent's process group and returns what it said on stderr when it closes. This could be `_bare_connection` generalised to take the client, plus a public initialize. Have both `_bare_connection` callers and the harness use it. Remove the harness's copies of `_kill_group`, the stderr drain, the spawn and the initialize call. Tests import only the public name.
- [1.3] tests/runtimes/test_policy_agent_harness.py:53 — assert_cleaned_up reads agent.pid and child.pid. The fake writes them only after importing `acp` and spawning its child, so with a 1-second deadline (and 2 seconds in the heartbeat test) the harness can kill the group before either file exists.
  Consequence: On a loaded machine (8 xdist workers), starting Python and importing acp in the fake takes longer than the deadline. `pids()` then raises FileNotFoundError, so test_an_agent_that_never_answers_ends_at_the_deadline_with_nothing_left fails. This is the flaky test the group's own 'Needs:' line names. test_each_command_judged_is_named_on_stderr_and_a_stall_is_heartbeaten also fails when three judgements do not finish within 2 seconds of wall clock. Both pass alone and fail under load.
  Done when: Neither test may depend on how quickly the fake starts relative to a wall-clock deadline. Prescribed fix: inject the deadline, so that `drive` takes a stop awaitable or clock (default: sleep for `deadline` seconds). The tests then pass one that finishes only after the fake has written both pid files (deadline test), or after it has judged three commands and at least one heartbeat line was printed (heartbeat test). Keep a separate check that the default deadline path ends a silent agent. Separately, have the fake write agent.pid and child.pid before importing acp.
- [1.4] docs/agent-runtimes.md:561 — Task 4.7 is not done. No real run's finding (how the first known agent signals a refusal by its deny list, and whether its approval step refuses anything beyond the list when the client allows everything) is recorded. There is also no statement that it could not be run.
  Consequence: Group 4's 'Done when' says the real agent's way of signalling a refusal is read from one real run and recorded. Without that, group 6 rests on the unverified assumption that a refusal means no terminal request, and design.md's UNVERIFIED items stay open with nothing saying why.
  Done when: Add a paragraph to docs/agent-runtimes.md giving what one real run over the harness showed: whether a refusal arrives as no terminal request, a tool_call failed status, or a rejected permission, and whether anything beyond the deny list was refused. Where the agent could not be run on this machine, say so there and leave design.md's UNVERIFIED items standing.

Optional:
- [1.5] tests/runtimes/policy_agent_harness.py:11 — The module docstring says a heartbeat is printed 'while none is' judged, but the loop prints one every `heartbeat` seconds regardless of whether a command was judged in that interval.
  Consequence: A reader expecting heartbeats only during a stall will misread a log where judgement lines and heartbeats interleave on a slow but healthy run.
  Done when: Either word the docstring as 'a heartbeat every HEARTBEAT_SECONDS until the run ends', or reset the heartbeat timer when a command is judged.

description.summary: Adds a test harness that drives an Agent Client Protocol agent over the policy probe commands, records which ones reach the client's terminal, and always ends the agent's process group. To support it, the protocol runtime's private connection helper becomes a public one.
changes: acp.py now exposes `agent_connection` and `initialize_agent`. `agent_connection` starts an agent in its own session, speaks to it through a client the caller supplies, and on close ends its process group and keeps what it said on stderr. The runtime's model and resume probes now use them in place of the private `_bare_connection` and `_initialize`.

tests/runtimes/policy_agent_harness.py drives an agent with one prompt per probe command. Its client allows every request and runs nothing. A command counts as reached when the agent asked the terminal for anything during that turn, however it spelled the request.

The run is bounded by an overall deadline, a progress line as each command is judged, and heartbeats. The run also ends on SIGINT or SIGTERM, or when a caller-supplied `stop_when` condition is met. Whatever the end, the agent's process group is killed and the harness's temporary directories are removed.

Fake agents (policy_fake_agents.py and policy_fake_agent_protocol.py) cover a silent agent, refusing, asking for permission, wrapping a command in a shell, and signalling the parent. They write their pid files before loading the protocol library, so the cleanup tests do not depend on how fast the fake starts.

docs/agent-runtimes.md records that the real agent's way of signalling a refusal has not been observed yet. It says why the run was not made and that the first acceptance run on a machine with the agent records the finding.

  Consequence: Task 6.3 asks that no agent process of the test's group remains after the run. Real protocol agents usually start helper processes (a node runtime, an MCP server, a shell), and those processes share the leader's process group. Take a run where the harness's group kill misses, or a child survives in the group: the leader has exited and been reaped, so `alive(run.group)` is False and `test_nothing_of_the_run_is_left_behind` passes while agent processes are still running. The harness's own test (tests/runtimes/test_policy_agent_harness.py:54) checks both the agent and its child for this reason.
  Done when: Add a helper beside `alive` in tests/runtimes/policy_fake_agents.py, for example `group_members(pgid: int) -> list[int]`. It scans `/proc/[0-9]*/stat` and returns every pid that is not a zombie and whose pgrp field equals `pgid`. After the last ')', the fields are state, ppid, pgrp. Skip entries that vanish mid-scan (FileNotFoundError/ProcessLookupError). The test then asserts `group_members(run.group) == []` and names the pids it finds in the message. Optionally have the harness test use the same helper.

units.feedback:
The counting logic in ready_units and start_room is correct, and the new tests separate per-project counting from global counting: each one fails under the old global count. 188 tests pass across the new and touched files. Two small things block approval: a docstring that is now false, and a count written twice. The full-queue line in the status still uses the global start_room, and the tick's build pool and the `[:slots]` slice in _evaluate_round are still global. Groups 7 and 9 fix those, so they don't block this unit.

Required:
- [1.1] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/units.py:955 — The ready_units docstring still says `max_units_in_progress` bounds the units in progress "across all repos". It also says the concurrency cap limits how many units are built "at once". The function now applies both to each project.
  Consequence: The docstring of the function this unit changes now says the opposite of what the code does: the limit counts each (repo, project) key on its own. The next reader will assume a global limit, which group 7's callers must not.
  Done when: Say the concurrency cap limits how many units of one project are built at once. Say `max_units_in_progress` bounds the units in progress in each project (repo and project, `project_key`). Say a ready unit of a full project, or of one with no free slot, is skipped and the next ready unit is considered.
- [1.2] src/agent_build_kit/pipeline/units.py:886 — start_room counts the in-progress units of a project with its own inline sum and filter.   Consequence: Two copies of "units in progress per project" are added in one module. If the rule changes (for example, what counts toward a key), both must change together. Meanwhile `project_counts`, the function the spec's 'grouped by key, no total' test pins, is dead in the product, so that test proves nothing about the code that schedules.
  Done when: Build start_room from project_counts: `counts = project_counts(graph)`, then `limit - (sum(counts.values()) if project is None else counts.get(project, 0))`, floored at 0. Then no second per-project counting expression remains in units.py. The existing tests in test_start_room_per_project.py and test_project_key.py pass unchanged.

- [1.3] tests/pipeline/test_ready_units_slots_per_project.py:1 — Task 6.3's last clause, 'a repo with one project starts as many as before', has no test in the file it names. It is covered only by the existing single-repo cases in tests/pipeline/test_units.py (around lines 312-316).

description.summary: The limit on units in progress and the build-slot limit now count each project (a repo and its project) on its own instead of across every repo.
